Quote: blue_tetris, Jul 5 2005, 10:51 PM
Increasing the density of something does not provide it with more gravity. Its mass will remain constant, and therefore, its gravitation will remain constant.
While this is true, you've overlooked something. The strength of a gravitational field is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the object which creates it (for all those who aren't good at maths, that means gravity gets MUCH weaker over distance). The radius of Earth is about 6000 km. The radius of a pea is about 1 mm, which is 6000 000 000 times less. This means at the surface of our pea-sized planet the pull of gravity is 3.6 * 10^19 times stronger (that's 36 000 000 000 000 000 000 times). Trust me, it's a black hole.

So why isn't there a black hole at the centre of Earth? Because when you are inside an object, the pull of the matter on one side (partially, unless you're at the centre of gravity) cancels the pull of the other side.

And to all those who say the flow of time is absolute, you're wrong. The relativity of time has been experimentally verified, and if we didn't take it into acount many modern devices wouldn't work. A GPS, for example, requires precise syncronisation between an object on Earth and a satellite with a relative velocity of several km/s. The clock on the satellite must therefore be constantly adjusted to account for the relativistic effects.

So there.

In addition (on the nature of time and our perception of it):

Time is merely the interval between events, in the same way that distance is the interval between objects. This interval may be different for every frame of reference, just as the distance between Australia and the USA is different to that between Austalia and Europe. Events still occur in a logical order (i.e. no causes before effects - at least, in our universe, and as far as we know), but events may occur at a different rate for each observer, and events that are simultaneous to one observer may be asyncronous to others. Time is just another dimesion, although possibly twisted at a weird angle to the rest, so to speak (for those who don't know, space and time are both distorted in various ways, including by gravity and relativistic effects caused by a difference in velocity between observers. In fact, they are usually unified and referred to as 'spacetime' by physicists).

And moving on to psychology... Psychological studies have shown that young people experience time as though it were flowing more slowly than our elders, because each second is longer compared to our accumulated experiences. For example, when you're five, ten years is twice as long as you've lived for, and seems like ages. For a forty-year-old, it's just one-quarter of your life, and qualifies as the near future. This doesn't make creatures that have lived longer more sluggish - it is merely their perception that changes, not any physical property. You could say the world seems to move faster for them, and as part of that world, they naturally keep pace. It's just that the earlier parts of their life now seem to have gone so very slow by comparison.

In case anyone hasn't guessed, I'm studying for a BSc.

#90423 39 2005-08-13T03:59:31Z Atilla
I am agnostic, for a number of reasons.

Firstly, because it's impossible to ever tell. When someone is struck by lightning, the religious say "He must have been a foul sinner. God struck him down for his evil." The atheists then reply "No, it was because there was an accumulation of charge in the clouds and he happened to be standing on a mountain holding a copper spike in the air." To which the religious people reply, "Ah, but God caused the accumulation of charge." After this, the conversation degenerates to the equivalent of people screaming "IS NOT!" and "IS TOO!" at each other.

Secondly, because there are thousands of religions out there, and most contradict not only each other, but themselves. The probablilty that the one you believe in, or indeed any of them at all, is right is next to nothing.

I believe most of the self-contradictory elements in a religion are caused by sociological influences. Take Christianity. God is supposed infinitely merciful, yet condemns the unrighteous to eternal suffering. Surely a program of rehabilitation would be more appropriate. And what's the point of telling people about heaven and hell? Even criminals can be bribed and blackmailed. They are, however, very useful for keeping the plebs under the influence of the Church. I find the fact that the first commandment is to worship no other god rather suspicious, too. "I may be a murderer, but at least I'm not heathen scum". And if you look at the history of Europe, you will find the word of the Church is more powerful than that of God. Do the Crusades, Inquisition and burnings sound like justifiable acts in religion that advocates loving thy neighbour and commands followers that "Thou Shalt Not Kill"? It's not an ad. You can't have small print saying unbelievers, heretics, criminals, prostitutes, and old women who wouldn't be so weird if their kids visited once in a while are excluded.

In fact, I think justification of any act by saying "God says..." is ridiculous. You can say that about anything. 'It happened, so clearly God meant it to happen. He is omnipotent, and could have stopped it if He wished.' Furthermore, many religions say no mortal can know the mind of god. They then tell us what he wants. Notice a discrepancy?

That said, it isn't impossible for there to be an element life beyond the physical. Perhaps a kind of god exists through the belief of humans - things are regularly done because 'God wills it', whether or not that god actually exists. Defining what exists and what doesn't is difficult in any event - money, for example, is just peices of plastic. In fact, in this high-tech age, it's more often just magnetic fluctions or patterns of light (better known as numbers). However, it's still incredibly powerful. Something doesn't neccesarily need physical form to exist - humanity practically IS things with no existance in time and space. And time and space are limited. What we like to think of as reality may just be a simulation, like the Matrix. Our universe may be an experiment in quantum mechanics by aliens. There may be endless ranks of universes, one for every possible sequence of events, so that nothing is real - there is merely the probablity of reality.

That said, we need to realise that we are just a clever animal with limited perception. Where everyone really lives is in a small universe which orbits, quite conveniently, around the inside of our heads. Everything we percieve is tainted by own perceptions and prejudices. Attempting to apply a human reason to things like the creation of the universe is foolish. A god may have created it because that is a function of godhood - just as being inquisitive is a function of our humanity. In one sense, the universe was never created - it has existed since the beginning of time and will until the end of time. It must have - what is time without a univirse for it to elapse in?

Anyway, that's my two cents (although it's probably more like 2 dollars).

By the way, has anyone read Strata or Small Gods, by Terry Pratchett? If not, I reccomend them (and all his other books for that matter).

On prophecies:

The big problem with such things is what is known as selective reporting. For example, it is a very common misconception that sharks are horrifyingly dangerous man-eaters, because of the sensational media reports every time someone is injured by one. In fact, sharks don't really like the taste of humans (especially ones wearing synthetic wetsuits). Think about it. Some surfer gets his leg bitten off by a 'man-eater' and survives. Do you really think a one-legged, badly bleeding human could outswim a creature designed by four billion years of evolution (or by a deity, if you're so inclined) to kill swimming things? No, they survive because the shark doesn't WANT to eat them. Uh, where was I? Oh yes. You never see "SHOCK! SWIMMER FAILS TO BE EATEN BY SHARK!" in the newspapers, even though (or rather because) it happens so frequently. Coconuts, on the other hand, are regarded as benign despite the fact that they kill more people. My point is that it's very hard to judge how many prophecies someone failed to fulfill after 2000 years, because everyone's been standing around going "Wow! That guy Jesus fulfilled another prophecy!" for the last two millenia. So we have no sure way of knowing just how well he did fit such prophecies as there were.

And furthermore, on the spaghetti appendage thing:

In a spirit of equality, I have devised two scientific hypotheses that can explain any apparently 'supernatural' phenomena.

THE COMPLICATED ONE

At the quantum level, it is theorised that particles do not have a single position in time and space; rather, they exist 'smeared' across a range of possible positions. Extrapolating from this, I theorise that our universe is just one of infinite ranks of universes, one for every possible sequence of events. Some differ from our own by the orbit of a single electron; others are not even recognisable as the same universe. These infinite worlds, which lie a shadows' thickness from our own, may interfere with each other in places where the fabric of reality is stretched. This is common at a quantum level because the huge forces concentrated in such a tiny area stretch the fabric of time and space as thin as a very thin thing indeed (Yes! Pratchett references for all!). However, interference may still occur on a macro scale; ghosts, for example, appear when photons get confused and think they're in a universe where the deceased still lives. QED.


THE SIMPLE ONE

Humans are opportunistic, dishonest, and easily decieved.

Um, because that means one Joule of energy can be created for 662.6 billion-billion-billion-billionths of a second. An object which weighs one kilogram contains 9*10^16 Joules. #95862 42 2005-08-31T10:46:52Z Atilla
Quote: Trogdor007, Aug 31 2005, 01:26 AM
It's apparently happened in hospitals when patients were on life support.
that'd suck, wouldn't it?

'Spontaneous combustion' in hospitals is usually the result of an electrical discharge, or heating due to an electrical field. People with breathing difficulties are often placed in oxygen-rich chambers, and static buildup on their clothing, skin and blankets can sometimes create a large enough spark to start a fire. In scans that use strong magnetic or electrical fields, if a cord is touching the patient's arm, for example, the field can induce a current around the the arm and wire (which form a closed circuit). Because of the the high resistance of the inulating materials, and the resistance of the person's flesh, much of the electrical energy is converted to heat and the patient can suffer severe burns. Or, indeed, catch fire. In fact, there are many, many instances of 'spontaneous' combustion which can be attributed to a discharge of static electricity.

Psychological studies have shown that most dreams (which are recalled, of course) have to do with things which the dreamer has observed or been thinking about during the day. It is believed this occurs because the brain becomse disconnected from the sense to sorting through the day's memories (not unlike the Disk Defragmenter), experiencing them again as it goes. #100744 216 2005-09-15T11:38:53Z Atilla
@macaddict: Evolution is not a myth. We can see it in action.

In northern America, there is a certain species of moth. This moth is usually a light grey shade, which blends in with the bark of the trees it lives on. There are occaisional throwbacks with dark wings. These get eaten fairly quickly by birds, since they are easier to see. On occasion, however, there is a forest fire. The grey trees are blackened, and now it is the light moths that stand out. They are nearly all eaten - the overwhelming majority of the remaining population is dark. And so is the next generation, because the colour of a moth's wings is a genetic trait. And so is the next generation, except for some throwbacks. However, by this time, the trees are recovering from the fire and becoming light again: the dark moths are gradually picked off and, within a few generations, nearly all the moths are light again. This has been recorded. We know evolution occurs because we can go and look.

Secondly: We know how old fossils are not only because they lie in a certain strata, but also through the use of advanced techniques such as carbon dating.

Thirdly: Believing someone cannot have any morals unless they agree with you is incredibly foolish and arrogant. It is this sort of behaviour which leads to atrocities like the Spanish Inquisition, the Crusades, and, indeed, September 11. Read my sig, dammit!

Fourth: You still haven't explained why your religion is better than any of the others. You're outnumbered, so you'd better have a good reason.

Fith: How do you know it was the hand of a Christian god that supposedly wrote this "moral code", and not the Noodly Appendage of the Flying Spaghetti Monster? Or the hand of Ganesh, God of Compassion?

Sixth: It is entirely possible that we percieve actions as right or wrong because it is an evolutionary advantage - it makes us cooperate. After all, humans aren't particularly strong, or fast. We don't have big claws and teeth, we don't have armour, we can't fly, we have a relatively poor sense of smell and hearing, and our vital organs are in a somewhat exposed position. Therefore, we have to work together to survive. And, of course, any organism's greatest competition is other members of its species, since they want exactly the same resources.

Furthermore, in the example which was most like a real game, the controller acted "just like a mouse", which doesn't sound too revolutionary... And it doesn't have enough buttons for my liking, either. I can see it would be good for some games, but it seems it would make others impossible. Of course, it's hard to make a judgement without actually trying it, so I'll keep an open mind.

Blue Tetris, you think Nintendo is releasing original games? What the...? Aren't we up to about Mario Pary 246 by now? Didn't they have to slap a hasty licence on Dinosaur Planet because they can't bear to release a game which isn't part of a fifteen-year-old franchise? Didn't the Wind Waker have a near-exact clone of the Ocarina of Time's engine? Aren't a lot of GBA games just SNES or NES titles with some extra graphics? Yeah, there are a lot of generic clones on other platforms, but Nintendo isn't that much better. I, personally, think they have been in decline ever since the N64, when they lost loads of third-party support. The DS looks more promising, but they aren't so hot in the console stakes.

And yes, I can see better games being made with conventional consoles. I love RPGs and strategy games, and dream of the day when processing power and memory are sufficient to give every NPC their own individual behaviour and statistics. With a good-sized population, of course. Innovation is always good, but I want some evidence that this new controller is going to improve the playing experience for veteran gamers such as myself before I jump on the Nintendo wagon. They're going to have an uphill struggle to get third-party support and I suspect their software library will be somewhat limited. It's software that really makes or breaks a platform, and untill Nintendo have a game which demostrates why their controller is superior to a standard pad, a joystick, or my good old mouse and keyboard, I'm reserving judgement.

Why are shopkeepers too stingy to give me a 50-GP healing potion, despite the fact that my party is all that stands between the world and complete annihilation at the hands of the Dread God Zaxytaryx and his Accursed Legions?

Why does a group of four untrained teenagers have to save the world? Where's the military?

How does that 2m long staff fit in that cubic .5m chest?

If you've noticed something 1) odd or 2) horribly cliched in your travels in RPGland, this is the place to post it. If you enjoy yourselves, feel free to create a Why is it...? for other genres. (Why are there roast chickens in the oil barrels in scrolling beat 'em ups? Anyone?)

Quote: macaddict, 2005-09-22T03:08:56Z
And for the last half of #3, did you know that science owes almost all that it is now to Christianity?All the pagan beliefs before the Church age believed that the world was constantly chaos and subject to no rules because of the unsure behavior of the gods.  But Christianity started the idea that nature behaves according to rules, thus effectively inspiring science to begin again.

No it doesn't. Long before Christianity began, Greek philosophers founded the notion that the universe followed certain rules. They differed from scientist only in that they sought to determine such rules from reason alone, without reference to observational evidence. Many of those who instigated the rise from psuedo-science to true science were dabblers in arts that went against the Christian faith because they were deemed to be pagan rituals or unholy sorcery. Furthermore, many organisations, religious or otherwise, encouraged a strong sense of order and rigid laws. The Roman Empire was particularly notable for this. Buddhists believe in supernatural beings, but only in the same way they believe in people - they are a part of the world order, not some force outside it. The whole purpose of Confuscianism is to promote order and law. In Taoism, everything is believed to follow the grand universal harmony. In any event, whether science "owes" anything to Christianity is irrelevant. They are entirely different; one is a religion and the other a system for recording and analysing observations as objectively as possible.

Quote: macaddict, 2005-09-22T15:17:44Z
A single cell is infinetly more complex than even an airport.  Simply the number of requirements that must be met for a single celled organism is just improbable.

The chance of molecules randomly coming together to form a single-celled organism is low. However, that is not how it happens. Smaller, self-replicating chemical reactions develop first, and later combine to form more complex cells. In fact, we can create such reactions in a lab by creating a mock 'primordial soup' (water, nitrogen, CO2, some other stuff) and passing an electric current through it, although I haven't heard of anyone letting them sit long enough for cells to form. I also point out that even if something is improbable, it's had billions of years to happen in, which raises the chances quite a bit.

#104413 3 2005-09-29T11:53:04Z Atilla
Mmm.. pretty good. Your use of semi-colons was a little odd. Some sentences also have too many commas, too many conjunctions, or a poor choice of words. I recommend going through each sentnce and having a serious look at the length and structure, then running through it with a thesaurus.

A few examples...
Quote
The sky blazed with warm, soothing colors

I don't think "Blazed" and "soothing" really go together. Try a softer, gentler word... something along the lines of "glowed", perhaps.

Quote
He walked towards the park bathroom to get some paper towels to blow his nose, and as he reached for the door, he noticed an peculiar looking man.

Too long, and clumsy. Split it into two sentences, eg "He walked towards the park bathroom, looking for some paper towels to blow his nose. As he reached the door, he noticed a peculiar man."

Quote
looking as sharp as ever

This isn't normally used when referring to a stranger, because you don't know how they normally look. Up to you, though.

Quote
Yet, his eyes; He had two eyes that were as golden as the buttons on his shirt.

Phrases seperated by a semi-colon should be able to stand alone, as sentences. "Yet, his eyes." is not a coherant sentence. You have to have something like "His eyes were quick and intelligent; they shone gold, like the buttons of his shirt." Specification of two eyes is unnecessary and looks bad; since he has been called a 'man', the reader assumes he has the normal number of limbs, orifices and organs unless stated otherwise.


Quote: TornadoTK, 2005-09-29T06:58:39Z
Awkwardly enough, nobody even took a glance at him, no matter how bad he stuck out. It's almost as if Joe was the only one meant to see him, like a ghost. He shrugged it off and entered the bathroom.

You changed tense between these sentences. "It's" should be "It was". "Awkwardly enough" is a little... well, awkward. Use the more common "Strangely enough", or just "Strangely".

Quote
The stench was pretty bad, as you could imagine in almost any public bathroom.

Looks awkward. Cut some of it - "The stench was pretty bad, as you can imagine" or "The stench was pretty bad, as it is in all public bathrooms". You could also change the sentence completely - "It was filled with the stench that permeates public restrooms everywhere." "Like all public restrooms, it reeked of stale urine".

Quote
He faltered for the slightest moment, as it would be human instinct to do so. Yet, he regained his composure, opened the stall, pulled some tissue from the roll, and suddenly froze.

"He faltered for the slightest moment in response to some ancient instinct" or just "He faltered instinctively" would be more elegant. In the second sentence, the word "Yet" should be removed. I'd also consider splitting it, although it's not too bad - "He regained his composure, opened the stall, and pulled some tissue from the roll. Suddenly, he froze." I think the full stop gives greater dramatic effect than a comma and "and", but it could just be me.


Sorry if I sound too critical. As I said, it's pretty good. And it is, after all, just a draft. I'm sure the final version will be excellent.

(Anyway, if you get published, you'll probably have to put up with editors doing this instead of me)

#104432 7 2005-09-29T14:27:49Z Atilla
@TornadoTK: Heh, thanks.

And I just want to emphasize something - you need to be more careful with your tense. Changing tense suddenly really disrupts the flow.

@stepself: I think structure is very important. It looks so much more professional, and flows so much better, when a story is well structered. It's okay to use unusual sentence structure - especially for dialogue - but it needs to done deliberately, and you have to be clear about the purpose. Readers will usually find the 'proper' structure easier to read, because they are used to it. Writing the whole narritive with odd structure generally just confuses people (although it is possible to pull it off well). The majority of a story should therefore be written with normal sentence structure, and the unusual bits saved for dramatic effect.

#104908 20 2005-10-02T09:42:13Z Atilla
Quote: blue tetris, 2005-10-02T06:51:44Z
Republicans against the "liberal media"
Ironically, the Liberal Party are the conservatives in Australia.

A brief overview of Australian politics, for anyone who cares:

Australia has a bicameral system at both state (Legislative Assembly / Legislative Council) and federal levels (House of Representitives / Senate). We also have local councils. The leader of the Federal Government is called the Prime Minister. The PM is backed up by the Cabinet (or front-bench), members of his/her party whom he has allocated a portfolio (such as Treasurer, Minister of Defence, etc). The next largest party forms the Opposition, led by the Opposition Leader (duh) and the Shadow Cabinet (Shadow Treasurer, etc). The Queen's representative (Australia is a constitutional monarchy) is called the Governer General, and proceedings in Parliament are controlled by the Speaker. The same applies at state level, except that the leader of the Government is the Premier, and the Queen's rep is just the Governer.

The Coalition consists of the Liberal Party and National Party (formerly Country Liberal Party). The Nationals focus on rural seats. The Liberals are much more powerful and hold mostly urban and suburban seats. The coalition is moderate conservative, and their strengths are traditionally economic management and growth, fast and on-budget completion of major projects, and the encouragement of business, trade and free enterprise. It is traditionally supported by business owners, white-collar workers and the upper class. They usually get voted out because the public feels they are not supporting public services enough, or that they are not helping the lower classes enough. The Coalition is currently in federal Government, and has been since 1996.

The Labor Party (ALP) forms the Opposition, since it is the only other party which has a hope of taking government. It is traditionally supported by blue-collar workers, the lower classes (except for small business owners, who like the Coalition) and trade unionists. Labor is generally popular for increasing funding to public services and welfare, and increasing the rights of employees. They usually get voted out for economic incompetence, excessive union strikes, and inablility to complete projects on time or on budget. Although they have traditionally been moderate Left, Labor has wobbled towards conservatism in recent years, and started focusing more on the middle classes. There has also been a great deal of infighting between various factions within the party, which hasn't helped their election prospects. The ALP holds every state government.

The minor parties are the Greens (strong Left) and Democrats (not anymore - they self-destructed after internal bickering), and there are a few independants. The One Nation Party also occasionally crops up (widely bagged for being racist, probably the closest to extreme American conservatives) and the Family First Party (religious strong Right) has recently entered Parliament.

#108913 13 2005-10-17T12:11:47Z Atilla
I've heard this sort of thing before. However, I don't believe it covers all points. There appears to be an element of randomness in the universe, as iangb said; it is entirely possible that the fate of the universe is not predetermined by cause and effect. This doesn't negate the fact that nothing has any meaning whatsover, of course... in fact, it is worse - in means that nothing exists, only the probablity of something.

Another thing to think about is whether there is truly a "reality", or if the universe is only our perceptions. According to the Theory of Relativity, for example, an object becomes shorter in the direction of motion when it moves relative to your reference frame. Consider then a very fast car and a tunnel. This tunnel has a door over one end which opens instantly when the rear of the car passes through the start of the tunnel. When they are at rest relative to each other, it is just longer than the car, so you can drive through it at low speed safely. However, imagine now the car is travelling at nearly the speed of light, relative to the tunnel. From the tunnel's point of view, the car is rushing towards it, so the car becomes shorter and fits through easily. From the car's reference frame, the tunnel is moving near the speed of light, and gets shortened dramatically. Which means the whole car will no longer fit in the tunnel, so the door won't open and they car will crash... What happens? Does the universe split in two, depending on which reference frame you inhabit? Perhaps everything is created by the observer; there is no time or motion, it is merely our perception flicking through nearly-identical universes and stringing the sensations together, like the eye does with disparate frames of a movie. Whatever happens, we will never know.

This is, of course, why I am agnostic. We can never say with absolute certainty that what we percieve is real or true, or even that there can be the concept of reality. Our limited senses can always be deceived. We could be just brains in a tank somewhere, tricked into believing in the world. Our universe could merely be the latest virtual reality sensation, and we are all enjoying a bit of role-play after work. We may be having a long and complicated dream. We may, in fact (and against all the odds), be right about Life, the Universe, and Everything. But we cannot tell, nor will we ever be able to. It is our fate to be fascinated by the workings of the universe and its origins, if indeed it has any, because we are humans and that is a part of our humanity. We convince ourselves that things like truth, justice and mercy are real, because our genes dictate it, or god dictates it, or because it is something we have decided for ourselves. And who can say they are not? Reality may not be defined merely as molecules and atoms; things do not necessarily require physical form to exist. It matters not, because people will act as people regardless. All we can do is get on with our lives as best we can, whether they are dictated by chemical reactions, by the gods, the stars, or our own free will.

#111854 36 2005-11-02T01:59:43Z Atilla
The "halves" paradox is created by faulty logic. Your position is space is continuous, not discrete. Think of it like a graph in the cartesian plane. There is a single, precise point in time where you are exactly at the end of the street, like the x-intercept of a graph. At any other time, you are to one side or the other. By choosing to only walk half the distance, you are deliberately choosing not to cross the intercept, but to approach it from one side in progressively smaller intervals. There is no reason why you cannot reach it. The length is finite. You are just electing to travel smaller and smaller distances so you will not reach it. It's like saying "Hey, it must be impossible to walk a metre, because if I don't move I never reach a distance of one metre from my original position! Even if I keep failing to move forever! Wow!" or believing that anything you can't (or choose not to) see doesn't exist.

Pressing 'S' saves the level data TO THE CLIPBOARD. You must then paste it into a text file (of course, copying normally works just as well). The intructions for doing this are in userlevels.txt and also in the manual, which I suggest you read if you haven't already done so.

I won't even go into the way an alien might move itsself. That depends completely on its environment. It may not need to move at all.

What is difficult to think of is a means to produce organic energy and a how to reporduce. We only know of the ways terrestrial organisms produce energy, there is no reason that aliens would not ingest things much like we do. Reproduction is even more difficult to imagine, one would have to understand much more about the alien to understand how it reproduces.

These aspects should be constant, meaning that all life no matter how alien should have some of these characteristics. Does anybody think that some of these characteristics are not constant, or have any more characteristics that they believe are constant?

Movement and ability to sense stimuli are not required. (Algae and fungus don't move or have any senses, as far as I'm aware...)

#117097 17 2005-11-23T00:37:23Z Atilla
Quote: Maniac, Nov 22 2005, 12:28 PM
Well, no, but rocket launchers in particular suck up a lot of memory because each frame they:

1. Look for the player
2. Find out if there's a rocket on the screen already
3. If it can see the player, and a rocket isn't on the screen already, fire a rocket
4. Move a rocket if it's on the screen(which isn't a simple algorithm, mind you)

And that's just a single rocket launcher. Put a whole lot in there, along with gauss turrets and drones, and your computer slows down enough for you to notice.
2. Only requires a flag, and therfore a single "if" statement. The others will use some memory, yes. But on the other hand, for the ninja:

1. Collision detection with tiles (complicated)
2. Collision detection with objects
3. Gravity
4. Momentum
5. Player input

And you neglect the fact that if there were two players, enemies would then have to either
1. Have an algorithm to decide which player they target, which increases memory consumption
2. Target both players simultaneously, thereby doubling the number of calculations necessary. Ouch.
3. Always target one player, which removes many of the benefits of multi-player.

With two players, there is also likely to be twice as much interaction with objects, which will increase calculations. I maintain that two players will almost double the lag.

#118617 11 2005-11-28T01:53:31Z Atilla
Quote: The Daily Llama, Nov 27 2005, 06:32 PM
Yes... Attilla- do you really think that rating one map- or ten maps- or even 100 of the highest rated maps- will really have that much effect, when there are 20,000 or so maps on NUMA?

And, is this really a lot greater incentive to rate maps down- raising your percentage, that only you can see, and only then when it's in the top 50%- moreso than wanting you to rate higher on the 'all authors' tab?

I don't think it will have much effect, but crazy noobs might. It isn't a lot greater incentive, but it is an incentive. The reason given for this scheme is that it would give you something to strive towards - that is, people will want that percentage, which only you can see, to be as high as possible. Rating others poorly is one way to help achieve that. It could also result in a more subtle form of low rating, such as "This map deserves a 4.5... but that would put it above my maps. I'll give it a 3.5 instead".

In any event, I don't see much point. If you want a slightly more accurate rating than the current one, ask Arachnid to put the actual average rating as a floating point number on the map page. It should be easy to do. You could also add a "number of results" display to the search function, and allow searches for maps above/below a certain rating, which would let you get a general idea of how many good maps there are.

I'm going to clarify on football terminology and culture in Australia, just to try and drag this back on topic. In the event that this fails, it's locking time.

Australian Rules Football is most popular in the state of Victoria, which has a disproportionately large number of teams. Many Victorian supporters follow their team with religious zeal. It is also popular in South Australia, and (I think) Western Australia and the Northern Territory, and is followed to a lesser extent in other states. In Queensland and New South Wales, the rugby codes (League and Union) are more popular than Australian rules, and are often referred to as football; in the other states, football is generally Australian rules football, except in ethnic groups in which soccer is popular. American football is NOT the same as rugby, and is referred to as gridiron. The AFL (Australian Football League) has recently been trying to gain support for the sport in other states, particularly Queensland and NSW. I live in Victoria, and support the Collingwood Magpies. I have no interest in rugby or gridiron. I don't mind playing soccer, but I don't watch it because 1. It's usually televised on SBS, which I can't pick up and 2. I often find it a bit tedious.

Quote: nevermore, Dec 22 2005, 03:09 PM
I get deja vu very often. I think I read somewhere that it's that your brain is processing something slowly. Once it's done processing what you've just percieved, it feels like you've seen it before, because of how long it took.
Does that make sense?

According to my psychology classes, the sensation known as "deja vu" occurs when there is an error in the transmission of sensory data to the brain. Partial or corrupted data is processed, the problem is found, and the same data is then transmitted again (hopefully correctly, this time). You then have a strong feeling you've been in this situation before - and you have, a fraction of a second ago.

N-Ball is an odd little physics-based platformer, not a noobish "sport" map. Well, actually, it's probably both, but I'm discussing the former. Basically, you have to guide a bouncing ball to the end of a level filled with various physics-orientated (including ragdoll) objects, preferably as quickly as possible. There are no enemies - only holes, and red platforms which must be avoided. Graphics are simple, but effective. Watch it spawn a thousand suggestions along the lines of "We should have physics object X in N" . As for the name, I have no idea whether it's coincidental or not. The game IS a little similar to N...

Pogo Sticker is another game where you must guide a bouncy thing to the goal as quickly as possible, this time a vaugely humanoid one. It uses only the mouse - your character leans in the direction of the pointer, and the direction they bouce (and, to a lesser extent, their movement in midair) is determined by the angle they lean at. Ragdoll mechanics are involved, so it can often be a challenge to stop the #*^&$% thing swinging back and forth like pendulum and actually go where you want. The mouse button can be clicked to increase the bounce power. Waiting a little while gradually restores the power to its normal level. Once again, no enemies, just an obstacle course - you have to avoid bashing your head too much or getting stuck, bounceless, on the scenery, though.

No, I'm sorry, it's "$level name#author#type#level data#". And MetaNinja's 'level data' was outside the quotation marks, you'll notice - it was not part of the format.

I think he wishes to watch the demos for userlevels. This can be achieved in two ways. Firstly, you could open the level in debug mode, paste the demo data in the appropriate box, click outside the textbox, press '3', press 'Q', and, finally, press 'P'. Oh, and make sure caps lock is on. The second option is to copy the v 1.4 level data, go to userlevels from the main menu, paste the data into the demo data box on the left, type a #, then paste the demo data after it, followed by another # (so the format should be $level#author#type#level data#replay data#), and click the watch replay button. Oh, yes, and you can watch your personal bests again by clicking on the box that displays your best time, just to the right of the associated level. This will also put the PB's demo data in the appropriate box in the same format as you would paste it in, so you can grab it if you want to post it.

#131790 8 2006-01-12T01:59:37Z Atilla
Face-to-face and internet discussions both have advantages and disadvantages. In an internet discussion, you can nip off to Google a stack of evidence, you can also take more time with the phrasing and construction of your argument, and people can't shout you down or talk over the top of you. However, because you cannot interject or clarify the way you can in a face-to-face discussion, and because writing often lacks the nuances of expression and tone present in speech, people are often misinterpreted. I suspect I am particularly prone to this problem, because I tend to write long and complex responses. Then again, I do that when I speak, too.

#132510 4 2006-01-15T01:35:44Z Atilla
Sounds like you have NaNs.

What's an NaN? It stands for Not a Number. What happens is that the user - that's you - pastes the level data into the appropriate text box, then presses L to load. Unfortunately, since the cursor is still in the text box, this also puts an 'L' on the end of the level data. Since N only deals with numbers and some punctuation, it is designated as Not a Number. When the level is loaded, this NaN is then intepreted as some random, undeletable object in a silly position. The solution is simply to click outside the text box before pressing anything. You can probably rescue your old level data by going through and deleting all NaNs, but since you've already remade it there is no need. Just be careful in the future.

Maps are put in the playable or non-playable sections purely based on their category. You chose to classify your map as N-Art, which is a non-playable category (look at some of the other N-Art). It should be in action, even though it has a theme.

Some of the problems with the level are:

There's loads of gold stacked in the top left corner for no good reason.

There are mines caddishly hidden behind gold. This requires the player to be psychic rather than skillful, especially since the placing is rather inconsistant.

There is gold which adds little to the playability of the level. Gold should generally be used as an incentive for doing things the difficult way, or a reward for doing something well (such as jumping from the very edge of a platform).

There's a large, empty bit with no enemies and no flow. This is not always a problem, but in this case it makes part of the level a bit boring.

Possibly a bit drone-heavy. It could cause lag on slow computers.

Still, it's not too bad for your first level.

Quote: The_Juggler, Feb 2 2006, 04:27 PM
Atilla, did you not even read b_t's post? I should have put your name on the retarded list. They were developed by people that did not have access to bladed or even metal weapons, so they used the few tools that they had.
Does nobody else realize how awesome it is when some guy with a stick kills a samurai with armor and a sword.
No, I just have a brain and a capacity for research. Nunchaku are considered relatively inefficient weapons even by martial artists because they are hard to use and ineffective against long bladed weapons - like, say, the katana you would expect a samurai to wield. Weapons such as the sai (which can be used as a sword breaker), bo (quarterstaff), tonfa and kunai were favoured. The bo, for example, is easier to wield, good for defence, and has longer reach than nunchaku, while kunai have a wide range of uses, are easy to conceal, and can be strapped to a staff to create an acceptable spear (contrary to popular belief, they were not generally used as throwing weapons). My statement was intended as a comment on the fact that many people misunderstand nunchaku and think they are some kind of ultimate weapon because they're all cool and exotic-looking, when in reality an unromantic, 6-foot long pole is more practical. I also point out that modern nunchaku are more effective than ancient ones, since they have been altered extensively because they are used exclusively as a weapon, and would be useless as a farming implement. While nuchaku were certainly used as weapons at some stage (although possibly not by ninja), they were by no means a weapon of choice, even among the limited arsenal of a peasant.

Oh, and sai and kunai are both metal, although they are not sharpened. Ninja did have access to some metal tools.

#138807 22 2006-02-03T00:28:50Z Atilla
Quote: Teh Dude, Feb 2 2006, 11:58 AM
That is the underlying assumption of having the map ratings. This measure is based on the assumption that in general maps are correctly rated. If the ratings really are all incorrect then why bother having them?

Let me explain in more detail the problem.

Calculating the root mean square of the distance of every vote by every user from the average on every map they've rated is impractical. There are 20000 maps and thousands of votes and users. Every time a map was rated, you would have to do the calculations again for every user that had rated that map, because the average is not different. Clearly this will not be implemented before the use of quantum (or at least optical) computers becomes widespread, being hideously complicated and requiring too many operations.

The alternative is to only compare the vote to the average at the time the vote was made, which hits the following problem:

Say Noob Map A is posted. Noobs 1-5 come along and vote it an average of 4.5. I then rate it 1.5, as it deserves. Skilled Mapmakers 1-5 then give it likewise poor ratings, dragging the average down to 2.5. Skilled Mapmaker 6 then rates it 1.5.

The problem is that I now have a deviation from the average of 3, while Skilled Mapmaker 6 has a deviation of 1 (ignoring RMS for the moment), even though we gave identical ratings, which makes this statistic innacurate, pointless and without merit.

Even with the first method, if I rate Noob Map A poorly and Skilled Mapmakers 1-7 don't appear, I look like a sniper even though my vote was legitimate. I dislike this because what it basically says is you must agree with everyone else or you're a sniper/don't know what you're doing.

Quote: Teh Dude, Feb 3 2006, 10:39 PM
Explicitly, in your example, you are forgetting that your difference would be averaged. So yes you may have a difference in this circumstance of 3. However, averaged over many maps this difference would be reduced.

However, as Sweep pointed out at the beginning of this thread, there is currently a large number of new users who give excessively lenient ratings. Another thing to remember is that snipers also often multiaccount and rate all their own - or their friends - maps up. #141159 39 2006-02-09T03:59:12Z Atilla
Quote: Teh Dude, Feb 9 2006, 12:54 PM
The appeal of a film is that you can passively observe another world. Generally films have much better stories than games. Plus films last less time than games and as such have more story content per minute. Also it is easier to portray your vision as a film director than it is in a computer game.

I am very much a substance-over-style person. As such, on the few occasions that I have played RPGs, I have stripped away the story and looked at the gameplay. Of course you can argue that games are not just about gameplay but about the experience as a whole. I find that good gameplay becomes immersive; I forget any distractions and just flow.

The only MMORPG that I have tried is RuneScape. To be honest, trekking across maps for minutes on end in order to retrieve an arbitrary collection of items is not my idea of fun. Sure, at higher levels you can teleport and whatnot, but I don't want to invest that much time performing repetitive tasks in order to get mediocre pay-off.

For those of you who do play RPGs/MMORPGs; when I play online FPSs like Quake II and Day of Defeat, I progress in terms of my skill at the game. My reactions sharpen, my aim is better, I learn tactics, etc. I would imagine that a similar thing happens when you play N a lot. When you play RPGs, you obviously get skill points for your characters. However, how do you as a person improve in terms of skill?

(Please note that I am not assuming that you don't get more skilled at RPGs, I just wish to know the nature of this skill.)

The key word here is "generally". FF is not generally. It is a series renouned for having very strong storylines. Furthermore, I disagree entirely with your belief that movies generally have stronger storylines than games. And the story IS (part of) the substance of a good RPG. You're trying to compare them to action games, which isn't really valid because the whole concept and goal is different.

As I said, the combat is definately the weak point of FF, since there is little skill involved (although there is some skill in choosing the right equipment and right party for any given situation). This is not true of all RPGs, however. Guild Wars is an MMORPG which requires considerable skill. Try also the Phantasy Star Online series although it's an ARGP. D&D-based games require correct tactics to make the most of your party members' skills (should you cast web first, or try to disintegrate the enemy mage? Should your rogue try to backstab someone, or lurk where it's safe and use her bow?), and of course you have to choose the right skills in the first place. Diablo and its sequels require you to know the strengths and weaknesses of various enemies, and of your own character (chain lightning or fireball? Perhaps lurking with a ranged weapon would work? Or should you just run in and hack it as quickly as possible?). Baten Kaitos, as I mentioned earlier, has a rather unique card-based battle system which requires quick eyes and very quick fingers.* Then, of course, there are strategy-RPGs like the Front Mission series. These RPGs require substantial skill on behalf of the player. FF, regretfully, less so.

*It's like this. All actions and items are represented by cards. So to attack, you might use the "sabre" card, while to defend you would use a Robe of Fire, chainmail etc. Each card has up to four numbers on it, associate with four directions on the second analogue stick. Getting a straight (eg. 8 7 6 5 4) or only using sets of cards with the same number (4444 or 443333, but not 4443 or 44432) will increase the damage/defensive power/healing of the cards you use. Furthermore, there are six elements arranged in pairs (water/fire, light/dark, wind/time) plus physical damage. Only the opposing element reduces damage from an elemental attack, only physical defense prevents physical damage. After you pick the first card, you have about half a second to pick each subsequent card. In the later parts of the game, you can use nine cards in sequence. It takes a bit of skill to regularly match the numbers on 9 cards without using any conflicting elements.

TEH BIG EXPLOSION!!!), and others never use them. Myself, I find it's a bit hard to hit anyone skilled with grenades, although they are useful for taking out vehicles (and occasionally dropping around a corner for someone to walk into).

Realism in game design is an acceptable goal so long as it doesn't inhibit gameplay, because it adds to what you might call the flavour of game, just as atmospheric music and appropriate graphics do. Sometimes realistic elements can become important strategic considerations (only being able to carry two weapons, for instance). Indeed, some games are based around such realism, such as the Total War series. The important part is that this realism should be intended from the beginning and integrated into the mechanics, rather than being slapped on and screwing the gameplay because of some obsessive-compulsive designer.

It's been suggested before and shot down. I dislike it. For a start, it would be extremely difficult to make a level which caters for all, or even a substantial portion, of the abilities. You would then end up with levels designed to played with one specific ability, in which case you may as well just do away with the abilities. Most existing levels would also work extremely poorly with the abilities. Secondly, it would prevent people choosing their favourite colour, because that would alter the mechanics - not to mention that some people suffer eye strain with some colours. Third, you'd need to alter replay data to include what flavour was used. Fourth, it requires a fair bit of programming, which might be better spent on other things. It might be acceptable as a mod, but I wouldn't want to see M&R spend their time on it when they could be doing other, better stuff.

*Pokes head in*

I don't have time to keep up with this big debate, so I'm just going to state my views .

* Marajuana is harmful, particularly over the long term. This is not unique. Many legal drugs are also harmful.
* Smoking of marajuana should remain illegal. Why? Because it has a considerable effect on your mental state. Passive smoking could therefore interfere with the daily business of others, especially those who need to refrain from use of certain drugs - for example, surgeons and people operating heavy machinery. The risk from this may well be tiny, but since such people have a duty of care to the public they are legally obliged to abstain from use of drugs which may interfere with their functioning. Tampering with duty of care laws would be messy and inevitably result in loopholes.
* Before anyone accuses me of hypocrisy, I also believe smoking should be banned in all public places (and possibly banned outright).
*A milder oral form of marajuana could be made legal, if such a form was available at reasonable cost. It would need to be regulated properly, of course, and to reduce the risks should be comparitively weak. This would make the drug comparable with alcohol.
*More extensive research should be done into the long term effects of marajuana use. In particular, it appears to increase the risk of psychosis or mental disorder at a young age, which is rather worrying. Legalisation without such research should be avoided if possible (think of the suppresion of research documenting tobacco's harmful effects), but if it is really necessary then legalised marajuana use should be carfully monitored. Such legalisation should be considered as a trial only.

Quote: Daddaluma, February 28, 2006 10:54 am
Quote: Atilla, 2006-02-25T07:56:12Z
* Smoking of marajuana should remain illegal. Why? Because it has a considerable effect on your mental state. Passive smoking could therefore interfere with the daily business of others, especially those who need to refrain from use of certain drugs - for example, surgeons and people operating heavy machinery. The risk from this may well be tiny, but since such people have a duty of care to the public they are legally obliged to abstain from use of drugs which may interfere with their functioning. Tampering with duty of care laws would be messy and inevitably result in loopholes.

This is the worst argument for keeping marijuana illegal. It's logically unsound and intellectual vaccuous. And yet so many people use this idiotic reasoning when arguing against legalizing drugs. You know what else could interfere with the daily business of others? Cough medicine. You don't see anyone up in arms trying to make that illegal do you?

There's only a case here if you can show that using marijuana somehow increases the likeliehood of a person to go do things that endanger other people. And I can guarantee you you'll find no such claim made by any researcher anywhere.

There's a certain amount of personal responsibility that has to be assumed when creating laws. Take driver's licenses for instance. The government only requires a simple test before they'll hand out a license to drive what amounts to a deathtrap on wheels. That's a huge good faith assumption right there, and you know what? They're right to make that assumption. People in general are responsible enough to handle being behind the wheel of a car.

Yes, OF COURSE there are people that will fuck it all up. It's just going to happen. You don't make driving illegal because some people are guaranteed to hurt, maim or murderdeathkill someone with their car. The same logic applies here. Just because there exists the possibility that idiots will choose to smoke and drive doesn't mean you ban pot altogether.
You misunderstand me. I am not suggesting everyone would turn into crazed, pot-smoking murderers if marajuana was legalised. People of some professions have a legal obligation to remain drug-free because they have a duty of care to their clients, just as athletes have an obligation to avoid drugs which may be perfomance-enhancing (even if these drugs would be used for a legitimate reason, rather than in an attempt to cheat). If such people were exposed to passive smoking of an hallucigenic drug, they may be liable should an accident occur in the undertaking of their job - even though it is extremely unlikely to have caused the accident and they had no intent to use the drug in the first place. Avoiding this would require altering existing duty-of-care laws, which would be slow, messy, and leave too many gaps for possible exploitation. For this reason, the smoking of marajuana - especially in public places - should not be legalised. Note that I specified smoking, and not just marajuana. Use of marajuana in a way which will not result in passive inhalation would be acceptable, as I stated in the paragraph following the quoted one. If someone wants to legalise marajuana gum or somesuch, I don't mind, but no smoking!

And I've yet to hear of passive cough medicine ingestion. That comparison would only be relevent if, when you took cough medicine, everyone within 20m was forced to take a little bit as well.
#150142 15 2006-03-01T04:54:16Z Atilla
Atilla's Student Snack 1 ("I-Can't-Believe-It's-Not-Pizza")

Ingredients:
Bread
Cheese (Extremely-tasty-indeed cheddar is Atilla's cheese of choice. But tasty, extra-tasty, or extra-sharp will do.)
Tomato sauce
Ham and any other toppings you feel like.

Method:
1. Toast bread. It must be crispy enough not to go soggy when you put the tomato sauce on it.
2. If you have sliced ham, it should be put on first so the sauce doesn't make it slip off. Alternatively, apply extra cheese in Phase 4 to prevent slippage.
3. Pour tomato sauce on toast. Remember that it will expand when heated, so don't put too much on unless you enjoy removing sauce stains. Covering about two-thirds of the slice should be fine.
4. Put everything else on top of the sauce. The cheese must go on last so that when it melts, it will hold everything else down.
5. Microwave it until the cheese melts (probably around 30 sec + 15 for each extra slice). You can also use a griller if you really have to, but microwaves are so much quicker and easier.
6. Eat. Be careful not to burn tounge on red-hot (ahahaha) tomato sauce.

*GASP* Mine's actually moderately healthy! How can this be?!

#153899 18 2006-03-12T00:25:28Z Atilla
ANZAC Biscuits (Atilla's Improvised Version)

Ingredients:
Flour
Golden Syrup/Honey/Sugar (whichever happens to be lying around in sufficient quantity).
Butter
Oats
Any decent nuts you can lay hands on (peanuts and walnuts are good)
You can stick corn flakes and suchlike in too, if you want...

Method:
1. Grind the oats and nuts (and any other dry, chunky ingredients) into itty bitty pieces. Putting them in a freezer bag and beating them mercilessly with a rolling pin is generally the easiest way to do this, and is also good for relieving aggresion. DIE, UNRIGHTEOUS OATS! DIE! BWUHAHAHAHAHAHAAAAA!
2. Chuck the flour and the stuff you just beat to a pulp in a big bowl. Don't go too heavy on the flour (somewhere around 50/50 is generally all right, but I like more nuts...)
3. Melt the butter. If you have sugar, melt that too.
4. Pour the butter and syrup/honey/sugar in with the dry ingredients. Mix them into dough.
5. Make the dough into balls, put it on a baking tray, and stick it in the oven 'till they look golden-brown. Recommended temperature is about 200 C.
6. Scarf them all immediately. They're better when they're still warm. Alternatively, put them in an airtight container and they'll last for ages.

Also, Catholic Encyclopedia: Animals in the Bible:
Quote
BEHEMOTH, is generally translated by "great beasts"; in its wider signification it includes all mammals living on earth, but in the stricter sense is applied to domesticated quadrupeds at large. However in Job, xl, 10, where it is left untranslated and considered as a proper name, it indicates a particular animal. The description of this animal has long puzzled the commentators. Many of them now admit that it represents the hippopotamus, so well known to the ancient Egyptians; it might possibly correspond as well to the rhinoceros.

You should also look up badger, basilisk, cockatrice, demons, dipsas, dragon, griffon, hippopotomous, lamia, leviathan, mildew, phoenix, raven, ringtail, satyr, sea-monster, spider and whale, all of which demonstrate translation and clerical errors, confusion between various animals (and, in some cases, plants and/or inanimate objects), use of one term to refer not only to several species but to a mythical creature as well, use of a mythical or poetic description which actually refers to an ordinary animal, use of mythical descriptors to indicate the animal in question was unspecified, use of a word in a way which conflicts with its modern meaning (for example, 'mildew' now commonly refers to a mould-like growth rather than an animal) or use of an animal's name in a symbolic sense. Picking out a passage and claiming it is most definately and assuredly a dinosaur is probably not a good idea, given the trouble scholars and translators have had even with animals we know existed at the time.

#7545 1 2006-03-21T05:37:16Z Atilla
If it weren't done by committee, it would be intelligent design.

*Ahem*

ANYWAY, as we all know, the human species is riddled with design faults. As the Committee for Human Redesign, it is our job to create a better one. It must be a carbon-based lifeform with DNA, be able to reproduce, and be physically feasible (ie not be too heavy to support itself, be able to acquire and process sufficient food, etc.). It should also be sapient, sentient, able to communicate, and capable of building temples and worshipping the Committee.

Now, there are some bits of humans that work reasonably well, so I think we should start from the current model, identify the problems, and attempt to fix them rather than trying a redesign from scratch. Suggestions for enhancements and optimisations on those components which, while passable, are not suitable for a product of this calibre will also be welcomed. Bear in mind that the finished product is not required to resemble the previous model - if there is good cause and it is physically plausible, a full restructure is to be welcomed.

This thread will probably be moved to either intelligent discussion or messageboard games, depending on who gets the first few replies in and thus sets the tone. Hopefully it will be the former; I want to see some biologically viable alternatives.

And just to get you started, here's a little list:

Problems:
*Air passage crosses digestive tract, leading to unneccesary suffocation. Recommend seperation of tubes. Also to be considered is a membrane which can be lowered to cover the breathing hole and act as a filter, allowing homo superior to survive in otherwise fatal atmospheres and preventing inhalation of dust, etc., but this may be impractical.

*Limbs and organs do not regenerate if removed. Reccomend altering, as in case of lobster claws, so that any missing component can be rapidly replaced. In current state, important organisms can be permenantly crippled with relative ease, which is a unpleasant to the victim and a burden to others of the species.

*Important organs (digestive system and reproductive system) are in an exposed position on front of organism. This makes them vulnerable to predators, given human's tendency to stand upright. Possible solutions include relocation, inclusion of auxillaries, implementation of rapid regeneration, better blood control, and placement of bones, scales, thick fur, or chitinous plates to protect these delicate areas. More bones or armour will probably limit mobility, so a redesign of the torso to allow protection of all organs is probably the best bet. Scales and fur are also feasible, though they would be less effective.

*Teeth rarely fit correctly. There are too many of them, and the shape of the mouth and face is poor. Possible solutions include redesigning the skull, and replacing some or all of the teeth with other mechanisms, such as mandibles.

*The sinus are always blocked or infected or something. The head needs better plumbing. I suggest a complete redesign, which will also help accomodate the seperation of the breathing and digestive tracts.

Improvements:
*Unnecessary body parts (appendix, tonsils). Remove them.

*Introduce dual-lensed eye, for zoom function? It could possibly be achieved by placing a larger sphere with a lens around the current eye. By distorting to become elliptical, the distance between the lenses - and thus the level of magnification - could be altered.

*Sensitivity to infrared radiation. There should be an eye-like organ, or possibly an addition to the normal eyes, which could detect infrared radiation of the wavelengths emitted by a objects which are approximately 300K in temperature. This would allow homo superior to see without external illumination, especially other creatures (which would be ~310K). Noise from the organism's own body heat could be filtered by having an insulated group of receptors to provide a background reading. Similar (albeit mechanical) systems are already used.

#158750 57 2006-03-28T06:43:31Z Atilla
I'm not convinced that non-predictability is an acceptable definition of free will, nor do I believe that knowing the outcome of a choice means that outcome was deterministic. If you toss a coin, call heads, and it lands heads, this does not mean there was never the possibility of tails*. If you do this a thousand times, it still doesn't mean there was no possibilities other then the predicted one. If you do it for every event in the universe, once again, it doesn't mean that no other events were possible - it merely means they didn't happen.

On a different tack, consider quantum particles. You can measure the position of the particle. You may even be able to explain why it should have such a position. But until the measurement is made, the particle doesn't have a precise position - it occupies many possitions simultaeneously with various probabilities. After the measurement, you know the outcome, but you still can't say definitively why that outcome occured. We can consider a choice in the same way - there is a chance an individual may make many different choices, and once the choice has been made, you can say that it happened because <InsertReasonHere>, but this does not prove that there wasn't really a range of possible outcomes in the first place. As for omniscience, that simply means that from a God's point of view, all the choices were already made, all the measurements already taken - although He knows the outcome, it does not mean that no other results were possible.

Furthermore, as Daddaluma has pointed out, what is generally considered free will is far from random or unpredictable. As the word 'will' implies, free will is generally considered the ability to determine your own actions with a specific goal in mind - to impose your will upon the world, rather than being constrained to a single set of actions. Since you will generally choose to take actions that are beneficial to you or that appeal to certain values or opinions you hold, this makes your choices predictable - even though you could do otherwise if you wished.

*ignoring for the moment wrangling about the air resistance on each side and so forth.

[physics]Actually, that's incorrect. The Doppler effect means that you percieve a wave (in this case, sound) as being a higher frequency (which determines the pitch, for sound) when you are moving towards the source (or vice-versa), and lower when you/it are moving away.

Sounds are louder when you are near the source because the sound wave has only a so much energy. As it travels, it spreads out, so the energy being transferred from the wave in any given area (in this case, your ear) is less. This is unrelated to the Doppler effect.[/physics]

#161266 23 2006-04-03T05:32:37Z Atilla
Plural possesives should have the apostrophe after the s. As in, "The Swans' home ground is the SCG." Group nouns, however, should have the apostrophe before the s. So "The flock's breeding ground was nearby" means there is only one flock, while "The flocks' breeding ground was nearby" means there are multiple flocks.

Too can also be used to mean, uh, "also". For exapmle, I could have said that too can mean "also", too.

We're is also often confused with were, because people are slack and leave the apostrophe out.

Questions may also be asked by altering the word order. For example, "That is true." is a statement and "Is that true?" is a question. Questions also often begin with "is", "are" ("Are you hurt?"), "do" ("Do you like my shirt?"), "does" ("Does this shirt make me look fat?"), "can" ("Can you read Japanese?"), "could" ("Could you please hold this for me?"), "would" ("Would you still support the Bill if these amendments were added?"), "will" ("Will you please leave me alone?") and "should" ("Should the engine be making that noise?").

A question mark followed by an exclamation mark indicates that a question is rhetorical (ie, that an answer is not expected): Eg. "Are you insane?!"

Edit: "have", "had", and "has" are also commonly used to start questions.

Quote: stepself, April 11, 2006 02:37 am
another one of science's generalizations. There are even more phases than those four. It's for the sake of convenience that only the basic three are taught to most people. Most people think there's some huge distinction between each phase, and while they are clearly different, it's more of a gradient. Subcooled liquids, superheated vapour, supercritical fluid, gels... they all occupy places in between (or beyond) the standard phases.

There are important differences between states. Solids have a (semi) rigid structure, for example, and liquids don't expand the way gasses do. Most people only know about four states (the standard three and gels) because they're the only ones they'll ever need to refer to. The average guy on the street doesn't need to know what a Bose-Einstein Condensate is.

My point was that you responded to the wrong part of the post, although I appreciate that this may have been unclear. You should have said that you do not believe recording the sounds would be considered decompiling, disassembling, or reverse engineering the software.

"Decompile" is a term used in programming, and is the opposite to compiling (converting source code in one language to object code in another). Look it up on Wikipedia if you want more information. You might also wish to look up assemble/disassemble, which have technical meanings distinct from their everyday use.

Anyway, let us consider that both our posts were ill-written and move on. Here is the full license:

I, of course, am not a lawyer, but it's probably better just to ask them about the rights for the sounds. As I said, they may provide you with access to the originals, and it can hardly hurt.

#8241 1 2006-04-22T05:33:19Z Atilla
Vertigo Games

In particular, take a look at Liquisity and Ore No Ryomi 2.

Anyway, Liquisity is a puzzle/action thing wherein one must guide the bouncing ball to the goal, avoiding and/or utilising obstacles such as spinning platforms, pinball-style bumpers, and bubble streams which push the ball around. It is not difficult, but it's still kind of fun. You'll probably finish it in a hour or two. It also includes a level editor.

ONR is an odd cooking/management sim, which requires you to put out fires, wash dishes, and empty the trash whilst a line of impatient customers waits. After closing for the day you may invest in such things as automatic dishwahers, new types of food, a tip jar, and advertising. The main part of the game is frantically trying to prepare food (usually by hitting the correct sequence of keys), which is fun although rather repetitive. If you play for a while, you may be invited to the "Iron Cook" show, which features food preperation challenges (such as serving 25 perfect beers in 60 seconds) and silly (but funny) voiceovers.

Yes. "Algorithm" means a predetermined set of rules/instuctions for completing a task or solving a problem. In this case, the algorithms for pathfinding are "Go straight until you hit a non-empty tile, then turn clockwise" and so forth. The algorithm for baking a cake would be turn the oven on, mix the ingredients, etc. But I digress.

Anyway... 96-4 has plenty of zap drones. Note how they go in different paths around the tiles, and treat the doors as a solid barrier. 86-1 has a nice display of drones constrained to a rectangular path. 80-1 shows a prisoner-type level. 85-4 is another one with lots of drones, syncronised this time. 95-4 also has many drones. There are plenty of others, but those should be enough to get started. Er, although I realise they're mostly a bit late in the game. They're just the ones I remember because I've played them more recently.

These days, psychopathy is defined in psychiatry as a personality disorder characterised by lack of empathy or conscience, poor impulse control and manipulative behaviors. Hare describes psychopaths as, "intraspecies predators who use charm, manipulation, intimidation, and violence to control others and to satisfy their own selfish needs. #175601 32 2006-05-14T03:41:19Z Atilla
From one of my previous discussions with B_T:

Quote: Atilla, 2005-10-02T09:42:13Z
Ironically, the Liberal Party are the conservatives in Australia.

A brief overview of Australian politics, for anyone who cares:

Australia has a bicameral system at both state (Legislative Assembly / Legislative Council) and federal levels (House of Representitives / Senate). We also have local councils. The leader of the Federal Government is called the Prime Minister. The PM is backed up by the Cabinet (or front-bench), members of his/her party whom he has allocated a portfolio (such as Treasurer, Minister of Defence, etc). The next largest party forms the Opposition, led by the Opposition Leader (duh) and the Shadow Cabinet (Shadow Treasurer, etc). The Queen's representative (Australia is a constitutional monarchy) is called the Governer General, and proceedings in Parliament are controlled by the Speaker. The same applies at state level, except that the leader of the Government is the Premier, and the Queen's rep is just the Governer.

The Coalition consists of the Liberal Party and National Party (formerly Country Liberal Party). The Nationals focus on rural seats. The Liberals are much more powerful and hold mostly urban and suburban seats. The coalition is moderate conservative, and their strengths are traditionally economic management and growth, fast and on-budget completion of major projects, and the encouragement of business, trade and free enterprise. It is traditionally supported by business owners, white-collar workers and the upper class. They usually get voted out because the public feels they are not supporting public services enough, or that they are not helping the lower classes enough. The Coalition is currently in federal Government, and has been since 1996.

The Labor Party (ALP) forms the Opposition, since it is the only other party which has a hope of taking government. It is traditionally supported by blue-collar workers, the lower classes (except for small business owners, who like the Coalition) and trade unionists. Labor is generally popular for increasing funding to public services and welfare, and increasing the rights of employees. They usually get voted out for economic incompetence, excessive union strikes, and inablility to complete projects on time or on budget. Although they have traditionally been moderate Left, Labor has wobbled towards conservatism in recent years, and started focusing more on the middle classes. There has also been a great deal of infighting between various factions within the party, which hasn't helped their election prospects. The ALP holds every state government.

The minor parties are the Greens (strong Left) and Democrats (not anymore - they self-destructed after internal bickering), and there are a few independants. The One Nation Party also occasionally crops up (widely bagged for being racist, probably the closest to extreme American conservatives) and the Family First Party (religious strong Right) has recently entered Parliament.

Heh... Australian politics are confusing, with conservative Liberals and two major parties which can both be abbreviated to "ALP", even though only one ever is.
