#8764 1 2006-05-17T13:03:39Z Atilla
Welcome, pupils! Since N-Vision is suffering from terminal server problems I've put together a small large map pack which demonstrates many aspects of play, including some basic things for beginners and more advanced tricks for experts. The file is formatted so that you can simply paste a level's entry into that big box on the left of the userlevels menu to watch a replay. Note that it now has "&userdata=" at the top - rename it "userlevels.txt" and put it in the same folder as N (you'll want to move or rename your existing userlevels.txt, of course) and all the levels will be available through the userlevels menu. Alternately, copy everything below the "&userlevels=" line and paste into your normal userlevels.txt. If you want to play an individual level, you should enter debug mode (also known as Ned), copy the whole level entry (You know, $levelname#author#type#leveldata#demodata#), paste it into the "level data" box, click outside the box, and hit L. N will automatically prune out the unneccesary stuff and load the level for you.

For the most part you don't have to do the levels in order. Some levels do require a skill or trick from previous levels - this will be mentioned in the description.

The teaching staff now includes myself, Mr Ngaged, Mr Sketch, Mr thecalcgenius, Mr Zres, Mr jeca, Mr Borealis , Mr Qix, Mr Dark Ball Y-E, Mr Bufar, Mr jtbandes, Mr Scythe33 and Mr Zapkt. Say "good morning," class! Also, thanks to the people who posted levels which were not included, or who made other suggestions. I'm not going to list them all, because I doubt people want to read through dozens and dozens of names, but rest assured that I appreciate your effort.

On the curriculum (Updated 1:26 PM (GMT+10) 21/9/2008 (9/21/2008 for Americans)):

The Inclined Plane
Demonstrates several handy tricks using slopes - the perpendicular jump (release the arrows and jump whilst on a slope), the triple jump (jump onto a slope, then into the wall, then off the wall in quick succession), and using them to avoid splattering all over the pavement (just land on them, preferably moving downhill). The little pit on the left of the exit isn't required, but if you want you can practice a more difficult triple jump - you only get a small slope to aim for, unlike the jump to the exit. You'll need to time the first jump better, and get the timing of the next two jumps more accurate as well.

The Double Reverse Jump (zapkt and Atilla)
Another slope trick. Run towards a slope and jump just before you get there, exactly as though you were doing a triple jump. However, when you hit the slope you should release left/right and press jump, performing a higher perpendicular jump than normal.

Dangerous Tunnelling (Dark Ball Y-E)
Downhill slope jumps. Press and hold right (ie downhill) just before you hit the first slope, and jump pretty much as soon as you land. You should fly through the gap of mines, with a fairly flat trajectory (note: if you jump while running downhill, your trajectory will be lower, and if you jump whilst running uphill, it will be higher). Still holding right, jump from the next slope as soon as you land. Note that you go a little higher because this slope isn't as steep. Then simply jump onto the one-ways and run into the exit - or try a perpendicular jump from the steep slope if you're feeling skilled.

The Slope of Skill (Dark Ball Y-E)
The compainion to Dangerous Tunnelling, this one demonstrates uphill slope jumps. Jump from slope to slope to build up speed, then do a perpendicular jump from the last platform to reach the exit.

Bite the Curb (Sketch)
Just a short level for practicing slope jumps. You'll need to use the perpendicular jump for this one (release left/right and hit jump whilst on a slope). Remember, the more speed you have, the higher you'll go, and hopping from one slope to the other will prevent you losing speed in the corner. Although only one way is shown on the demo, it's possible to reach the exit from either slope. Also, note that if you stand where two slopes meet you'll be able to jump straight up, like you would on a flat surface.

And away!
Your basic launchpad high jump. Just hit the jump button straight after bouncing off the pad while you're against the wall.

Knees of Steel!
Surely you can't survive that... or can you? Clipping the edge of a block can save you from even the hardest of falls, as long as you hit it in the right spot. Incidentally, this trick will occasionally let you skip quite a large portion of some levels.

What momentum?
Strangely, the deceleration from a wall jump doesn't kill you, but hitting the ground does. This means hopping off the wall is a great way to stop fatal falls. It doesn't need as much wall space as sliding, so you can use it when you don't have much to aim for.

Floating in the Breeze
This level shows the odd floating effect when you jump into a roof. Float over the first bunch of mines just by taking a running jump (make sure you hold the jump key all the way). Get past the next two by jumping into the roof just in front of them and releasing the button, allowing you to fall between them. This might take a bit of practice, since you have to be fairly accurate.

Ding! (Sketch)
You walljump much higher than usual if you jump whilst running up a slope or curve, then quickly jump off the wall. This will be used a lot, so it's important to be able to do it consistently. Run up the slope, press jump when you're about halfway up (still holding towards the wall) and walljump.

Feels Like No Grip (Zres)
I'm sure everyone has discovered (much to their annoyance) that walljumping on doors, one-way platforms and thwumps is different to tiles. They lack tiles' "toggle-stick" function, so you must hold towards the object when you jump, or you'll just fall.

Feeling Tipsy
Avoid the explosive roof! In this situation, you will often be able slide down the edge of your platform and walljump across, as demonstrated in the first jump. Otherwise, you'll have to lean over the edge. To do this, move N *very* close to the corner (until one foot is hanging off, basically) and stand still. Don't move towards the edge too fast or you'll fall off. Pressing towards solid ground will make you tip slower, and if you do it while you're almost upright you can walk back onto the platform. Note that this trick only works on tiles, locked doors and trapdoors - you'll just fall straight off one-ways, bounceblocks, and other objects.

Bent
Argh! Those loathsome curved tiles often cause problems for beginners. You get used to them after a while, though. For the convex (outward-curving) ones, you should avoid walking towards the outside - you'll often fall off if you try it. Jump, then start moving sideways if it's at all possible. Jumping as soon as you land can also help you avoid slipping off. Note that if you're struggling to walk up the steep side, jumping will help. With the concave (inward curving) tiles, either hold towards the centre or jump to avoid slipping. If you want to keep moving, they're quite similar to slopes - jumping off one will send you higher, and you can use them to change your direction quickly.

Overhung (Zres)
Jumping into tiny gaps is also irritating. To get into the first gap, hop off the wall (not too high!) and try to fall in. If you hit the corner, a very small (and very quick) jump should get you in. To get out, you should lean over the edge a little, as in Feeling Tipsy, and jump up to the wall. For the second one, jump to the wall beneath the gap (remember, a walljump will stop you sliding off) and just climb into it.

Do the Double (lord_day)
It's possible, though difficult, to jump from a tile or object which is only one block high, and you'll have to do it in a variety of circumstances to finish this level. There's no real trick to it - you just have to hit the jump button fast enough. If you like, you can try "double shifting" - set the the shift key to jump, and press left shift while releasing right shift. This technique can also be used to jump rapidly up chimneys (one-tile wide shafts). Note, however, that it's entirely possible to finish this level without double-shifting.

Much Ado About Thwumps
Thwumps aren't always your enemy. Hitching a ride on them is going to be necessary at some stage. The first bit it fairly easy - just jump onto the thwump when it comes and inch along on top of it. When Thwumps move sideways, they don't take you with them, so you'll have to keep tapping forwards.

The second part is the most difficult. You must run towards the slope. Jump off the slope, then quickly off of the Thwump (like the triple jump), still holding right. If you time your jumps correctly, you can keep jumping off the Thwump all the way up. Two jumps should be enough here, though - and remember, if you release the jump button you'll lose your upward momentum faster.

The third part isn't too hard. Just jump into the back of the Thwump, hold towards it, and keep doing small hops to stay on. The forth is also fairly straightforward - just like the first, but much faster.

Finally, the Thwump jump. If you leap from the top of a thwump while it's moving upwards, the momentum will carry you higher than a normal jump.

More Ado About Thwumps (Borealis + Atilla)
Almost getting squashed by a Thump can give you a speed boost. It's much easier with a jump pad, but a similar trick is possible without one, though your trajectory will be different. To do it, stand underneath the Thwump, near the jump pad, and hold left when you're about to become ninja-pancake. It's not likely to be terribly useful in the main game, but it crops up occasionally in user levels, and if you don't know about it it can sometimes be used to cheat your own levels.

"But how do I get to the exit?!" I hear you cry. Well, Thwumps will also push you through one-way platforms (bounceblocks, too, for that matter). Just lure the Thwump up and stand beneath it. Once you're safely down, waltz over to the Thwumps facing the wall on the right. There's a glitch with Thwumps that makes them move slowly backwards when you approach if you place them one pixel away from halfway through a wall. In this state, they'll go right through walls, but you can still stand and walljump on them. You should set them off when you open the door - get through the curved corridor before they squish you, then wallslide and jump on them to get through the mines.

Thwumper Cars (Qix)
A couple more tricks with thwumps. In the first section, you should run toward the twump and jump so that you hit the roof just before it touches you. You should be able to squeeze past with the right timing. The second is another variant of the thwump-launching shown in the last level - this time you get sqeezed from between two thwumps rather than a thwump and the floor. Just jump in between the thwumps when they're moving backwards to do it - the later you leave it, the faster you'll fly out.

When Blue Octagons Attack (Atilla + Sketch)
This one just shows how drones move, and the seeking and passive variants. You shouldn't have a problem with the first three - just remember they don't go into partially solid tiles (like slopes and half-tiles), and time it right. Get past the next two by luring one down and jumping through the gap (note: they won't chase you into the side corridors because they're made of half-tiles stuck together). Then, reach the exit switch by luring the seeker drones into the trap on the left. Also, note the Zap Drone following the surface of the block in this area - there are several ways drones can move.

Tall People Need Not Apply
You can make it past zap drones by standing on some slopes (the 1, 2 and 3 tiles, namely) and the concave curves - just. The start is simple - just let yourself slide into the little pothole. For the shallowly sloped section, the gold marks the tiles you can use to slip under a drone. It just needs a little timing. For the final part, I recommend running under the drone at the first slope, as depicted in the demo, but it's also possible to slide under on the other side. Steep slopes are quite similar to the 45 degree ones when it comes to drone dodging, except that you have slightly more room and slip off much faster.

Trampoline
Shows four types of bounceblock jump. The first and simplest requires you to push the block down, then jump when it's moving upwards. Note that if you aren't moving sideways (however slightly), the block won't sink properly - just tap back and forth if you wish to stay in the middle. The second (the double jump) starts like the first, but rather than waiting for the block to spring up, you should tap jump at the lowest point, then quickly press and hold. You can go even higher with a triple jump (rap jump twice, then press and hold) if you're fast enough. The third is the sideways double jump. Run towards the block and jump into it. Still holding towards it, tap jump. Quickly press and hold jump and press away from the block. Finally, you'll need to do a sideways triple jump, which will send you much higher. Like with the vertical triple jump, you just need to tap jump twice, quickly, then press and hold.

Touchy (bufar)
Sometimes, being able to push bounceblocks around is dangerous rather than helpful - usually when there's something unpleasant beehind them. In this level, you have to avoid pushing the bounceblocks too far. This means reducing your momentum as much as possible before hitting them (try not to fall onto them from too high if you're coming from above, don't come in too fast from the side) and jumping off as quickly as possible. You can also avoid the mines by standing on the very edge of a bounceblock. This is difficult and unreliable, so I don't reccomend trying to stand still, but landing near the corners can give you a bit more leeway with your jumps.

This level is by bufar, but I edited it slightly to show that you can avoid mines even when they're right inside the bounceblock you're trying to jump off.

Wading Pool (Qix)
Shows how to push bounceblocks out of the way. The first one is the hardest. I reccomend running back and forth between the bounceblocks (remember to jump over the gap or you'll lose speed) until you've got some speed up. Then run into the right bounceblock, and just before it starts pushing you back jump furiously (still holding right). You should be able to squeeze past. Next, head up to the exit switch. You'll need to force your way past by performing rapid walljumps. To get back down, fall on the block from a great height, and keep moving sideways slightly while you're on it. You should fall through (note that you'll sometimes do this by accident in other levels). Since bounceblocks don't always return perfectly to their original position, you may also be able to push the block aside by running along the ground. For the next block, just drop onto it from a decent height and run out. Now, for the final section, there are many close packed blocks. The trick is to try and force yourself into the gaps between them, rather than straight into the blocks. Jumping furiously may also help, but for the thinner barriers timing and good aim will probably be more useful.

Linear Algebra
Lasers are fairly simple. They take a little while to charge up, they fire in a straight line, and they don't change their aim once they've locked on. Note that they have to rest for a brief period after firing in addition to charging, which will give you a little more time to get where you're going. And remember that the best way to get around them is generally to make them fire the wrong way then nip past while they're torching empty space.

Laser Pointer (Qix)
Shows how to get past a laser in a long, narrow shaft. Stand just close enough to one edge for the laser to fire, then slide down the opposite side of the shaft. As soon as it stops, drop from the wall to make it past. Note that most shafts are short enough for you to just drop past.

Target Acquired
A brief introduction to homing missiles, which will detenonate on tiles and doors, but not bounceblocks, one-ways, etc. Remember, they have limited speed and turning radii. Moving quickly will let you avoid them, particularly if you pass them while close - they'll lose time turning around. This is also a good way to guide them into walls and floors. Note that trying to turn around while a missle is near is often a bad idea, since it takes you a while to accelerate, but remember that walljumping can help you change direction quickly if you need to. Also, remember that there are times when it's advantageous to prevent a rocket hitting the walls - sometimes it's easier to avoid a rocket trailing behind you (after all, you can just run away from it...) and sometimes the laucher is in the way and you need to stop it firing (each launcher will only have one rocket in existence at once).

These Puppies Bite (Qix)
Floorguards for all! They're fairly simple - they just charge towards you when you're at the same height and there are no tiles in the way. Note that they can't change direction until they reach the edge of the platform or any non-flat tile - you can sometimes use this to give you a bit of extra time. Note also that they don't particularly care about doors, and will come straight through them. To avoid them, either run very quickly away from them (walljumping or deflection from slopes/curves will give you a bit of momentum if you don't have room to accelerate) or just jump over them - if there's room.

I Need More Space (Zres)
Introduction to Chaingun Drones. Unlike lasers, they'll still aim after they start charging. To avoid being shot, you need to move out of the way *just* before they fire. Or find something to lurk behind. Also, remember that their aim drifts slightly while firing. It's actually possible to slip between bullets, but I don't recommend trying to do it deliberately.

Tiptoe
Yes, you can stand on the points of those sloped tiles. It's quite tricky, however. Try to land with the ninja's centre right above the point, not too much momentum, and jump again as soon as possible so you don't tip off. This one's probably going to take some practice, I'm afraid.

That's Not Normal (thecalcgenius)
Somewhat similar to Tiptoe - you can stand on top of doors, even the ones that open when you approach. Keep the momentum as low as you can, but make sure you go high enough for them to close.

Precision (Sketch)
Beginners often have trouble walljumping off a half tile. Timing and practice are necessary, but many also find it easier to get some speed up and jump towards the tile, as is shown at the beginning of the demo.

Gripping the Ungrippable (Qix)
If you land on the exact top of a curve, it will be considered flat and you won't slip down. In a similar fashion, you can do a normal walljump off the side of a curve. It's fairly straightforward, but requires precise aim. Just treat it as a normal walljump, but make sure you hit jump when you're next to the vertical side of the curve. I find a little sideways momentum makes the timing easier.

Slippery Sides (Sketch)
Shows how to climb a wall with overhangs - this feature is common in jumping puzzles, but the technique is also useful in other maps. When you're trying to jump around an overhang, make sure you don't hold toward the wall when jumping - you'll go higher and wider.

All That Glitters
As requested, how to jump on diamond-shaped blocks. For shallow and middle slopes, don't aim for the centre - it's hard to maintain control on the point. Land on the sides instead. As with circular blocks, hold towards the middle to stay on, or jump quickly. Remember the slope jumps you've learned - it will make it easier to get where you're going, and you can often skip some areas. For the steep slopes, your best bet is to hop from point to point, as in Tiptoe, unless you have a little upslope momentum, which will stop you sliding off too quickly. However, if you don't already have upwards momentum, you won't be able to jump very high from the slopes and you'll fall off very quickly.

Clear Shot (Jeca)
Gauss turrets can take a bit of practice to get used to. Even if they can hit you, they won't fire unless their crosshair is within a certain distance (NOT exactly on you) and they have had time to focus. The crosshair will focus while it's pointed in your general direction, and will lose focus (or focus more slowly) if you're moving very quickly, hidden behind something solid (tiles, doors), or if the angle between you and the turret changes radically. Note that it stays focused after a shot, so if you're still nearby, the turret will fire again quite quickly. Their aim is a little slow, so jumping out of the way at the last minute or falling/running quickly past the crosshair is generally OK. The exception is when moving directly towards or away from the gauss, since even though the shot is aimed at a point behind (or in front of) you, you'll still be in the line of fire. Note also that, since jumping back and forth in a narrow space won't alter the angle between you and the turret much, it will still focus on you. Remember that the crosshair changes slightly and there is a charging noise before firing, which will give you some warning. Eventually, you'll be able to predict when a turret will fire without these signs, which is just as well because you need to watch where you're going.

Oh, and the section with the mines is a little tricky. If you're a beginner, don't be bothered too much if you can't finish it. And you'll probably find the bounceblock jumps from Trampoline useful in the second section.

One-and-a-Half Ways (Ngaged)
This shows how to exploit a problem with the collision detection for one-way platforms. If you walljump while you're just below a downward-facing one-way, you can jump right through it. It takes a bit of practice to get the timing right, though.

I'm A Mime! (Dark Ball Y-E + Atilla)
More collision bugs with one-ways - they don't work properly on some slopes, and and you can collide with them even when it looks like you shouldn't, forming an invisible wall. Putting one-ways inside walls like this is generally considered poor design, precisely because it messes up the collision detection.

In the first corridor, the one-ways in the floor will stop you just walking through. Jump over them to get past. Then, jump up the shaft whilst holding towards the left wall. As long as you keep holding left, you'll get caught on the one-ways inside the wall - allowing you to climb up without hitting the mines. Next, just fall down the other shaft and saunter casually through the one-way on the slope - it won't effect you unless you jump into it. Finally, inch along (and, indeed, right off the edge) of the last one-way so that you can jump into the shaft. This is one of the more irritating bugs - if you try to drop past a one-way, you'll occasionally find yourself standing on it instead.

Porous (jtbandes)
Another bug with one-ways - it's possible to tip through them if they're placed at the edge of a tile, which can be used to cheat some levels. The first one should be fairly easy - just walk towards the gap slowly enough for you to tip over the edge, as in Feeling Tipsy. Repeat to pass the second section. If you want to get the gold on the left, stand on the slope above the entrance, and slide down slowly whilst holding towards it. You should fall through the one-way. For the third section, you can get the gold on the right by jumping so that you just catch the edge of the tile. You should hold towards the tile, of course, and you should also try to keep your momentum low (scraping the underside of the tile is a good way to do this). It's quite difficult, so don't expect to get it first try. The fourth section should be handled the same way as the others, but it's more difficult because of the steep slope. You'll have to jump onto the slope. Mind you don't go too high, or you'll land on the one-way instead (and remember the collision bugs from "I'm a Mime!" - even if it doesn't look like you're going to hit the one-way, you'll still land on it) . The final section is similar to the area with the extra gold in the third - try and land right on the corner of the tile, and keep the upward momentum low. Make sure you come from beneath, not above - you'll just land on the one-way otherwise. Finally, slip through the last two one-ways, just like you did for the gold in the second and fourth sections.

Tunnelling Phenomena
It's possible to squeeze through some small gaps - if you can get the right angle and enough speed. The first one should be easy - just fall onto the slope and run down. For the second, take a running jump into the gap, then hit jump again when you're partway through (jumping upslope will give you more speed, remember). The third is similar, but you're going to have to walljump into it, and since you'll probably have less momentum, you'll need to get your aim and timing better. For the fourth, jump to the top and slightly to the left of the gap, then fall into it moving slightly downhill. It will probably take a few tries to get the angle right, and watching the demo will be helpful at this point. Anyway, the last one should be fairly simple - jump into the gap with a bit of horizontal momentum and just run through.

'Gainst Whom No Lock May Stand (Ngaged)
It's difficult. Very difficult. But it's possible to jump through the locked doors. I recommend rapping jump at an incredible rate, although some might prefer good timing. When you watch the demo, maximize N so you can see me shoot through the roof at a ridiculous speed.

Unlocking the Unlockable (Dark Ball Y-E)
You've probably seen gold delay used in DDAs. Well, due to the same quirk of collision detection, you hit only one switch when there are two on top of each other, though it will require very good timing. I find the easiest way is to wall jump just as you touch the switch, but you can also clip it as you fall or jump past. Note that this also applies to gold and mines, and that it works when there's more than two objects on top of each other as well.

I Retract That Statement
That is, the one where I said I couldn't do corner kicks, let alone instuct others...

Ahem. For those who don't know, it's possible to jump further and higher than normal if you take a flying leap into the corner of a tile and hit jump just as you hit it. As you can imagine, this requires near perfect timing, and even skilled players have trouble with it. The one in this level is set up at a convenient distance and height, so it should be a little easier than normal. As usual, they key is practice. Loads of it.

You can also kick off the convex curves in much the same way. This is often easier than a corner kick (though not so much in this map, because the height and distance aren't quite so nicely marked for you).

I Reverse That Statement (Qix)
It's also possible to do a reverse corner kick, which will send you upwards and slightly backwards. It's done pretty much the same way as a forwards corner kick, but you should release left/right (or press the opposite direction, if you prefer) just before you kick.

Revenge of the Corner Kick (Qix)
Next week, we'll be showing the Return of the Revenge of the Son of the Corner Kick, Part II.

Anyway, it's also possible to do a falling corner kick, for extra distance and little height. Fall away from the corner, then just before you hit it press towards it and jump. If you get it, make sure you press left again straight away or you won't make the distance.

Hello, my naem is... (scythe33)

It is possible to launch yourself a long way horizontally when doing a super jump from a launchpad. This definitely one of the hardest tricks in the book, if not the hardest. It's almost impossible to do it every time, and there are different "degrees" of the jump, with one of the most extreme being necessary to complete this level. The easiest way is to hit the launchpad diagonally, as shown in the demo. You need to be a little bit away from the wall, or it'll just be a normal launchpad superjump, and you've gotta hit jump quickly, because otherwise he'll be too far away from the wall. I can't stress this "a hair away from the wall" part too much - you can't be falling next to it.

...

Any suggestions, comments, requests or questions are welcome, of course. And if any experienced players have suitable levels, please send them to me with a demo and brief description.

#177522 2 2006-05-19T00:32:51Z Atilla
Do you have a working NUMA account? If not, create one by opening N, going to the configure menu, filling in the boxes in the bottom right, and clicking "Create new user".

Once you have an account, go to NUMA and sign in. Then click on "Submit map". Fill in the level description, name, type, and so on. For the level data, use the raw data N produces (NOT "$Name#Author#Type#Raw data#" like you would in your userlevels.txt).
#177554 32 2006-05-19T01:46:45Z Atilla
@ian: That's my point. Acceleration due to the curvature of spacetime is not distinguished from acceleration due to other forces. Therefore, if a universe curved back on itself, the twins paradox would not arise because you still can't get back to your starting point without accelerating.
#177556 3 2006-05-19T01:50:37Z Atilla
Also, make sure that the syntax is correct. Each level should have the format "$Name#Author#Type#data#". If you leave the # off the end, for example (easy to do) the levels after it won't show up correctly. If this doesn't work, check if any of your level titles have unusual punctuation in them (&, #, $...) and remove it.

#180242 5 2006-05-25T10:33:24Z Atilla
Open debug mode (Ned). Paste the level data into the imaginitively named "Level data" box, and load the level (L). Then paste the replay data into the replay box (check the level's page on NUMA. If there's no replays, ask at the forums), load it by pressing 3, hit Q to initiate playback, then P to start watching. And make sure caps lock is on.

Alternately, paste the replay and level data into the replay box in the userlevels menu using the syntax "$Levelname#Author#Category#leveldata#demodata#". If you're not sure what I mean, follow the St Atilla's College link in my sig and look at the .txt file attached to the first post.

I've thought about this before, except: everyone finds yellow as more difficult to read against a white background than the other colours. That sort of disproves it for me (plus, the emotional connections with colours, ie. blue = cool).

To others, yellow may look like what you think blue does, but they still find it difficult to read because of the design of their eyes and brain. Despite what many people believe, much of what you actually "see" is created and/or erased by guesswork and extrapolation by the brain. Otherwise your vision would be covered with a network of veins and odd diffraction patterns. And there'd be a hole near the centre of your vision where the optic nerve connects to the retina. Anyway, many colour associations are conditioned - for example, things which are hot often glow red or orange, so it would be rather odd not to associate the colour with heat - even it it looked green instead of red.

How To Select the Level Data Easily (For Windows):

1. Go to the end of the level entry.

3. Place the cursor in front of the #

5. Hold shift and hit right a few times to deselect the name, author etc.

#181665 7 2006-05-29T01:13:52Z Atilla
"Evolution" in the general sense means that something changes gradually, usually to a superior state (otherwise a word such as "degeneration" or "decline" would be used).

In biology, the Theory of Evolution postulates that organisms may change from generation to generation due to pressures on reproduction. This is in turn based on several observations:

1. There is variation in organisms. Even within a species, not all members are identical.

2. Some of these variants are traits which may be beneficial/harmful to an organism's chance/rate of reproduction and/or survival.

3. These traits may be inherited by the offspring of an organism.

4. Current organisms are the result of this process.

The Theory of Evolution doesn't really include the spontaneous generation of life, since it deals with what happens when you already have organisms. However, the process of evolution may be used to describe the developement of self-replicating particles which could not yet be considered life. Note also that it is important to distinguish the general theory from other, more specific theories - for example, punctuated equilibrium.

The process of evolution is a fact (that is, it can be observed - as in the breeding of dogs, the appearance of new bacteria which are resistant to old antibiotics, etc.) and may also be used to describe more general cases where selective pressures effect the propagation of a design, idea or variant. For example, computer chips and artificial intelligence have been developed by producing random variations, selecting the ones which most resemble the behaviour you want, then generating another batch with minor variations and mixtures of the selected specimens and repeating the process until you get something that works well. You could also speak of cultural evolution and how ideas that have traits which will result in their being propagated are more likely to be enduring and widely known. From a purely sociological viewpoint, religions are a fine example.

And please, please remember that the words "fact" and "theory" have different meanings in science to everyday use.

#181731 2 2006-05-29T07:05:22Z Atilla
You're probably loading the demos incorrectly. Either that or your browser is corrupting the data.

Anyway, try the following:

1. Open N, go to debug mode, and load the level, as normal.
2. Go to NUMA and click in the textbox with the demo.
3. Press Ctrl+A to select all the data. Unless you're using a Mac, in which case I believe it's Cmd+A or somesuch instead.
4. Copy the data with Ctrl+C or the equivalent command for Macs.
5. Switch back to N and select all the data in the demo box by clicking in it and hitting Ctrl+A again.
6. Press Ctrl+V to paste the demo data you copied earlier over the junk data in the box.
7. Click outside the text box.
8. Press 3 to load the demo, Q to begin playback, and P to start watching it. And make sure caps lock is on.

If this doesn't work, look at the data you're pasting and make sure it is a similar format to this:

235:0|33554432|139810|etc|etc|lots|more|numbers|and|vertical|bars

If it isn't, you have a problem. Try using a different web browser.

The legal definition of meat also includes pretty much everything that isn't classified as 'offal' (brain, heart, kidneys etc.), meaning snouts, tendons and blood vessels can be used to fill a meat pie. #9164 1 2006-06-01T02:01:10Z Atilla
Previously it has been suggested that one might be able to create folders to keep userlevels organised. Instead, I propose that N be able to handle multiple text files instead of just userlevels.txt.

It would work like this. Instead of loading userlevels.txt when you enter the userlevels menu, there would be file called include.txt or somesuch, which would contain something like

&files=
"userlevels.txt"
"legacy.txt"
"LA^3.txt"
"atilla_and_co_training.txt"
"my_levels.txt"

The userlevels menu would parse this file, and display the file names like it currently does the levels (maybe descriptions/authors could also be included). Clicking on one of the files would then load the levels from that file as is currently done for userlevels.txt. Of course, a "change file" button would be added to the level menu, allowing you to go back and select a different one.

This seems technically feasible, and shouldn't require too much extra programming (particularly since you should be able to grab most of the code from the already-existing functions for parsing userlevels.txt). It would also have a large number of benefits - it would be *very* useful for level packs, it would let you keep things organised, it prevents parsing a large amount of unnecessary data, and it prevents me having to constantly rename a buch of text files. The only downside I can see is that it might be little confusing to newbies, but then, the current system isn't terribly user-friendly, either.

EDIT: Since it doesn't actually mess with the userlevels file, the level data, or the parsing itself, it would also be totally backwards compatible.

Thoughts, anyone? Is this impossible for some technical reason I haven't thought of? Is it just too much programming?

Quote: Qix, June 04, 2006 08:47 am
How should the two shepherds fairly divide this money?

Go to court to ensure fair division of assets, and end up giving it all to the lawyers?

(The real answer is that the shepherd who had 5 loaves should get 7 coins and the other only one. 8 loaves among 3 people means two and two-thirds of a loaf each. The shepherd with 3 loaves therefore gives one-third of a loaf to the hunter, and the shepherd with five gives 2 and 1/3 loaves (that's seven thirds). Between them they have given the hunter eight-thirds of loaf, seven of which belong to shepherd who had five loaves. So he gets seven eighths of the money.)

#184385 19 2006-06-04T05:48:58Z Atilla
Quote: Keron Cyst, June 04, 2006 02:02 pm
Well, Wells' The Invisible Man has it so the person who was successfully able to render himself invisible (through chemicals he drank, not a cloaking device as the article says) was able to see because his corneas were very, very faint but not completely invisibleso if you had extremely good eyesight you would be able to see two tiny dots moving around the room (and would probably think you were hallucinating or something ).

His corneas? The cornea is the clear bit on the front of your eye, and is supposed to be transparent. I believe you mean the retinas.

Anyway, you'd still be near-blind. And the light wouldn't be focused at all because your lenses and corneas would still be invisible. "But aren't they transparent anyway?" you may ask. Yes, but you can still see them, in the same way you can see glass objects - because they refract the light passing through them. To be invisible they would have to cause no rerfraction. (Incidentally, baby oil has about the same refrective index as a lot of glass. So, if you get a jug, put a glass in it, then fill the jug with baby oil, the glass becomes virtually invisible. It looks particularly weird when you use a beaker with markings on the side - it seems like they're floating in the middle of the jug.)

Quote: Trogdor007, June 06, 2006 11:16 am
I'm sorry... What is malware?

Malware is an abbreviation for "malicious software", and includes adware (generates pop-ups constantly, changes your homepage, etc), spyware (reports your browsing habits, personal information to someone via the net - which slows down you browsing because it eats bandwidth), viruses, and various others. Adware and spyware are more common than viruses, but usually also less harmful to your computer (although perhaps not your privacy). Unfortunately, there's a distinct lack of security software for Macs, so if you do get infected annoyingly difficult to fix. My badminton racquet is made of graphite. I wouldn't recommend eating it.

And calling pencil graphite pencil lead for historical reasons is far from the worst case of linguistic imprecision in English. For example, Catholic priests are called "Father" despite being celibate, and despite the cliche many people call a spade a shovel. A steam engine is produces steam, but a fire engine doesn't produce fires. A metal rod is made of metal, but a lightning rod isn't made of lightning. Wineglasses are often made of plastic or crystal instead of glass, depending on your financial state. If you live in America, the "silverware" is probably really stainless steel. Which can, in fact, be stained, although it doesn't rust quite so easily as normal steel or iron. And "irony" does not describe something kind of like iron. And so on. And on. You get the point.

Ok, here's another thought for a level. Make a map that shows new players that objects can be hidden under other objects. You could make the exit switch have a trapdoor underneath like in 00-1.

#189293 11 2006-06-14T12:11:51Z Atilla
Listen closely, young'uns, to the story I am about to tell you, for I shall speak of Clovic and how he brought suffering into the world.

A long, long time ago, when the world was new and fresh, all manner of animals lived in peace, including humans. No animal hurt or killed another and for a time, everyone was happy. Except for plants and fungi, which were being eaten at an alarming rate due to the uniform vegetarianism, but nobody cares about them anyway. They're not like us, after all.

There was, amongst the humans, one called Clovic. One day, young Clovic looked around and thought that, although all animals were equal, some were clearly more equal than others. Humans were not as agile as cats or as strong as bears, nor as numerous as rabbits or insects, nor did they have dogs' wonderful sense of smell, nor could they fly like the birds or swim like the fish or change colour like the chameleon, except when it was cold and they went an unhealthy shade of purple, for they had no fur and had to huddle together for warmth. The animals were always very polite about this, but Clovic believed they secretly sneered at the weak, fragile humans.

So, one day, after an ant had been particularly and infuriatingly polite to him, Clovic decided he would even things up. He remarked casually to the birds that the insects had been saying rather unkind things about them - he was shocked, of course - and that they might wish to have a chat about it. The insects denied this, of course, and so the birds returned to Clovic, asking why he had said such things. "Well, of course they'd tell you that", he replied, and went on to describe in detail just what the insects had been saying. So crafty were his words that the birds were infuriated, and immediately set upon the insects and devoured them.

Realising what they had done, they were horrified. But Clovic went to the insects, and said "Look what the birds have done to you. They have devoured your family and friends, and for what reason? You must teach them a lesson. Go forth, bite and sting, show them the price they must pay for destroying the peace." And so the insects did. The birds, who were feeling guilty and were just on their way to apologise most humbly, were attacked by a fearsome swarm of insects; and they said "Look at the treachery of the insects! They are our enemies after all, and we are right to eat them." And so, even now, the emnity between birds and insects remains.

Clovic continued in this manner, spreading dissent and hatred amongst all the creatures, so that bear hunted fish, fox hunted rabbit, and even amongst their own species, animals would know jealousy and envy, and fight their brothers for the lion's share (which is why the lion tries to eat so many mammals these days). And when killing was accepted, and all the animals fought and feared each other, Clovic took up a stick, and sharpened it; and seeing the warm hides of the other mammals, which he had always envied, he killed them and took their fur for himself, that humans would no longer have to fear the cold. However, there were some animals he could not bear to kill; the dogs and cats, who were humans' loyal friends, and who had huddled together with the humans to keep them warm. And so these creatures remained friends of humans, and are to this day.

Then the gods of the world, who had popped out for morning tea, returned and saw the havoc that Clovic had wrought. And though they could not repair the shattered peace, they decreed that Clovic should be punished for his crimes. And so Clovic was filled with all the pain and grief of the world, which he had wrought on other creatures and must now suffer until peace returned. And so Clovic wanders the world in despair, even as we speak, seeking to end the emnity between all animals.

And that is the story of how Clovic became the first emo.

---

I'm so sorry, Clovic, but I couldn't resist... and it's no more evil than all the other emo jokes.

#194623 10 2006-06-26T03:23:26Z Atilla
Quote: Keron Cyst, June 25, 2006 06:17 pm
Evolution dictates that if it isn't useful, it shall be thrown out.
No, no, no! That's not how evolution works! You're thinking of it from an "intelligent design" perspective. Contrary to the slogan, evolution is not "survival of the fittest", merely "survival of the fit enough". As long as an extra finger isn't killing you, it'll probably hang around - the species doesn't think "Hey, this finger is unneccesary. Let's get rid of it". Not all evolved features are optimal - otherwise no further evolution could occur. Many just happen by sheer chance. For example, the crossed air and food pipes of land animals lead to choking, and are clearly not the best design imaginable. But we have them because that was the mutation that first lead to air-breathing life. At the time this windpipe developed, there was no competition on land, so you could happily survive and thrive even with your ill-designed breathing apparatus. By the time the land was heavily populated enough for competition to play a significant part, the crossed pipes were prevalent. Of course, it's possible that a mutation with seperate eating and breating pipes could occur, but other factors would be more important since choking was not a primary cause of death. The numerical superiority of the crossed-pipe creatures would mean they would overwhelm the non-crossed lineage, because the advantage afforded by the latter was too small. Fingers are a similar case; we had to have some finite number of fingers, and it turned out to be five. Since we now have numerical superiority to the six-fingered mutation, and they recieve no significant advantages from their extra finger, we will form the majority until there is some pressing need for extra fingers (or, in a freak accident, a meteor wipes out 99% of the five-fingers and leaves the six-fingers unscathed). Since it's not actually killing them either, six-fingered people can (and do) exist as a minority.

As for 3... that's one of the worst arguments I've heard. Firstly, not only are cells not conscious, but evolution is not a conscious process. Fish do not suddenly decide "Hey, I wonder what's on the land? Let's grow some legs and see!" Nor does evolution have a definite end point or goal, or because being alive is in some way more enjoyable than being dead, so creatures want to live. One of the common misconceptions about evolution is that it is driven by some kind of imperative to reach a state which is "desirable" or "superior" in some way, which is entirely untrue; it is merely a byproduct of how the world works. Consider flipping a coin twice. You may end up with one head and one tail, two heads, or two tails. The first is the most likely; if you repeated it a million times, you would expect that there you would end up with one head and one tail more often than with two heads, or two tails. This does not mean that the macrostate with one head and one tail is somehow superior, merely that it is more prevalent because of the laws of statistics. This is also the priciple behind entropy and much of thermodynamics.

Quote: Banannakid, June 26, 2006 12:20 pm
That doesn't make sense. Nothing is contributing to the universe's intertia anymore, but friction is helping to slow it down and gravity is slowing it down, too, and will pull being to pull it all back together.

But not fast enough - gravity drops off with distance, remember. Say, for example, that a particle's speed starts at one and decreases by half its current value each second (not realistic, but nice and simple). So, initially s = 1. After 1 second, s = 1/2. After two, it equals 1/4. After 5, s = 1/32. After 8, s = 1/256. After 10, s = 1/1024. Note that, although the speed of the particle is always decreasing, and the particle ends up going extremely slowly, it is still moving away and will continue to do so until an infinite number of seconds have passed (in other words, forever).
#195103 16 2006-06-27T01:36:54Z Atilla
Things like this are the reason you have to be careful about saying things like infinity/infinity = 1. It's not neccesarily true, because infinity is a process rather than a number.

Consider the functions y=10x and z=5x. lim y as x-> infinity = infinity. lim z as x -> infinity = infinity. However (lim y)/(lim z) = 2, not 1. It's a common mistake in exams...

Quote: Banannakid, June 26, 2006 02:06 pm
That's not how it works. The friction doesn't discriminate according to the amount of kinetic energy in the object in question. The speed doesn't decrease reverse exponentially (or what ever the term is). Otherwise, you could roll a ball and it would remain rolling indefinantly if left to its own devices.

Not only is friction working on the expanding universe, but gravity is as well.
It was a simplified example to prevent integrals. And friction occurs between objects in direct physical contact which are moving relative to each other and opposes the direction of motion, so it certainly does depend on the velocity of the objects. The effects of gravity on the object will reduce with time because the object is moving further away, at a rate which is dependent on the velocity - which is why I just approximated a = -v/2.

Time for integrals, from scratch, because 1. I screwed up last time 2. I was viciously attacked by the word filter and 3. I think I can explain it better using a slightly different approach.

Ahem. The force due to gravity, F, = GMm/r^2. To find the amount of energy needed to move an object from some initial distance r[i] to r = infinity, we integrate the force due to gravity from r[i] to r = infinity. An object at r = infinity will experience no gravitational acceleration, since GMm/(infinity^2) = 0; therefore it will not slow down any further.

∫ GMm/r^2 dr between r[i] and infinity (if only I could stick the terminals in as well...)
= GMm ∫ 1/r^2 dr btwn r[i] and inf.
= GMm[-1/r] btwn r[i] and inf.
= GMm(1/inf. - 1/r[i])
1/inf = 0, so
GMm(1/inf. - 1/r[i]) = -GMm/r[i]. (It's negative because it's a potential energy.)

Now, if we have more kinetic energy then GMm/r[i], we have enough energy to move the object to an infinite distance and some left over - it will still be moving away, and no longer decelerating. In practice, of course, you're never an infinite distance away from something. However, since you have enough energy to keep going until you reach infinity (never) you'll just keep getting further and further away forever.

Much better. Hopefully the brackets will remain in tact this time.

#197337 174 2006-07-01T06:21:40Z Atilla
Whether Buddhism is a religion or not is uniportant at this stage, since you were discussing evidence of Christ's divinity; specifically, I believe the fufillment of prophecies was the issue, with maximo saying he thought it was too unlikely for someone to fulfill the prophecies Christ did by chance.

Firstly, let us consider the general nature of the prophecies. For a starting point, prophecies predicting the birthplace and lineage of the Messiah have been mentioned. As I see it, it is not unreasonable to assume these requirements will be fulfilled by many potential saviours; after all, many people are born in any given area, and many people share a lineage. To paraphrase Morrowind: "So you are born on a certain day of uncertain parents. But there are many who share your birthday, and many who do not know their parents. This does not make you the Nerevarine, but you are one who may become the Nerevarine."

Anyway, the important thing is that we end up with a pool of potential Messiahs, of size uncertain. Then come prophecies about things that should happen to the Messiah, or that the Messiah should do. As has been pointed out, some of these could be fulfilled deliberately, while some would depend more on either chance or divine guidance, and some are more likely than others. For example, it was prophesized that the Messiah would be beaten before he was crucified. Now, given the history of casual violence associated with many military and police groups, I would not consider it suprising or at all unlikely that a prisoner would be beaten before execution. As has been previously stated, crucifixion was not uncommon. Then, of course, there are the less likely prophecies; I believe maximo, for instance, mentioned that it was predicted that none of the Messiah's bones would be broken, and that broken bones were the norm for those who are crucified. Ultimately, it becomes a question of whether the number of potential Messiahs since the prophecies were first spoken is high enough for it to be more likely that someone would have fulfilled the prophecies than not. With our current knowledge, I do not believe it is a question that can be adequately answered; and even if it could, it would not be undeniable proof. It is entirely possible that a billion-to-one chance comes up on the first try, or that a 50-50 chance fails 100 times. Then, of course, there is the possibility that the evidence of our senses is not actually correct (please insert Matrix reference here). And I think I'll stop at this point before I wander too far into a discussion of agnosticism.

I would also like to point out that evolution and creationism are not mutually exclusive, despite what many people think. For example, it has been said that God is instrisically logical. Would it be so far-fetched, then, to believe that God created our universe, subject to logical physical laws, and did not interfere with these laws for miracles and suchlike? After all, since He is all-knowing and almighty, He would have forseen that humans would eventually evolve and come up with Christianity. God still would have created humanity - just by using the laws of physics, rather than breaking them.

#9859 1 2006-07-03T03:57:25Z Atilla
Now, as far as I'm concerned, science and religion are NOT opposed to each other. Certain theories or observations may sometimes contradict Holy Text X, but that doesn't mean science and religion are by their very natures opposed; even close friends disagree sometimes.

What some people fail to understand is that science is simply a system for predicting and modelling physical systems based on empirical observations. No more, no less. It cannot be used to prove or disprove the existence of the supernatural or spiritual because it deals only with the physical. That said, it may be used to disprove beliefs about the physical world which are associated with certain beliefs about the spiritual; the traditional example is the belief that Earth is at the centre of the universe.

People also often forget that science is based on observations and evidence, and there is always the chance that accepted theories will change based on new observations and better evidence. Scientists to not claim to be arbiters of ultimate truth, and what is proven today may be debunked in fifty years (or, more likely, modified until it works). Take gravity, for example; it used to be thought that Newton's theory of gravity was all you needed to know. Then Einstein came along with relativity, which explained what Newton's theories did not. But that doesn't mean Newton's ideas were foolish or stupid. They work very well for everyday objects, and are still commonly used. Similarly, classical mechanics don't work on a quantum level, but are still fine for everyday calculations. Furthermore, scientific theories descirbe what is currently thought to be the most accurate or most likely explanation, rather than some kind of ultimate truth.

As such, don't go around saying "I'm not religious because I believe in Science". That's treating science as a religion, which it most certainly is not. "Believing in" something implies that you have faith, and faith should not be part of science; as I said earlier, it is a system which is rooted in evidence and observations. Scientists even calculate the odds that their experimental results were a fluke, and how much they can expect results to deviate from a prediction due to inaccuracy of equipment, minor uncontrolled variables (gravity is slightly different depending where you are on Earth's surface, for instance) and so on. You can believe a specific theory is correct, or believe that the scientific method is a good way of doing things, but don't go around capitalising science and saying you Believe as if it's some kind of monolithic entity you can throw your faith behind.

Also, please refrain from saying "Oh, scientists disagreed/changed their mind once, so they're unreliable", "This one experiment went wrong, so the whole technique is unreliable" or "It's only a THEORY". Firstly, it is good that scientists change their minds; it means that when something doesn't fit the evidence, a better explanation is found. The newly accepted hypothesis is likely to be more reliable and more accurate than than the old one. Constantly changing and refining accepted theory makes science more reliable, not less. Secondly, please learn the correct technical usage of "theory". In science, a theory is an explanation which has been extensively tested and verified by many independent sources (and the details of the experiments conducted by said sources have been examined by still others, and the experiment has been shown to be repeatable). Theories are therefore among the most reliable parts of scientific knowledge. This extensive testing process also catches out flukely results, due to an error in the experiment, problems with equipment, misinterpretation of results, and so on.

Finally, don't get in a huff because scientific theories disagree with your personal beliefs. Scientists are just reporting what they observe, and as I have stated earlier, scientific explanations are restricted to the purely physical. If the most likely physical explanation for the facts is not the same as your spiritual explanation, then just consider that their explanation works as best it can within the restraints of science. Even if it's not actually true, it lets them predict a few useful things, and that's the important part. At this point, someone will no doubt complain that scientists deliberately ignore the supernatural, and therefore promote atheism. No, they do not. Science is restricted to the physical because it is useless otherwise. If supernatural explanations are allowed, any observation can be explained as the whim of a deity, and there can be no predictions; after all, what man can fathom the mind of a god?

So, in short, science describes the physical world, and religion the spiritual, and for the most part, they don't intersect. Scientists are not trying to determine how much an evil act weighs (how many can you perform before your heart outweighs a feather? And what kind of feather is it?), or to calculate exactly how hot the fires of hell are. Nor do religions attempt to calculate the efficiency of a Carnot cycle between resevoirs at 600K and 300K. Occasionally, things wander into an area which some think is physical and others think is spiritual, and then there is a clash of opinions; however, this by no means implies that science and religion are fundamentally opposed.

Also, please read my previous rant on a similar topic.

Quote: Atilla, 2006-07-03T03:57:25Z
What some people fail to understand is that science is simply a system for predicting and modelling physical systems based on empirical observations. No more, no less. It cannot be used to prove or disprove the existence of the supernatural or spiritual because it deals only with the physical.

As soon as you start bringing gods into it, it's not science anymore. Also, one of the primary goals of the scientific method is to keep things as objective as possible. Applying an external agenda - in this case, a Christian one - is likely to introduce bias and thus invalidate any observations.

Christian Scientists believe that illness is the result of fear, ignorance or sin, and can be cured solely by prayer and meditation. They also believe that the world which we commonly consider "real" is actually an illusion created because we cannot properly comprehend the true, spiritual world, among other things.

EDIT: This is another reason why one should not capitalise "science" indiscriminately. A Christian Scientist is very different from a Christian scientist.

Bias in science makes it less reliable and less useful, and should be avoided whenever possible; you will note that I said applying any external agenda is detrimental, and that in this case it happened to be a Christian agenda. Obviously, this is not an ideal world, and there will always be some bias in any human undertaking, but this does not mean we should just give up and allow any manner of bias to proliferate. Scientists often go to considerable lengths to try to minimise their own unconscious bias - for example, you may have heard of the double-blind proceedure, in which a researcher prevents him/herself coming into contact with an experiment's human participants in case he/she influences them without being aware of it (eg. through body language, slight modulations of voice).

Another example would be the 'tainted research' conducted by many companies which wish to advertise the product as "clinically/scientifically proven". Even disregarding the often flawed or obviously biased nature of the experiments themselves, many companies will throw away 1000 reports saying their product doesn't work, keep the one that indicates it does (despite the fact that the researches themselves say something interfered with the experiment) and claim the product is "proven". That's not proper science. Other forms of bias are equally detrimental.

And, I say once again, science can not be used to prove of disprove the existance of supernatural entities. Anyone who attempts to use it in this manner, whatever their religious affiliation, is displaying a blatant disregard and/or lack of understanding of the nature of science, and the reasons this nature must be upheld.

They both have advantages and disadvantages. My way prevents N having to examine every text file in the folder. Because the file names are being read from one source, and the name of every file you're going to read will be explicitly stated, the code will probably be easier to read and maintain. However, it's somewhat incovenient for the user since they are required to edit mysterious text files. Yours prevents this, making it easier to use. But it is also less efficient, and punctuation in some text files could cause errors. This would either have to be coded around, or all .txt documentation would need to be placed in a seperate folder.

Roll up, roll up, see the Amazing Atilla and his Quintilogy of Five!

DOWNLOAD! The text file!

PLAY! The levels!

GASP! At the 'Shroom of Doom!

STARE! At the needlessly dramatic level names!

CURSE! That ----ing drone. You know, the one that gets you every time, which I put there specifically to annoy you, not people in general, but you personally.

TELL ME! that I'm a talentless hack (or, alternately SCREAM! my name and THROW! underwear at the stage)!

SWOON! At the fact that I actually managed to make this many levels. It's almost more than I have on NUMA.

FLAIL WILDLY WHILST MAKING CHICKEN NOISES! For no good reason. Be sure to record it and post the video.

Questions That Haven't Been Asked Frequently But Undoubtably Will Be:

Q: WTF?!

A: A small cottage made of teapots.

Q: How do I distinguish a level pack from other packs?

A: Thrust your hand vigourously towards it. If your arm suddenly goes AWOL, it's a pack of wolves. If your fingers are kissed, you're talking to a politician, and it is therefore a pack of lies. If it ends up spread over the table, the floor, the bench, and the person sitting opposite you, it's a pack of cards. If you discover that you've just destroyed your $700 computer monitor, it's a level pack.

Q: Is this actually any good?

A: Play it and see. Some levels are good. Some are not so good. Many are debatable, depending on your tastes. This level pack is somewhat quick and experimental - if there are a significant number of levels that people like, I will consider making another pack with more exacting standards.

Q: How come you made a level pack?

A: Because I felt like it. Also, it lets you distribute levels which would not be appreciated on a "stand-alone" basis - those which are too short, too odd, too difficult or too easy to be submitted to NUMA.

Q: You just wanted to write this silly description, didn't you?

A: Lies! All lies!

Q: A couple of these maps look familiar.

A: That's a statement, O Foolish One, not a question.

Q: Why do a couple of these maps look familiar?

A: There are three I posted in the Neddis thread. The rest are all new, though.

Q: What's with the name?

A: Well, it's five episodes consisting of five levels each. A quintilogy of five, you see. I wanted to make it three episodes just so I could legitimately call it a trilogy of five, but I ended up with too many levels.

Q: So, are you a total lunatic or what?

A: I prefer to think of myself as eccentric. In truth, I am either a minor genius or mildly insane depending on your point of view. But then, what man could live without being a little insane?

Quote
The chemical senses are the olfactory (smell) and gustatory (taste) sensations. The olfactory sensors are located in yellow pigmented areas on each side of the inner nose. These areas are about 2.5 cm2 in area each, and contain chemoreceptors, which are nerve cells responding to certain chemicals that are carried to the sensors as gases. The detailed functioning of these cells does not appear to be known. The axons of these nerves apparently are received in olfactory bulbs under the front part of the brain, on both sides. Here there are glomeruli, each receiving signals from some 26 000 receptors. The olfactory bulbs on either side are cross-connected. Finally nerve fibres reach the olfactory areas in the anterior lobes of the brain. The types of olfactory sensations are given as fruity, flowery, resinous, spicy, foul, and burned. The olfactory sense is some 10 000 times as sensitive as taste, and is primarily responsible for the flavours of food.

Quote: Obby, August 06, 2006 01:01 am
I would just like to say that you are entirely wrong.  The God of the Jews and God of Islam and the Catholic God are all the same.  The three religions are called the three Abarahamic religions because they split from the God of Abraham.  And by this I mean that they practiced their beliefs differently.  Its all one God, but the followers practice their specific bleiefs differently.
I am aware of that. However, whether Christians worship the same god as Jews is debatable. The concept of the Trinity, for example, renders the Christian God quite different to that of the Jews and Muslims - you say that Jesus was God, while the others say he was a man. That's a fairly large difference, in my opinion - large enough to call the Jewish and Christian gods different, though certainly related, even without considering the other difference between the religions. Besides, many religions have borrowed bits from others, or share a common heritage. Consider the Bah' faith. They believe that all religions spring from the one god. Following your logic, this would mean that all gods are one, which would seem to prove the Bah' correct. It would also mean that the Christian god is the same as Kali, Pluto, and Horus, which I don't believe is something you would agree with. Furthermore, Christianity has absorbed many pagan myths over the years, declaring the old gods and kings to now be saints, angels or demons, and re-naming their holy days to fit with Christianity. Christmas, for instance, is considered by most scholars to be a Christianised version of the Roman Saturnalia, which was originally dedicated to Saturn and later to Mithras. I'm fairly sure you don't think Mithras or Sataurn are the same as the Christian God, even though it appears one of Christianity's most improtant festival periods sprang from their worship. In short, while the Christian God is certainly similar to the Jewish and Islamic gods, I think the differences are great enough for them to be considered distinct. The religions share a common heritage, but then, so do many others.

Quote: Guest, 2006-08-07T04:04:35Z
@agnostics.  They believe that their is a god, but they are unsure of wich one.  By believing that their is a god, they believe that there is a type of supreme ruler in the universe.

That's incorrect, even for agnostic theists (who believe in a specific god, but don't claim they know their religion is fact). It certainly doesn't apply to agnostic atheists. Agnostics may believe one of the following:

1. They, personally, do not have sufficient knowledge to consider the existence or non-existence of supernatural deities (in general, not in particular) proven.
2. Nobody currently has sufficient knowledge to prove the existence or non-existence of deities
3. It is impossible to ever prove the existence or non-existence of deities.

In short, agnosticism is the belief that we (or just you personally) cannot currently tell whether or not gods exist, and therefore that declaring either case to be true is a leap of faith. Failure to support either side is therefore usually considered the most appropriate path, though agnostic theists choose to follow a religion despite their doubts.

#213461 74 2006-08-09T04:09:49Z Atilla
My contention is that the statement "atheists believe they are above God" is at best misleading and at worst totally innaccurate and meaningless.

To keep things clearer, let us focus on the first of these for the moment; that is, I shall begin with an attempt to demonstrate that "atheists believe they are above God" does not give an accurate impression of the beliefs of atheists.

Firstly, if you asked atheists whether they believed they were above God, I'm fairly sure most would say something like "No, I don't believe in God." Furthermore, defenitions of atheism rarely refer to believing you are "above God"; atheism simply refers to the lack of belief in gods, or belief in lack of gods. The statement "atheists believe themselves to be above God", then, is not useful in understanding an atheistic worldview, because it does not describe their core beliefs.

To demonstrate this point further, let us consider other worldviews. If atheists can be said to think themselves above God because they do not believe in Him, then it must be equally true that Christians think themselves above Ganesha (a Hindu god) because they do not believe in him. However, what does the statement "Christians believe they are above Ganesha" tell us about Christian doctrine? Next to nothing. If you were asked to describe the beliefs of Christians, I doubt you would say "Christians believe themselves above Ganesha" at any point, because this is only an incidental consequence. If Hinduism had never existed and there was no concept (note: concept, not the thing itself) of the god Ganesha for Christians to believe themselves above, Christianity would remain unchanged. So it is with atheism - when you say "atheists believe themselves to be above God", you appear to be connecting atheism with the concept of a Christian (or at least monotheistic) god. This is extraneous to atheism; as in the analogy with Christianity and Hinduism, atheism can exist perfectly well without the concept of any specific god.

Finally, the statement "atheists believe they are above God" is misleading because it implies that this is a belief specific to atheism, which is untrue. All non-Christians (or non-Abrahamic religion followers, depending on your intepretation) also fail to believe in your God, and by the same logic must believe themselves above Him - though they may, of course, believe in their own gods.

#10737 1 2006-08-20T12:45:28Z Atilla
A couple of nights ago I was lying in bed reading.

"Kriiiiii... Kriiiii... Kriiiii..."

I look up. The noise stops. I go back to reading again.

"Kriiii.... Kriiiiiiiii..."

Again, the eerie chirping. It can't be crickets, surely? I've never heard them around college before. It's in the city centre, after all, and I can't help but think crickets have trouble digging tunnels in concrete. I get up to investigate - it sounds as though it's coming from the room next door - but the noise stops again. I wait a while, then return to my book.

"Kriii... Kriiii... Kriiii..."

This time the noise continues after I get up. When I walk across the room, I notice that the noise seems to be emanating from the small bin in my room.

The noise stops.

I look at the garbage bin.

It looks at me.

I prod it with my foot.

"Kriiiii....."

I look at it again. There's not even anything edible in there, just some plastic packaging. Surely it couldn't be insects? I prod it a few more times, and every time it makes a noise, but whatever is actually generating the chirping doesn't seem inclined to show itself.

There can be only one course of action at this point. I must remove the bag of garbage from the bin in an attempt to find the offender. I wish to go to bed shortly, and I'm sure as hell not putting up with that noise all night.

So, I gingerly hook the bag with one finger and lift it our, fully expecting some hideous bug-eyed thing with skittering legs to rush out of the bag, antennae flailing wildly, leaving a swathe of filth and decay in its wake.

Nothing.

I place the bag onto the floor, whilst keeping an eye on both the bag and bin.

I peer into the bin. Nothing there.

I look at the bag. It's your generic, semi-transparent, cheap plastic supermarket bag. I can't see anything that looks remotely biological inside.

I kick the bag.

Nothing.

Steeling myself, I remove a couple of things from the bag.

Still nothing. The bag is empty but for a few lonesome bits of plastic. But the noise was definately coming from the bin! And nothing has left either bin or bag! It must be coming from the bin itself! Ganesha preserve me, it's ALIVE!

I reunited the loving bin-bag couple, and the noise did not return.

I can only assume that two bits of plastic were rubbing together as they settled (tsk, tsk... packaging has no sense of decency these days) and that lifting the bag sperated them. And that's the tale of my bizzarre, but rather anticlimactic encounter with the Living Trash Can.

The comparison to the word "retarted" "stupid" "crazy" and "queer" are not valid. All of them have an intrisic negative meaning. #218330 11 2006-08-22T03:44:00Z Atilla
@B_T: I was referring to the original meaning of the word "queer" - that is, strange or odd. I agree that in its modern usage it isn't really negative.

You'll note that I said that "retarted" was borderline, precisely because it can be construed as discrimination against the handicapped. I consider it to have a more negative meaning than "gay" because it describes an medical condition in which your learning abilities are reduced - and I really doubt anyone would want to be in such a state. In a similar manner, someone who has a sprained ankle may be described as "lame" because their physical strength is reduced, even though they are not lame in the medical sense. Being "gay", on the other hand, means you're either homosexual or happy, neither of which are intrisically negative (although being gay can have unpleasent social consequences due the homophobic attitudes of many). If you're retarted, you cannot do some jobs and perform some tasks because of your condition. Likewise if you're lame - you obviously can't be an athlete. Gays, on the other hand, are fully capable of anything heterosexuals are, except perhaps for engaging in sexual relations with the opposite sex. Why, then, should the word "gay" be used to mean stupid or unjust? Why not "straight"? Why not "negro" or "British"? There's really no difference. Would you consider the sentence "Shooting down your allies' aircraft is such an American thing to do" to reflect negatively on America? Would most Americans? I'm using the word to mean "stupid" rather than refer to the country, of course, but I'm fairly certain most Americans wouldn't be terribly happy about it.

Furthermore, statistics show that in Australia, the younger you are, the less likely you are to be homophobic - except for the 14 -17 year old age group, which just happens to be the group that commonly uses "gay", "poof" and "fag" as insults. "Gay", a word which was previously positive, just happens to become a derogatory term shortly after it's used to describe a group which is widely discrimated against. The word "straight", the opposite of "gay" had and still has possitive connotations. What a coincidence. This doesn't prove that those terms are responsible for homophobia, of course, and certainly doesn't mean the people who use them intend them to be homophobic. But when we see such correlations, you need to look seriously at usage of such terms and consider subcoscious factors, such as the halo/horns effect and association fallacy.

Quote: TornadoTK, 2006-08-22T02:23:59Z
It's offensive to be called a female dog?

Yes. Animal names as insults refer to a negative trait of the animal - for example, pigs are considered messy, so people who are untidy are called pigs. Bitches are often snappish during pregnancy, or when protecting their pups, so someone who is touchy is described as bitchy. In the same manner, using "gay" as a derogatory term presumably refers to a negative trait of homosexuals - since they don't differ much from heterosexuals, the most likely trait is homosexuality itself.

Quote: TornadoTK, 2006-08-22T02:23:59Z
I don't want to have to say "That's something that I dislike" instead of "That's gay/stupid/retarded/garbage/poor/dumb/bullshit/crappy"

Firstly, I don't think garbage, crap or bullshit are likely to complain about your usage of such terms, since they're inanimate objects.

Secondly, the word "stupid" has never had a meaning which is not negative, as far as I'm aware, and doesn't really refer to a specific social group. There are plenty of gay groups, and plenty of people who proudly identify themselves as gay, but I've yet to see the Stupid People's Association of Australia or a Stupid Pride march.

For some reason, people often become less friendly when they see you wantonly slaughtering innocents.

Also, I agree with Maestro. There is not an endless supply of civilians who are both willing and able to fight. If the military is getting slaughtered, drafted civilians are just as likely to desert at the first opportunity as march out to get shot. Not to mention that many people simply refuse to fight - for example, in 1970 a whopping 100,000 people flooded Melbourne's streets to protest against conscription in the Vietnam war.
