#223181 14 2006-09-03T12:56:35Z Atilla
Quote: jeca, September 03, 2006 10:23 pm
Quote: maestro, September 02, 2006 02:31 pm
Electrolysis requires electricity, which needs to be produced by other energy resources. Usually, it's not efficient enough to be worth it.
But isn't it the same basiscs you use with fussion(dunno spelling in english)? I don't mean that you should put a small fussion power plant in each car (now that'd be the day) but to me that seems like a fairly good solution.
It's fusion, not "fussion". And no, fusion is a totally different process to hydrogen burning. In the latter, you simply split water into it's component atoms, using some energy to do so, then recombine the hydrogen with some oxygen, getting less energy back because the process is not 100% efficient. The advantage is, of course, that you can actually burn hydrogen, unlike water. In our current plans for a fusion reactor, deuterium and/or tritium* would undergo nuclear fusion to become helium, yielding extra energy that was previously stored within the atoms themselves, rather than in the bonds between atoms.

Hydrogen with one or two extra neutrons, they are present in lesser amounts than normal hydrogen. Deuterium is also called "heavy hydrogen" Both occur naturally, though trituim is somewhat scarce due to a relatively short decay time. They can be produced from "heavy water", which is water with deuterium instead of normal hydrogen.
#223184 16 2006-09-03T13:03:30Z Atilla
Quote: top predator, September 03, 2006 10:57 pm
the malasyan guy uses nanotechnology to slipt water into hydrogen to power a car he has done it and the car has moved so the production cant be 0.
He meant the net production. That is, we had to spend as much energy to make the car's fuel as we got back when we ran it (in fact, as I said earlier, we would get slightly less back). This means that hydrogen-burning power plants would be useless because they would consume more energy than they produced. Except possibly in space, where you could harvest hydrogen clouds rather than using electrolysis. It's like batteries. They're good for portable devices, but you need too much power to make them in the first place, which is why we don't have Duracell power plants.

Er, astronomical probably isn't a good choice of word. I mean, astronomical factors leading to the evolution of humans are usually taken to be things like meteors, the type of light the sun emits, the position of Earth, and so on.

Aside from that, what you said is incorrect. Life did not "evolve from nothing". Evolution occurs when you already have living (or at least self-replicating) things. It is thought that self-replicating molecules arose through natural chemical reactions and that evolution then lead to the development of more complex life. And the Big Bang is in no way comparable to a grenade. That's like saying planes are impossible because running along flapping your arms doesn't make you fly. You should also remember that the universe is a very large place indeed; if the chance of life appearing on any given planet is one in trillions, well... it certainly looks like there are trillions of planets, so the chance of it happening at least once would be quite high.

@iangb and Fol67: I admit I was too harsh. Therefore, you now get to put up with the long-winded, but clearer and less abrasive version.

I was attempting to highlight the fact that Fol's posts have become increasingly controversial, and suggesting that he may post progressively more outrageous things as a plea for attention. He started by saying that he was bisexual and sexually active at a young age (I was only one year out, and mistakenly remembered the age Fol said he hit puberty instead), which while somewhat unusual were not terribly shocking, and as a result did not gather undue attention. He then escalated to Christian-bashing, necrophilia and Satanic contracts signed in blood. Now, the percentage of the population that is bisexual is quite small. The percentage of the population that is bisexual, necrophilic, and 12 years old is very much smaller. The percentage of the population which belongs to this tiny minority and which is also sworn to Satan by some kind of blood oath is practically non-existant, unless I'm greatly mistaken. I therefore found it considerably more likely that it would be one of the large number of attention-seeking people in existance than that Fol not only belonged to such a tiny minority, but happened to wander onto a forum for a freeware game and start declaring it. The apparant contradictions in some of his posts, which have already been pointed out, did little for my inclination to see his claims as legitimate. Nor did it help that he often professed his views in a way which was insulting and aggresive - though perhaps I, too, am guilty of this. It may be that what he says is true, but it does seem a trifle unlikely. This is not intended to be a slander on him personally. It is simply a reflection of the fact that many people take the unique nature of the internet as an invitation to act in a manner which would not be tolerated in the real world. When anonymity is a given and the lack of body language and subtleties of voice makes it difficult to judge motives, it is much easier to get away with socially disruptive behaviour, and there are too many people willing to exploit this unfortunate cirmcumstance for me to take everything which is said at face value.

Fol67, if the statements about yourself you made are true than I apologise for having been hurtful. But I hope that after reading the above you can understand why your statements may appear to be deliberately provocative and disruptive to others.

Quote: Rincewind SW, September 19, 2006 04:56 am
So is a theistic agnostic someone who doesn't know, but has a certain belief that one of the other is true?
An agnostic theist does not claim to know a deity/deities exist, but chooses to believe in one/some anyway. It is akin to the statement "I don't know if I passed all my exams, but I'll make plans on the assumption that I have until I get the results" or "I don't know if we'll win, but I hope we do."

Quote: McP, 2006-09-19T01:03:00Z
Quote: Suki
On a scale based entirely on my own opinion, sanity increases moving to the right:
Theism -> Agnostic Theism -> Agnostic Atheism -> Atheism
BAHAHA
That made me laugh...your so unbeleivably biased, but then again, i am too in my own right...

Anyway, i also dislike agnosticism like Suki, but in a completely different fashion. Pick a damn side...Indecision is worse than the wrong decision i think.

What, you expect him to say his belief isn't the most correct? If he thought that, he'd change his beliefs!

Also, agnosticism is not synonymous with "indecision". Agnostics are those who viewed the available evidence and arguments and decided that they are insufficient to conclusively prove or disprove theism. We can make a comparison with politics: say you run a country in the Middle East. Some people claim that Tyrant X, who runs the neighbouring country, is planning to invade (theism - those who claim he plans to attack at 6 AM next Tuesday are followers of a specific religion). Others say TX is quite content to brutalise his own citizens, and scoff at the claims of a forthcoming attack (atheism). Your spies are fairly useless, and have been unable to provide sufficient evidence for either claim (agnosticism). You still have to decide whether you should make a pre-emptive strike to prevent an invasion that might not actually be coming (agnostic theism), or to hold off until there is evidence that an attack is immanent - if such evidence ever exists (agnostic atheism). Also, even though you're uncertain if the attack will occur, you can still argue that it won't happen at 6 AM next Tuesday because there's no way TX can mobilise his forces that quickly (saying a specific religion is incorrect, rather than religion in general, which is perfectly compatible with agnosticism).

EDITZORS:
Quote: Guest, 2006-09-19T01:22:04Z
And the whole theory looks to be based off that the simplest things are the best... Which is not always true...

A more correct statement of Occam's Razor is not that the simplest explanation is true, but the one that makes the fewest assumptions. For example, you could say that theists assume (1) the universe exists and (2) it was created by God, while atheists just assume (1). Personally, I find referring specifically to Occam's Razor to be rather useless in a debate - far too many people just say "I don't understand your view, so you're wrong. Occam's Razor." There's also the unfortunate fact that if you obeyed Occam's Razor to the letter, your explanation for everything would be "because it is". Why do rocks fall? "Because they do." Why is the sky blue? "Because it's blue." It tells you nothing, but it's the simplest explanation and makes the fewest assumptions. If someone's opinion rests on too many unfounded assumptions, just point it out and explain how making such assumption makes their explanation unreliable, rather than shouting "Occam's Razor!" and running away.

Quote: Bananakid, 2006-09-19T01:28:17Z

NO. Thou shalt not imply scientific principles are unreliable on the basis that they are "only a theory"! To do so is irrational and ignorant. How many times must I tell people this?

Quote: Atilla in the pinned thread at the top of Serious Discussion
...please learn the correct technical usage of "theory". In science, a theory is an explanation which has been extensively tested and verified by many independent sources (and the details of the experiments conducted by said sources have been examined by still others, and the experiment has been shown to be repeatable). Theories are therefore among the most reliable parts of scientific knowledge. This extensive testing process also catches out flukely results, due to an error in the experiment, problems with equipment, misinterpretation of results, and so on.

I claim that there was a great flood a few thousand years ago because Thor drank too much, and spewed forth enough bile to fill the seas**. This flood is historically verified. Should we believe in Thor and his drinking problem?

"The Quiet American" describes the actions of fictional characters during the Vietnam War. Many of the circumstances and events described are historically accurate. Is it wise to believe everything in the book is real?

What I'm saying is that there are many, many other beliefs which could account for said historical events. This doesn't necessarily make them correct, or even sensible.

*Obviously because pirates are so cool.

**This also explains why oceans are full of horrible slimy things.

Approach from the left. Stop in front of the first thwump, and wait for it to come down. Walk underneath it as it goes back up - the thwump on the floor will lift out of your way. Wait in the gap after the 2nd thwump for the 3rd thwump to fall, then walk under like before (or don't bother waiting- just run under it if you're feeling confident). Stand beneath the thwump that was on the ground when it goes up. This will lure the thwump on the roof down. Jump on top of it, then jump into the alcove with the exit switch. To get out, wait until the thwump next to you falls, then stand on it and walk underneath the thwump on the left when it rises. From there you can just repeat the process you used to get in. If you opened the doors on the right, head out them instead.

More Questions That Haven't Been Asked Frequently But Undoubtably Will Be (MQTHBAFBUWB):

Q: Uh, what?
A: A large cottage made of teapots.

Q: What is the Answer to Life, the Universe, and Everything?
A: Eight less than the number of levels in this pack multiplied by the number of episodes in the pack and divided by twice the number of levels in each episode.

Q: Aaah! How am I supposed to work that out? My mathematical ability is so low it's, er... what do you call those numbers below zero again?
A: "Make an abacus out of second-hand toothbrushes" and "negative", respectively. Also, I hope you don't manage your own finances.

Q: Why isn't blue more red?
A: Because that would imply that the specific gravity of cheese is less than the finite interval of a mollusc expansion in the X-Y plane, which is clearly not the case.

Q: How difficult is this level pack?
A: Average, on average. The earlier episodes are easier and the later ones harder, of course. The later levels of each episode are also substantially harder.

Q: Is this why you haven't submitted anything to NUMA for a while?
A: Yes, mostly. Although I had a break from mapmaking for a bit.

Q: My house is infested with beavers. What should I do?
A: Contact your lawyer and send them a notice of eviction. If they fail to comply, spread rumors that they have WMDs and wait for the military to take care of it.

Q: Why isn't your first level pack in the "Levels packs" section?
A: I blame trout-flavoured icecream.

Q: Is it really necessary to write such silly descriptions?
A: Yes. Always.

Q: I still think you're a total lunatic.
A: You still can't tell the difference between a question and a statement.

EDIT: Erk. Found a mistake in one of the levels (Like Moths to a Flame). Should be fixed now.

#235105 45 2006-09-29T11:35:05Z Atilla
Speaking from a non-American's perspective, Bush is not a good president. His foreign policies are abrasive, to say the least, and his administration appears willing to ignore, or even actively endorse, grossly unethical behaviour to further their own ideology.

Has David Hicks had any media coverage in America? He is an Australian who allegedly trained with al-Qaeda in Afganistan, and was captured by the US in 2001. They held him in a Guantanamo Bay detention facility without trial until 2004. He was supposed to be tried by a military tribunal in 2005, but in late 2004 America's Federal Court ruled that the trials were unconstitutional and biased. This decision was later overturned by the Court of Appeal on the basis "the President of the United States issued a memorandum in which he determined that none of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions "apply to our conflict with al-Qaeda in Afghanistan or elsewhere throughout the world"". In 2006, the Supreme Court overturned this decision, ruling that the military tribunals and treatment of prisoners contravened both US law and the Geneva convention. Also in 2006, five independant investigators from the UN Commission on Human Rights called on the United States to "close immediately the detention centre in Guantnamo Bay and bring all detainees before an independent and competent tribunal or release them." Their report also criticised the US administration for attempting to redefine "torture" to allow practices which would considered a breach of international conventions against torture, and said that the detainees at Guantanamo were being subjected to breaches of basic human rights.

Now, I'm not saying David Hicks not a terrorist. Indeed, it seems quite likely that he is. However, if they are so sure he is a terrorist, why can't they just try him and let the evidence speak for itself? When the president of the "land of the free" openly endorses a military tribune which is widely considered corrupt and unjust, breaches the Geneva convetion, and which has been declared to violate several basic rights by the UN, you have a problem. When the UN goes on to say the administration involved is also trying to legalise acts of torture which are considered unethical by the international community, you have a larger problem. And this is just one example.

#235405 3 2006-09-30T05:31:45Z Atilla
1. Jump into the bit with 3 pieces of gold just left of the start.
2. There's a drone going clockwise around the next platform on the left. Follow close behind it to the switch above the thumps, then quickly turn around and head back to the bit with 3 gold. Jump over the drone coming from the right.
3. Wait for the drones just to your left to get out of the way. Run left to the next switch.
4. Wait for the drone going clockwise around the leftmost platform to go past. Follow it to the exit switch. As soon as you get it, jump back up to avoid the thwump and head right.
5. Walk to the right across the top of the level. Watch out for drones, though they shouldn't give you much trouble.
6. Wait for any drones in the way to move, then drop down the rightmost shaft and run to the exit.

Quote: Black Sheep Boy, September 30, 2006 06:18 pm
Quote: Atilla, 2006-09-30T03:10:57Z
Firstly, I live in a democratic country and am granted the right of free speech, which allows me to criticise whomever I please.
I had a fleeting interest in this issue a few month ago. So some of what I say might be a bit... outdated or inaccurate. But I believe it's mostly correct.
Free Speech isn't protected under Australian law. There's plenty of anti- sedition stuff around, which isn't currently being abused but could, potentially, be used to lock up anybody who dares to disagree with the opinions of those ruling Australia at the time. Thankfully, this isn't happening. But it could, and there's very little to stop it.
Free speech in Australia is beginning to be protected by state governments, but this could be overturned by the Federal Government.
It's one of the major arguments for implementing a Bill of Rights into Australia, as Australia does not currently have one.
The sedition laws are rather silly, but I don't think they're quite that bad. There are disclaimers that disallow prosecution for pointing out problems with Government policy in good faith, which should prevent most abuses in anything approaching a fair trial. The High Court has also tended towards decisions allowing free political expression in the past.

Also, due to a rather strange quirk of legality, I believe Australian sedition law applies not only to acts of sedition committed outside Australia, but also to acts of sedition committed by foreign citizens - effectively allowing Australia to prosecute anyone in the world. I'm not totally sure, though, so if anyone knows better...

II. WAYS OF COMING TO KNOW GOD

The Catechism is available here, for those who wish to read it.

Also, I agree with Dave in that I think many people will be happier believing something which is clearly irrational than not. In this circumstance, it is both natural and logical to pick the choice which makes you happier. The choice itself is rational; the beliefs it leads to are not. However, I disagree with the belief that highly rational individuals can only act in a manipulative manner. That is looking only at one possible form of rationality. Equally, one might point to the irrational people who ride roughshod over others to further their own cause - religious zealots, for instance. Instead, a rational person may (somewhat) objectively consider the effects of an action on all parties, and present the option which will bring the greatest overall good. They may also act as a mediator between less rational parties which struggle to see each other's point of view. Ultimately, society needs the rational to moderate emotional responses, maintain adaptability and balance, and prevent stagnation (and, quite frequently, to ensure that things actually work). Likewise, a degree of irrational emotion is needed to prevent people acting in their own self-interest according to inflexible dictates of logic. Homogeniety breeds vulnerability, which is why all animals have a degree of diversity.

Reciprocal question @ theists: What would you do if you died and it turned out you had followed the wrong god/gods?

---

Also, I have an argument against faith from a theistic viewpoint. It is not holeproof, but it is quite interesting.

Now, it is said by many that the nature and existance of God may be discovered by observation of the natural order which prevades the universe. Let us consider for the purposes of this argument that this is true; that is, the existance and nature of God may be deduced from the existance and nature of the universe. Keeping this in mind, let us look once again at the order of the universe. We note that occurances within the universe are bound to mathematical laws - essentially, the universe runs on logic. We may infer, then, that God is instrisically logical, and furthermore that logic and order are pleasing to Him. Now, we earlier stated that the existance of God may be deduced from the existance and nature of the universe - in essence, we may determine the existance of God with logic and reason alone. Therefore, there is no need for faith. Furthermore, we can state that God does not wish his followers to have faith because the proof of His existence - which negates the need for faith - is an intrisic property of the universe, and therefore also a property of God.

The most obvious counterargument is that the initial assumption was flawed, and that the nature/existance of God cannot be discerned from the nature/existance of the universe. However, this leaves the question of how anyone knows not only that God exists, but that he approves of faith. It also makes agnosticism look increasingly logical.

Comments? Can anyone see the loopholes?

Assuming that there is no limit to his power and that he has no rules or scheme by which to operate, he will basically act randomly. In all likelihood, he will use a [random number] percentage of the things he can do at any given moment, and he will do them [random number] times per his favorite unit of time (but he doesn't really have to pay attention to silly things like time). When you have unbounded random numbers, which is a number from negative infinity to infinity, you tend to get a number that approaches one of those infinites.

That assumes that probablity still works without natural laws, which conflicts with the belief that supernatural things do not adhere to any semblence of order. It is also based on the assumption that a supernatural creature would not operate with any kind of goal or pattern, which is not a reasonable assumption. Pretty much every supernatural occurrance people believe in has some constraints or at the very least a pattern of action - the Christian God, for example, has the Ineffable Divine Plan, judges people according to the guidlines set out in the Bible, and so on. Vampires can't enter your house unless you invite them in. Mages have to throw bat guano and saffron seeds while speaking certain words to cast a spell.

Furthmore, most superstitions follow a consistant internal logic - just not the laws of physics. If you attempt to brew a potion five times, and it only worked the time you brewed it at midnight, a logical conclusion is that the potion must be brewed at midnight to work. Sceptics would say that this is mistaking corellation for cause, which is true - but the same thing can be said of many discoveries throughout history. Some of our current scientific knowledge undoubtably falls into this category, too - in particular, it's quite common when dealing with causes of disease, side effects of drugs, and so forth.

Quote: Tsukatu, 2006-10-10T15:41:09Z
One of the infinite actions the barbarian will in all likelihood take is to convert an infinite amount of the matter in every existing plane (more than 100% of the matter) into an infinite amount of random sorts of energy, essentially obliterating everything. He doesn't even have to do things that we can imagine - he can turn the next townsperson he sees from a human into an abstract idea, like a dance routine. He can microwave justice. And he likely does all of this an infinite number of times per second, constantly. Sure, he'll probably be small and ineffective for some length of time, but he can always change his mind about his actions over a stretch of time, and if he ever decides to not exist it is always his perogative to begin existing again, and afterwards deciding that he has always existed.
If you think that he's going to obey the town's silly little rules, or that the town is going to be completely unaffected because it has solid, obeyed rules, you're dead wrong. I might bet that the town will be okay for the first yoctosecond, but after that the chances are so damnably small that I may as well say for practicality's sake that the town is utterly annihilated and subsumed into the barbarian's swirl of senseless, conditional existence.

Other possible actions include leaving the town alone for all eternity, shifting the position of an atom by one nanometre, causing the sun to emit two extra photons per year, and so on. I recently saw a Penn & Teller's "Bullshit" on second-hand smoke. Apparently the dangers of second-hand are total hype, and that the smoker's lungs really filter out all of the bad stuff, or enough to leave only trace amounts for you to breathe in.

Never heard of the show, and forgive me for not changing my opinion based on a TV show when, as far as I can tell, most health authorities assert that passive smoking is harmful. Particularly when dealing with an industry that is known to have actively attempted to hide research showing its product was hazardous to your health.

Anyway, even ignoring cancer and suchlike, many people suffer from respiratory illnesses which are aggravated by smoking. There are also undeniable short-term effects; exposure to cigarette smoke always gives me a headache and makes me nauseous, and I know plenty of others who suffer similar effects. Even without specific bans on smoking, it would almost be possible to sue under nuisance laws. Then there are duty-of-care laws - if it turns out down the line that passive smoking is a health risk, restaurant owners may well face legal action, given that the general opinion is that passive smoking is harmful.

Personally, I think smoking should be banned in public places, but pubs and suchlike should be able to obtain some kind of "smoking licence", under a similar system to alcohol licencing. That way, smoking is still allowed, but it is not the default - which reflects the fact that non-smokers comprise 80% of the population.

#11872 1 2006-10-22T01:36:16Z Atilla
I'm not sure if this is actually a good idea, but I'm going to throw it out there because it's interesting. I don't think the whole thing has been suggested before, although some parts of it have.

What I'm suggesting is that there be an option to prevent anyone else seeing the ratings on your map, as is currently done for maps below five votes. This would be a compromise between the current rating system and the option of disabling ratings altogether.

What's the point of ratings if nobody else can see them? It's a quick and simple method for the author to get feedback. It may also improve the accuracy of the ratings you are getting. For a start, there will be less incentive to snipe - nobody else is going to see the results, it won't affect the all-authors list, and the author will just dismiss the offending vote anyway*. It will also prevent the more subtle effects of people being swayed by the existing score.

Basically, this option considers ratings to be a tool which helps authors to improve their mapmaking, rather than as a way to gain fame, or a way for the general populace to find good maps.

*A list of votes, which has been suggested several times, could aid in this. However, I don't think it's really necessary or even desirable. eg.
0: 1 0.5: 0 1: 0 1.5: 0 2: 0 2.5: 0
3: 1 3.5: 3 4: 2 4.5: 1 5: 0 Av: 3.5

#245293 20 2006-10-24T08:03:14Z Atilla
@stepself: I believe you're talking about energy/time uncertainty rather than a time quanta. Uncertainty does not mean there is a minimum time which we can measure accurately; it just means that when such a time is measured any measured energy will have a huge margin for error. Such relations can be obtained by applying unit conversions to the uncertainty principle, without reference to string theory. Many such pairs of variables can be found this way. Position/momentum and time/energy are just the two most commonly known.

EDIT: Actually, now that I think of it, it's possible to show that angular momentum, space, and energy are quantised using quantum mechanics. Time may also be possible, though I can't recall having seen it done.

#249360 45 2006-11-03T02:40:34Z Atilla
Quote: Dave, November 01, 2006 10:19 pm
P.S. I've never fully understood the nomenclature of Australian politics. Labor Party certain sounds liberal, but so does the Liberal Party. I'd just not vote at all and stay out of the confusion....

Nonsense. It's perfectly straightforward. The major parties are the Australian Labor Party (aka ALP, probably to disguise their American spelling) and the Australian Liberal Party (not the ALP, despite its initials). The Labor party is somewhat liberal and the Liberal party is conservative. The Liberal Party forms the Coalition with the National Party, which contests both state and federal seats. Then there's the Democratic Labor Party of Australia (DLP), which is not to be confused with the Australian Democrats or the Australian Labor Party, not to mention the Progressive Labor Party (PLP), Country Labor Party (CLP), People's Front of Judea, and Judean People's Front. Oh, and "the Labor Party" always means the ALP, not the others. There's also the Republican Party of Australia (RPA - no, not the Royal Prince Alfred hospital!), which is not an arm of the ARM (erm, the Australian Republican Movement), and the Family First party, which is only an accurate description if your family consists of conservative Christians. I award the Greens a special prize for having the most accurate and unambiguous name of any well-known Australian political party.

#250983 12 2006-11-07T01:27:21Z Atilla
The overall number of cones just alters your sensitivity to colour, not what colours you actually percieve. Having more cones would increase the saturation of colours (that is, things would look more colourful, and less grey). There are also different types of cones (three in normal people), which are sensitive to different wavelengths to varying degrees (check the absorbtion spectra on Wikipedia). Naturally, there is some variation in the number of cones an given individual has, and in precisely how sensitive they are to different wavelengths, but this is rather minor in most people. It might make you disagree with someone about whether aqua is blue or green, but it won't make you claim an object which someone else thinks is orage is actually purple. Therefore, having more cones overall should not produce a preference to certain colours, since it effects all colours (approximately) equally.

Rods, on the other hand, only detect the intensity of light, rather than the colour. They are more sensitive than cones, but they cannot provide as much fine detail and they are slower to respond to light. They are primarily used for night vision, which is why everything looks grey and blurry in the dark. One could hypothesize that men have more rods than women because they have traditionally served as watchmen and guardians, and therefore have more need to see in dim light.

Also, the whole blue/red/pink thing is almost certainly due to conditioning rather than any inherant preference of a gender for those colours. The colours have been opposite at several times in hitory - blue for girls and pink for boys.

I certainly support adult stem cell research, and I support ebryonic stem-cell research and cloning for medicinal purposes with a few reservations. I do not support reproductive cloning at this stage.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2006-11-09T06:43:12Z
Quote: Atilla, 2006-11-09T06:05:34Z
Or as well-informed as those who vote under a system where the winner is often determined by who has a larger campaign budget, funded by private groups with vested interests?

How does mandatory voting remedy this issue? Are you saying that people without vested interests in their government should be forced to cast their random opinion for an issue that other people care significantly about? Do you think the possibility of corruption in the government is remedied by making the electoral process more lottery than decision? Because that's how I view the compulsion to vote: a lottery. People forced to do something will do it with less concern. They won't take it upon themselves to consider the issues. They'll do it to get it over with. I think we can all understand why that might strip a little sincerity from the process.

You misunderstand. A substantial proportion of campaign funding in goes towards getting potential voters to actually turn up. Even if more people dislike your policies than like them, you can win the election by bombarding your supporters with encouragements to vote. Perhaps it's selective reporting, but politicians appear to spend more time preaching to their own supporters in America than Australia. In a compulsory voting system, however, almost everyone is going to turn up regardless of what you do. This reduces the influence of donations from special interest groups, because you have to focus on pleasing 51% of the electorate - not making the 30% that already like you turn up.

I also find it slightly strange that all these people who allegedly couldn't care less still seem to acquire an opinion when they enter the polling booth. If most of the population really had no opinion, wouldn't there be a huge number of invalid ballots submitted every election? Or wouldn't the guy listed first on the ballot paper always win because all the apathetic people placed a donkey vote? If the people who don't vote are those who don't have political opinions, why does the phrase "You didn't vote so you can't complain" come up so often in debates about American politics? It would seem to me that many people who don't vote have opinions which they will happily espouse with a little prodding.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2006-11-09T06:43:12Z
Quote: Atilla, 2006-11-09T06:05:34Z
Perhaps you meant as unbiased as the people who will be disowned by their family unless they vote Republican? Or as unbiased as a system in which certain demographics can be - and, historically, have been - prevented from voting by making it difficult for them to access the polling booths?

How does mandatory voting prevent the bias generated by controlling families and communities? A family member forced to get up off of her ass and vote Republican can just as easily get up off of her ass and vote Democrat. No one will ever know how she voted.

That's true, but how many are likely to do that? Compulsory voting ensures that the people who are actually voting based on who they like, rather than on family history, get to the polls. It comes back to my previous point. Why bother pleasing the majority when you can just focus on getting the hard-line party voters "off their asses", as you so succinctly put it? When everyone has to vote, it becomes much, much more difficult to win on party votes alone. You have to get at least some of the swinging vote on your side, and that means policies which are more representative of the population's true opinion.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2006-11-09T06:43:12Z
I don't think mandatory voting is a good way to protect a minority's right to vote.  Black people were once forced to sit at the back of the bus.  I think it's counterintuitive to force them to sit at the front of the bus in an effort to protect their rights.  Forcing someone to do something in an effort to protect their right to do it is a very bad way of going about it.  Hopefully, in the distant progressive-secular future, we won't be forced to have abortions to reserve our right to have them.

That's not the same. There are a limited number of seats at the front of a bus, and that would be compelling blacks to sit there instead of other people. It would be segregating them, giving them different status to others. The glorious seat of democratic voting, however, has room for everyone, and everyone has the same status. It would only be comparable with the bus situation if you made blacks vote twice or somesuch.

I also think it's a good idea to require people to be vaccinated against diseases such as polio and hepatitis. You might argue that this infringes upon their right to decide to be unhealthy. I would argue that it will prevent problems for them in the future, and also benefit others by preventing the spread of disease. So it is with compulsory voting. It removes a method by which a group may be discriminated against, and replaces it with the very slight inconvenience of having to fill out a small piece of paper twice every four years. It also ensures the government better represents the entire populace, and thus ensures that policy stays somewhat balanced.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2006-11-09T06:43:12Z
Quote: Atilla, 2006-11-09T06:05:34Z
I can definitely see how having the entire country vote - regardless of race, religion, or social class - would make the results unfair and biased. It's not entirely about the application of perfect government, to me. It's not about having the best electoral process EVAR. It's about protecting the individual's rights. I don't think we need to give up our rights to have a stronger government. The right not to vote is a legitimate right to retain. Granted, everyone should vote. Every last person should get off of their asses and vote! Also, no one should drink alcohol! Also, everyone should always brush their teeth! Also, everyone should play N!

I would argue to the bitter end that people should do all of these things. But I'd never force their hand in the matter. That's the difference, for me.

That doesn't explain how having the entire population vote somehow spontaneously generates bias in the election results.

What harm does it do you to vote? It takes, what, a couple of hours over a period of four years? You probably spend more time per year tying your shoelaces than voting. If it wasn't compulsory, you'd probably waste just as much time wondering whether you should vote and dealing with all the spam demanding you do. And if you really don't want your ignorant vote to pollute the system, you can just enter a blank ballot slip. I think compulsory voting ensures a fairer system which is more representitive of the electorate at a cost to the individual which is so trivial as to be negligable. I therefore fail to see what value a right to not vote actually has. It appears to be of only trivial benefit to the individual in the short term, and may well be detrimental to them in the long term. The benefits of compulsory voting outweigh the petty dent they make in the sanctity of personal freedom.

...says Mr US$200-A-Month-On-Booze-And-Miscellaneous-Indescretions. I'm spending about AU$80 a month (~$60 US). Who needs to spend less?

Let's do some calculations. Say you go to uni every day and study at night, so you can't work on weekdays. You then work from 9 to 5 on Saturday and Sunday, a total of 16 hours, for and hourly wage of AU$15. This gives you a total of AU$240 a week. About 20% of that will go in taxes, super, etc, so call it $200. Rent per week in central Melbourne for a student flat would be about $100. Quote: Dave, November 17, 2006 05:03 am
All that out of the way: What motivated you to criticize me, Atilla? That's what I was asking. Not "what did I do that made you want to criticize me" but rather "what about you makes you want to criticize people who say something that you disagree with"? There's no Socratic nature to this question. I actually want to know. It's probably a simple answer, and that's cool too. But what is the answer?

What motivates me to criticise people I disagree with depends somewhat on the situation. My goal is usually to cause the other person to alter their behaviour or opinion. For example, if someone was to post "All muslims are terrorist scum and should be deported," I would point out that there are many Muslims who are not terrorists, and furthermore that their statement is quite an insult to most Muslims. I would hope that they would either realise they were being unfair, or at the least learn that people are likely to take offence at such statements and consider whether they really need to make them.

Also, everyone makes mistakes occasionally. Some have immediate penalties, like tripping over. Social errors, however, can sometimes go unnoticed, and what consists of an error differs depending on your company. If other people do not indicate what they like or dislike, and what they find or do not find acceptable, it becomes more difficult to have a meaningful discussion. You can see this a hundred times over in the religious debates we've had - often, someone who is used to hanging around with Christians will be a bit confused by the standards of evidence the non-theistic members find acceptable, simply because they're used to different standards. Unless someone points out that the standards which are accepted here are not being met, both sides will continue to make arguments which seem absurd to the other, and nobody really gets much out of the discussion.

#258713 2 2006-11-24T00:58:52Z Atilla
To make a thwump move backwards, you should place it one-pixel less than halfway inside a wall, facing that wall. I find that the easiest way to do this is to use x-snap to place one halfway inside a wall, then go through the level code and change the number for the thwump's position by one. Thwumps have code of the form "8^767,564,0" where 8 indicates the object is a thwump, the first number is the horizontal distance from the left of the map, the second is the vertical distance (from the top of the map, for some reason) and the final number is the direction the thwump is facing. All you need to do is reduce or increase the horizontal or vertical position by one, depending on the direction the thwump is facing. The code above is for a glitched thwump at the bottom of the map, embedded in the right-hand wall, for instance (it was 8^768,564,0" before I edited it).

Quote: Obby, 2006-11-27T22:27:59Z
And what is so wrong with blind faith?

The problem with blind faith is that it offers no method of determining which of two conflicting beliefs is more likely to be accurate or useful. Consider. If you say the sky is green, I may respond with "No, it's blue. Look out the window and see." However, if you had blind faith that the sky was green, you would not accept this evidence. You would be sure the sky was green, no matter what I said or did, and come up with more explanations based on blind faith to account for the discrepancy between what you are observing and what you believe you should be observing.

To take a less extreme example, say that a man is accused of murder. It is known that someone was murdered - the body was found run through with a sword - but no evidence shows who was responsible. In the absence of evidence, two priests are to judge the man, on the basis that their god, who is just, would not let an innocent man be convicted, nor a guilty man walk free. The first priest states that, without doubt, the man is guilty. The second states that the man is surely innocent. Both have faith in their own verdict. Who is correct?

The belief that the universe started, and that it would be impossible not to have something start it, are both unverified assumptions. You may believe them, but you should not expect everyone to do so, unless you demonstrate that any other view is logically inconsistent. Also, the belief that the "first cause", which is itself uncaused, is a deity in the sense which the word is understood by most humans (ie. not just physical laws or suchlike) is a further unverified assumption.

Mind you, since time appears to be part of the universe, asking what came before doesn't really make much sense. If there was such a "before", we should recognise that it would not necessarily behave in a manner remotely similar to our own reality, and may well be incomprehensible to us.

Also true. In fact, science can work even if a god exists - as long as he isn't actually included in the scientific method, or scientific theories.

For example, say that a God exists. Now, if I drop a stone, it falls to the ground. You could say that it falls because God decides to push it to Earth, and that if God did not interfere it would float in the air forever. However, that isn't terribly useful - how can you predict whether God will decide to push things to Earth or not? What science does is assume that the stone falls according to certain laws, because then we can predict things based on our knowledge of such laws. Thus, God would not be included in the scientific explanation for gravity, even though we assumed He existed.

Scientific theory says "stones fall in this manner," because that is observed to be correct. It does not say "stones fall in this manner because God tells them to" or "stones fall in this manner because God doesn't exist" because these things cannot be observed, and are irrelevant to the model. Whatever reasons you choose to ascribe to these observations, the fact is that stones fall in a certain manner, and this manner is what science describes. God is thus irrelevant to scientific theory.

Quote

Rubbish.

1. The laws of mathematics say otherwise. Consider the function y=e^(-t), where y is the available energy, t is time, and e is a constant. This function is monotonically decreasing; that is, the amount of available energy is always decreasing. The time from t = (-infinity) to t=0 is infinite, yes? But the value of y at t=0 is 1, a non-zero number. Therefore, there is still available energy, even though the function has been going for an infinite time.

Unphysical because y is infinite when t = -infinity, you say? Possibly. Instead, let us consider the function y = 1/t + 2. When t = -infinity, 1/t = 0 and y = 2. (ie the universe starts with a finite amount of available energy). There is an infinite time between t=-infinity and t=-1, and y decrease monotonically in this region. However, at t = -1, y=1. That is, there is still usable energy, even though we started with a finite amount of energy and an infinite amount of time has passed. Therefore it is possible for the universe to start with finite energy, exist for an infinite period, yet still have usable energy.

2. Flawed reasoning. A universe which has existed for an infinite time can be finite. Therefore, the fact that the universe is finite proves nothing.

Even if 4a was correct, 4c would contradict the previous assertion that the universe is finite; if this is so, then the cause need only be larger than this finite size, and may thus be finite itself.

#261834 31 2006-11-30T01:20:44Z Atilla
@macaddict: X1 and Y1? You're using parametric form. You should be using functional form. Hit mode and select "Func" instead of "Par", assuming you're using a TI-83 or similar. The put Y1 = e^(-x). Note that although y decreases forever, it never actually reaches 0.

Now for the slightly more complicated on. Change Y1 to (1/X) + 2. Look at the graph. Remember that we are only considering the domain X < -0.5. Now, you should see that the graph has a horizontal asymptote at Y=2, that is, as X gets more negative, Y approaches (but never reaches) 2. To phrase this another way, the limit of Y as X -> -infinity is 2.

Now. Where we actually draw the origin is rather arbitrary; the laws of physics are still the same regardless of where we put it. We can consider, then, that -infinity is the 'beginning' of the universe, which comes with an initial 2 units of usable energy (ie Y=2). As time passes (ie. X becomes less negative), Y decreases. Now, the point X=-1 is an infinite distance from -infinity (the start of the universe), right? Look at the graph (or just substitute it into the equation). You should get Y=1 - that is, there is still usable energy left, even though we started off with a finite amount and our model of the universe has been going for an infinite time. This demonstrates that it is possible to start with some finite amount of energy, keep decreasing it for an infinite time, and still have some left. It's somewhat like Zeno's most well-known 'paradox' (the one with Achilles and the tortoise, you recall) - an infinite sum can give a finite result. In this case, it is the sum of energy lost over an infinite period of time rather than the distance traveled over an infinite number of intervals.

Why is this the equation for usable energy? It's not, necessarily... but it could be. As scythe said:
Quote: scythe, 2006-11-29T22:08:51Z
You're stating that the function has to reach zero if it is constantly decreasing. He's stating that there are counterexamples. Since you want to prove that it has to reach zero, you have to prove that it is not a counterexample. Until you do that, it might be one of the counterexamples, and since your result may be false, you haven't proven it.

#265447 7 2006-12-06T06:19:20Z Atilla
My worldview is closest to empirical agnostic atheism, also known as "negative agnosticism" and "weak agnosticism". I have not been given reason to believe that the existence of gods is more or less likely than the alternative. Therefore, I consider the most rational stance is to withhold judgment. I also consider that the probability of any specific religion being reasonably accurate is quite small. I do not pretend to know what happens after death, other than the obvious physical effects. I have some leanings towards apathetic agnosticism (the contention that whether gods exist or not is largely academic and irrelevant to daily life). I've never really felt that gods influence my life; they exist, they appear to be largely uninterested in me, or at the very least have a policy of non-interference.

I do not claim to know why the universe exists. However, once it *did* exist, I believe it (mostly) adhered to certain physical laws, which we have modelled through scientific means. I therefore think that, more likely than not, the universe as we know it expanded from a point about 13 billion years ago. I consider everything beyond this point speculation; you can say it appeared spontaneously or that God created it, but I don't think you can prove either.

I am a moral relativist. I judge what is ethical based on the ramifications not only of individual actions, but the underlying reasons or philosophy. For example, while enforcing the law may not have the most desirable consequences in a specific case, in the long term laws must be applied consistently if people are to respect and understand them. I also recognise that, as a human, I have ingrained sentimental tendencies, and that my judgments are unlikely to be totally objective. It is my opinion that such tendencies likely developed as a mechanism which encourages cooperation between humans, and thus increases their chances of survival, in accordance with the principles of selection.

#265852 52 2006-12-07T02:43:04Z Atilla
^ Agreed.

Consider this:

Quote: Douglas Adams
Imagine a robot that is designed to watch over a human baby in a crib. This robot is nothing but a computer, keyboard, one articulated arm, and an array of sensors for sound, motion, smell, movement, and whatnot. The robots primary mission is to gently rock the crib when the baby cries. But the articulated arm has many more capabilities. It could, if it were so programmed, kill the baby.

The programming for this computer is more complicated than a simple if-then sequence. The robot gathers input from its environment and increments or decrements counters in its memory that are the equivalent of human urges. If any of those urges reaches a 10 on a scale of 1 to 10, the robot is programmed to ignore all other program code and act according to a specific subroutine. Otherwise, if no special urges are redlining, the robot just does its job of gently rocking the baby when it detects crying.

So for example, the robot would have a jealousy counter. When the human parent enters the room, the robot detects whether its keyboard has been touched. Each time the baby gets attention but the computers keyboard is untouched, the robot adds 1 to its jealousy counter. If the keyboard is touched, the robot subtracts 1.

You can imagine the robot having a number of urges analogous to humans. It could have an anger counter that increases if the room temperature stays above 70 degrees for longer than a day. And the anger counter could be linked to the jealousy counter such that more anger makes the jealousy counter increment more than just 1 each time it is ignored. As you add more urge counters, and link them, eventually the robots state of mind becomes exceptionally complicated.

The program could be written so that some combination of urges, once they are maxed out, causes the robot to kill the baby. And just to keep things interesting, the robot routinely generates random numbers that alter how the urge counters are incremented. Sometimes an urge increases by exactly 1, other times maybe only .75 or 1.25 or even -1. The randomness isnt so great that the robot is entirely unpredictable. Most times it acts as you would expect and gently rocks the baby. But between the complexity and the subtle randomness, even the programmer cant know for sure what the robot will do next unless he manipulates the environment to some extreme, such as heating the room to 90 degrees to spike the anger counter.

The robot will, for all practical purposes, exhibit what we call choice. It doesnt have to kill the baby even if the environmental sensors pick up enough urges to do so because the randomness might decrement the urges just in time. And just for fun, the robots voice will say out loud I chose to do that after every action.

At this point I think those of you on either side of the free will argument can see that the robot is merely unpredictable and not enjoying free will no matter how often it states it is making choices. The challenge for those of you who believe in free will is to explain how the moist robots you call humans are any different. We have, for example, a basic program that keeps us from doing harmful things. But, if we get hungry enough, and our urge counters spike, we will become cannibals.

Does the robot have emotions, and is it acting irrationally?

Another example. Predicting the path of a ball which is thrown requires a substantial amount of calculus. Then, to catch it, you have to calculate the angle you need to rotate each joint to bring your hand into the right position and close your fingers around the ball, which requires trigonometry. But even people with no understanding of mathematics can do it. Why? Because your brain makes the necessary calculations without the conscious part needing to waste resources thinking about it.

Now, you may say that this isn't the way the brain calculates it, and that it instead looks back at the thousands of previous times you've tried to catch something and compares them to the current time, until it finds the closest one and makes the same movements. This may be true. But, once again, how long would it take you to (consciously) go through thousands of movie clips and analyse them all to determine which is closest to your current situation? Once again, your brain is making a judgment without bothering to inform the conscious bit what it's doing.

In the same way, when you feel hunger, your brain has remembered when your last meal was and how much food is currently in your stomach, and determined that you need to eat. You don't have to think "I last ate at 8 o'clock and my stomach holds 20% of capacity." You just want food. It's like using a calculator - you get the results and act on them, without the need to know every step taken to reach said results. This doesn't necessarily mean you are acting irrationally.

Let me state my previous arguments again, in different terms. Emotions serve a useful purpose, in that they encourage behaviour which is usually beneficial, without the need for lengthy decision-making processes which may be beyond the intellectual capacity of some individuals.

Take pain, for instance. Say you felt no pain. If you put your hand against a hot object, you would need to think "This object is too hot for me to touch safely. I must remove my hand." While you did so, your fingers would be badly burnt. However, with the current arrangement, your brain doesn't even enter into it - as soon as the pain signal reaches your spinal cord, a message is sent back to your arm telling it to move away from the source of pain as quickly as possible. Because this is so much faster than waiting for you to make a rational decision, you would suffer much less damage! Likewise, if you wife is getting savaged by a wolf, you don't have time to weigh every alternative and decide to help her. You just do it because you have an emotional attachment and instinctively feel that you should help.

Quote: Tsukatu, December 11, 2006 10:25 am
Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle is actually irrelevant. It pertains to human knowledge of an electron's speed and position at any given time. It obviously has both, we just can't know both.

That's not actually true, as far as we know. If the physical world was not constrained to obey the uncertainty principle, many of our explanations wouldn't work. This interpretation has been upheld by numerous experiments and is agreed to be better by most physicists. Indeed, the wikipedia article Keron posted includes quite a good discussion about it, as does the one about the Copenhagen interpretation which it links to. In particular, the belief that the motion of particles at the quantum level is somehow determined by "hidden variables" - which you appear to be implying you support - has been shown to be inconsistent with the laws of physics as we know them. You may choose disagree with the Copenhagen interpretation, but you cannot claim it to be disproven with any degree of validity, and must therefore acknowledge that you have made a leap of faith in believing in a deterministic universe.

Anyway, I think the whole question is largely irrelevant, because you can't possibly tell the difference. If you 'choose' to have orange juice for breakfast, was that free will, or was it simply determined by the state of your brain? Even if you use the Dagger of Time to go back and choose apple juice instead, who's to say you weren't fated to alter time and choose apple juice? (Not to mention that it's not really the same decision, since you have extra knowledge...)

Relative to one of the cars, the other car is moving at 200 km/h (just add the two speeds together: 100+100=200), and I am moving at 100 km/h (also add the two speeds: 0+100=100). Quote: Spiker, 2006-12-14T03:00:39Z
-When two spacecraft travel past each other at 60% the speed of light, the appear to move away at 60% the speed of light.

However, the situation with the cars only works for speeds considerably less than the speed of light. If two spaceships travel in opposite directions travel at 60% of the speed of light relative to me, one will not be travelling at 120% of the speed of light relative to the other; instead, you have use a complicated mathematical formula to work out the relative speeds, which will end up being a little below the speed of light (but still greater than 60% of the speed of light). It's counter-intuitive, yes, but that's the way the world works.

Quote: Spiker, 2006-12-14T03:00:39Z

It's also totally incorrect. Ignoring for the moment that you can't travel at the speed of light, the speed of light is the same for all observers, regardless of their motion relative to one another. No matter how fast you are going, light will still appear to move at a set speed relative to you. Also, in your own frame of reference, you are always stationary (you can't really be moving relative to yourself, can you?), and since you are carrying the mirror it is also stationary relative to you. You would therefore be able to see your own image in the mirror.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-19T21:43:40Z
But if evolution is driven by DNA variation, how can we model evolution without the DNA in the picture? Its like saying 'Origin of the Species' could change into 'The Holy Bible' without looking at the books' text.

You can identify a pattern without knowing the precise cause of every element in that pattern. In fact, this is how many scientific discoveries are made: you first identify a trend, and then seek the underlying causes.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-19T21:43:40Z
Also, my point in bringing this up was looking at not only the F1, but the F2 and F3 generations. So a 2 foot average suddenly recieves a 3 foot mutant. This is beneficial to the mutant, so it produces a 2.5 foot offspring. Then the 2.5 foot offspring mates and produces a 2.25 foot offspring, then a 2.135 foot offspring, etc. This continues, so the benefit of a length enhancing mutation is eventually nullified by the averaging effect in the population.

Except that it doesn't work like that. For a start, you've totally ignored selection pressure. If being tall were an advantage, the average would gradually rise because more of the tall creatures would survive and breed. Say, for example, that you start with 4 2-ft couples, and one 2-ft/3-ft couple (average height of species: 2.1 ft), each of which produces five offspring. Now say that the mortality rate is 40% for creatures shorter than 2.25 ft, and 20% for others. In the next generation, there will be 12 2-ft creatures, and 5 2.5ft creatures (average height of species: 2.147 foot). Let's say we end up with one 2.5 ft couple, one 2.5/2 ft couple, and five 2 ft couples, with one lonely 2.5 ft creature. In the third generation there are 15 2 ft creatures, 5 2.25 ft creatures, and 5 2.5 ft creatures. The average height is now 2.15 foot. Notice that the average height has increased each generation, even though there have been no new mutations. This is grossly simplified, of course, but it demonstrates that when selection pressures are present, you can't simply assuming mutations are "nullified" by the effects of averaging.

Furthermore, as has been pointed out, many traits do not average like that, and even when they do, the chance for offspring with the original mutation is increased if one or both parents have said mutation in their ancestry.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-19T21:43:40Z
Ok, photosensitive is a misstatement. What would you call cells that produce vision for an organism? Even if you got these cells, you'd need a highly organized nerve system to translate the reactions of these eye cells to the brain.

No, you don't. At the most basic level, you would have a cell (or patch of cells) sensitive to light, attached to a nerve. When light strikes these cells, the ensuing reaction sends an electrical signal down the nerve. If this signal is there, light; otherwise, dark. That's advantage enough for many creatures. After all, any plants move to face towards sources of light, and they are not renowned for their amazing brains and complex neural network.

Quote
The explanation so far is reasonable, even delightful, but what I find intriguing is that Darwinists are not troubled by the unfitness of the peahen's sexual taste. Why would natural selection, which supposedly formed birds from lowely predecessors, produce a species whose females lust for males with life-threatening decorations? The peahen ought to have developed a preference for males with sharp talons and mighty wings. Perhaps the taste for fans is associated genetically with some absolutely vital trait like strong eggshells, but then why and how did natural selection encourage such an absurd genetic linkage

The most obvious answer would be that the tail used to be more useful, but no longer is, or that it became linked with some other trait by chance. Also, as has been pointed out, it's not such a hindrance that it usually results in peacocks being killed. You have to remember that, contrary to the slogan, evolution is not survival of the fittest but survival of the fit-enough; as long as the problems with a trait are not large enough to get most of the population killed at an early age, the species can still servive.

Incidentally, I believe the tail can also be used to make the peacock appear large and intimidating, frightening off some predators.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-20T20:11:14Z
The birds which are flightless still have flight-perfect feathers, just not in the right places and not enough of them. What would have HAD to have happened then, as far as evolutionists are concerned, would be that the flightless birds evolved from flying birds.

It could go both ways, Say that you start with bellows-lung proto-birds with shoddy feathers, which can float short distances by flailing madly (rather like an inefficient chicken, if you will). They develop better feathers, which enable better flight. Some of these flying proto-birds develop the circulatory lung, enabling much more efficient flight. The bellows proto-birds start dying out because their flight mechanism wastes too much energy and is no longer effective for evading predators, which have developed better jumping and climbing ability to counteract it. The circulatory-lung birds then produce ground-dwelling variants which fill the niche left by the dying proto-birds. They are able to evade the predators despite their improved jumping ability because they they can fly further and faster due to their ancestors' optimisation for flight. Hence, circulatory lungs replace bellows lungs in birds.

Quote: Wikipedia
Some assert that evolution cannot create information, or that information can only be created by an intelligence. Physical information exists regardless of the presence of an intelligence, and evolution allows for new information whenever a novel mutation or gene duplication occurs and is kept. It does not need to be beneficial or visually apparent to be "information." However, even if those were requirements they would be satisfied with the appearance of nylon eating bacteria, which required new enzymes to efficiently digest a material that never existed until the modern age.

Japanese researchers demonstrated that nylon degrading ability can be obtained de novo in laboratory cultures of Pseudomonas aeruginosa strain POA, which initially had no enzymes capable of degrading nylon oligomers. This indicates that the ability of bacteria to digest nylon can evolve if proper artificial selection is applied. Recently, the same group found X-ray crystal structure of the newly evolved nylon-digesting enzyme. Using the structural results, the authors propose "that the amino acid replacements in the catalytic cleft of a preexisting esterase resulted in the evolution of the" nylon-digesting enzyme. This hypothesis still needs to be confirmed by detailed genetic studies.

..you can't all of a sudden have a cell possessing these specific photon-receptive enzymes without the DNA to code for it.

You don't have "these specific enzymes". You have others which aren't as effective as photoreceptors but have another use. Eventually you end up with specialised photoreceptors.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-27T18:09:47Z
It appears that the only answer for my argument (directly above) is that it can be done by computer stuff.

We point out that photosensitive molecules are common. We say that even cells which are not photoreceptors have a degree of sensitivity to sunlight. We tell you that many proteins with other uses also happen to be photosensitive. We point to creatures which have a eye which is missing several components, yet still provides an advatage. We show that a complex neural system is not required, since there are many organisms which lack such a system but can still perceive light. Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-27T18:09:47Z
Frankly, I dont understand a word of the computer thingie. Whats a logic cell? How exactly did they pass through it.

Very Basic Description of Evolution of Electronic Device Which Differentiates Between Two Signals:

1. Take a bunch of circuit components. Get computer to randomly generate a way of putting them together. Do this a bunch of times and run two different signals through the devices.

2. Toss out all the ones which don't do anything or behave randomly. Keep any that look vaguely like they might possibly do different stuff if you put signals of a different frequency through.

3. Randomly "breed" (mix) the remaining lot to produce another bunch. Chuck out all the useless ones and breed the remaining ones again.

4. Repeat 4000 times.

5. Get a device that produces a stable 5V output if one signal is put in, and nothing on the other signal. This fulfills the original goal.

It also produces a design which appears totally ludicrous and which no human engineer can comprehend. Some of the bits weren't even connected to the circuit. A human engineer would assume they didn't affect the operation of the circuit, but if you remove them it stops working. Even the guy who built it had no idea how the heck it worked. If it was part of an animal, people would probably say that it must be irreducibly complex because we couldn't determine a clear-cut route for designing it just by looking at the components. The point ian was trying to make is that humans are not good judges of precisely what is "irreducibly complex", and that it's therefore a bit silly to throw out a theory which seems to work well simply because there are one or two appendages we don't fully understand.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-27T18:09:47Z
Because of the complexity of the rules of English grammar, most English sentences are totally isolated

That's not true of all sentences. Furthermore, I could replace "grammar" with "grammer" and you would still interpret the sentence in the same way, but also deduce that I'm not good at spelling. Which leads me to my next point...

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-27T18:09:47Z
Isnt information by definition sensible or meaningful?

No, not at all. That refers to quality of information rather than quantity. "AAdjA" gives you the same amount of information as "House" (ie five characters). It just makes less sense two you.

Furthermore... you might say that you can draw additional meaning from "House", but this is not a quantifiable or objective measure. For example, I may have written a computer program in which the string "AAdjA" is a flag for user preferences, or "AAdjA" may be a codeword telling my troops to retreat. How can you say that "AAdjA" always means less than "House"? It's certainly not true for non-English speaking people, for a start. What I'm saying is that the "sense" and "meaning" is extrinsic rather than intrinsic to the information; that is, it depends on circumstance and who or what is receiving the information, rather than the information itself. Therefore, the amount of information present is unrelated to how much sense it makes to any given observer.

Did you watch the demo?

Get a good run-up. Make sure you're going as fast as possible. Tap jump *just* before you hit the slope, as shown in the picture. If you jump too early, you will be falling as you hit the slope and lose momentum; ideally, you should still be rising as you hit the slope, but you should be still be able to make it if you reach it at the peak of your jump. As soon as you land on the slope, hit jump again (still holding right), then again as soon as you hit the wall (also, release the right key now). Don't try and wait until you can clearly see the ninja touching the wall or you'll probably be too slow; anticipate when you're going to hit the wall.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-01-22T21:44:18Z
Investigators have many times acquired anomalous dates by the potassium-argon method as well as other methods. Consider the tests run on historic lava flows in Hawaii. (footnoted reference available upon request) Rocks from the Kaupelehu Flow, Hualalai Volcano, known to have erupted in 1800-1801, were dated with a variety of methods on several different minerals and inclusions. Although too young to have produced much radiogenic argon or helium, the rocks contained large quantities of these gases dispersed throughout. The article reports 12 dates, ranging from 140 million years to 2.96 billion years! The dates average 1.41 billion years! The authors go to great lengths to try to explain them away, claiming primarily that, as it rose, the magma brought with it older material from deep inside the earth, but the authors were unable to explain how the gases were retained, and why the different gases and minerals gave such different ages.

I request the reference. Because I suspect it actually refers to a report which tested xenoliths (foreign rocks) in the lava, and which further states that the apparent "ages" were not considered meaningful. Such tests are commonplace, and are used to determine which materials and in which circumstances radiometric dating may be considered reliable. I would also like the sources for the other studies you mention.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-01-22T21:44:18Z
The speed of light has slowed visibly within our lifetimes. Whos to say the average rate of the speed of light might not have been represented by f(x)=1/x? This way, many stars light could reach the earth quickly despite the distance. Even if its linear, the rate would have been significantly higher in the past.

Reference, please. Also, by our current understanding of physics, many other things are dependent on the speed of light. This would cause some odd effects, which we should be able to detect.

-----

Extra arguments: What about erosion and weathering? For example, we're fairly sure the Great Pyramid at Giza has been around for, ooh, about 4500 years, in which time it has - of course - suffered from some erosion. Now, there are many natural structures in somewhat similar conditions which appear to have suffered from much more severe weathering. This would seem to imply that they are far older than the Great Pyramid. How do you explain this?

We know of many large impact craters. An impact of sufficient force to produce them would cause great upheaval for much of the planet. We can also look at other planets and moons where erosion is less of a concern and note the extremely large number of impact craters visible. Obviously, our atmosphere stops a lot of the smaller meteors, but we must assume that Earth has suffered a similar number of large impacts. If these had all occurred in a short period of time, and humans had been present, there should be records of meteor strikes regularly wiping out whole countries and coating everything in dust for hundreds of kilometers around. Then, of course, we may compare the number of impact craters on an "old" surface and a "new" one - for example, a relatively stable part of Mars' surface and a part which has been covered by lava flows from one of its many volcanoes. The number of impact structures in these lava flows is much less than the number of impacts in a relatively undisturbed area of Mars' surface. Therefore, we can deduce that Mars is much older than these flows. Indeed, we can even see some craters which have been mostly filled with lava. Given that covering large areas with such flows takes time, Mars must be quite old. It seems unreasonable to assume that Earth somehow popped into existence a substantial time after Mars, so we must instead assume Earth is also rather old.

Finally, from what we know of astrophysics, it would take a long time for the Sun and the planets to form, and even more for the surface to become conducive to life as we know it. Unless you assume that the solar system somehow all appeared at once, in its current state, Earth must be quite old to exist as it does now. And, of course, I point out that it is logically impossible to support the notion that the solar system came into existence in its current form through empirical evidence, so there's no point trying to "prove" this occurred. Rather you must prove than accepted astrophysics is incorrect.

Er... not really. As far as we know, it's quite possible for huge floods and tsunamis to occur without divine intervention. A few centuries ago, people cried "Witch!" instead, because that fit with the culture of the time. A few millennia ago, gods were a great way to explain things you didn't understand - including natural disasters.

Then, of course, we have all the other physical features or events which are explained by Religion X. For example, the giant catfish Namazu is said to cause earthquakes when the god Kashima, who restrains the fish, lets his guard down. The scientific authorities were adament that the earth was the center of the universe, and called it heresy to say otherwise.

"Heresy" is a charge of defying a religion. Religious authorities, particularly the Catholic Church, were adamant that Earth was the centre of the universe. Indeed, Galileo was placed under house arrest and ordered not to hold or support heliocentric views. Even in ancient times, it was declared that heliocentric views were against religion in Europe, after the Greek astronomer Aristarchus proposed a heliocentric model in around 300 BC.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-01-29T21:38:55Z
Funkhouser, John G., and Naughton, John J., "Radiogenic Helium and Argon in Ultramafic Inclusions from Hawaii," Journal of Geophysical Research, Vol. 73, No. 14, July 1968, pp. 4601-4607

This was not a test of the age of a lava flow. It was instead a test of ultramafic inclusions contained in the lava (as it says in the paper's title, might I add) - that is, other rocks which were carried in the lava, but were formed earlier. Despite the fact that the paper clearly states from the beginning that it is not the lava which was being tested, Morris somehow claims this was an attempt to "explain away" the alleged problems with the dates. This is a gross and seemingly deliberate misinterpretation.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-01-29T21:38:55Z
Woodmorrape, John, "Radiometric Geochronology Reappraised," Studies in Flood Geology, Institute for Creation Research, 1993
Here's a decent rebuttal.

In short, it demonstrates that Woodmorappe does not adhere to commonly accepted standards for scientific reporting, misquotes many of his sources, and dumps large amounts of data with little context, all of which lead to misinterpretation of data. The results cited only appear problematic because they have been misconstrued.

Unfortunately, I'm having slight trouble accessing the others: I can't find several of them at all (are you sure you copied the references correctly?) and I'm required to subscribe to a journal to access the others. I would, however, also like to point out that:

1. Most of the references are from the 1960s, when radiometric dating was relatively new and less well understood. Why aren't there more references to recent studies? If radiometric dating was always inaccurate, surely there should still be problems in modern papers? For example, Morris says that K-Ar dating is often used incorrectly to support slow ocean floor spreading, but fails to refer to any publications where this occurs.
2. The fact that many of the papers are so old may be one reason they are difficult to find. This, in turn, makes it rather hard to actually verify what Morris claims.
3. Morris refers to K-Ar dating of very young samples. However, it is known that K-Ar dating is unsuitable for such samples. This means Morris is stating that applying an dating technique incorrectly yields inaccurate results, which is hardly surprising.
