@Sea salt:
Firstly, I note that the article "Sea salts loses its savour for evolutionsists", to which you linked, takes as its first and primary reference a study of processes which add and remove salt from 1899. I feel is is reasonable to dismiss that particular report on the basis that at that time, measurements could not be taken over a wide enough area to be meaningful and furthermore that there would be a relatively poor understanding of such processes at that time. Even now, our understanding is rather limited; how much worse was it a century ago?

Secondly, I note that you refer to measurements of the amount of salt going into or out of the ocean, not measurements of the actual salinity. This could be problematic. Firstly, we are not sure that we know of all processes which affect salinity. Secondly, changes in salinity are not uniform (1, 2 (PDF)). Wouldn't it be a bit odd for large areas of ocean to become less saline if all this salt was being dumped into the ocean and not removed?

Finally, the amount of salt present in the oceans is incredible. If you assume that the oceans started out fresh and that salt has since been deposited, where was it originally? It would surely cause problems, or at least large differences in the ecology, if it were all on land.

Quote: Atilla, 2007-02-07T00:21:28Z
Again, although there are some scientists who are outspoken atheists, this is not true of the whole community (or even the majority). Please stop trying to present scientists as some kind of antitheistic cabal. You've done it before, it's not remotely accurate, and it's not impressing anyone.

From where did you get this number?

One of the more well-known studies, a survey conducted by Scientific American, found that 40% of scientists with a Bachelor of Science professed "belief in a personal god and afterlife". Then there's this study (PDF), which found that only about 25% of scientists were actually atheists or agnostics. A substantial proportion believed in a higher power but not a personal god, or said that although they had many doubts, they still felt they believed in God. About 36% said they were certain that God exists, which would make up the 40% reported in the other study if you throw in some of the doubters. And here is a media report referring to another study which showed two thirds of scientists are religious. The fact is that, although there are a greater proportion of atheists in scientific institutions than in the general population, most scientists are religious in some form.

#295243 4 2007-02-09T01:12:11Z Atilla
^Thank you for those rather unhelpful comments. Now go away.

Ahem. Anyway...

Your personal best for the Metanet levels is recorded automatically, and may be viewed by clicking on your score for that level in the Highscores menu.

Demos are also recorded automatically for levels in the user levels menu. Upon completing a level, the level and demo data will appear in the box on the left, in the format $level name#author#category#level data#demo data#. If you want to post the demo on NUMA, you'll need to get just the demo data from the end. Note that you cannot record demos this way unless you actually complete the level.

If you wish to record a demo in debug mode (Ned), you should click outside the text boxes, reset the level, and press 1 to begin recording. When you finish the level/die/whatever, you should then return to the Ned menu, press 2, and copy the text in the "demo data" box.

The Rules (Rambling Version)

Atilla tells you. You are no longer a mewling kitten and have learned to keep secrets from Atilla, and so Atilla tells you.

In the beginning, there shall be Nine, and each shall fashion from the aether a tileset, which shall be sent to Atilla via the arcane mysteries of the PM button. And after the first week, Atilla shall engrave these tilesets upon a text file of granite, and place them in the forum square that all may see. And the people shall judge the maps, voting for their favourite; and the map which is most loved by the people shall be great in Atilla's eyes. If an author should fail to craft a worthy map, and receive not a single vote, then they shall be cast from the sphere of Heaven and a new god shall take their place.

Atilla will then say unto the Nine, take this tileset which was made for you, and create from it a level worthy of the vault of Heaven. And they shall each craft a fine level, and once more present it to Atilla. Again, Atilla shall show the levels to the people, saying "Which among these is the greatest?" And that which is deemed most worthy shall be taken, and the others cast aside, and any of the Nine who are unworthy shall again be banished, and another shall take their place.

Once more Atilla will speak unto the Nine, saying: "Take this, all of you, and playtest it. This is the map of your colleagues, which has been given to you." And the Nine shall take the map, and shall make small modifications. Once more Atilla shall place their maps before the people and ask which is greatest; and after their judgment, shall we know the One, True Map.

There are no turtles anywhere.
...it's so depressing.

The Rules (Clear Version)

Stage 1
I shall take the first nine authors to post here saying they're in (telling me on IRC works, too). Others may be taken later, so post if you want to participate even if more than 9 people are already in.
They shall each make a tileset, and PM it to me. Text, pastebin or NUPB is fine.
I shall put the tilesets into a single text file and post a voting thread.
Anyone who is not currently one of the Nine will vote on their favourite by means of a poll.
The map with the most votes will be used as the basis for the next stage.
If a map doesn't get a single vote, the author will drop out, making room for the next on the list.

Stage 2
Each author shall create a level based on the tileset which was chosen. Small modifications to the tiles are allowed - just treat it as if you were using a tileset from NUMA.
The authors shall PM their levels to me, and I shall post them for voting, just like the last stage.
The map with the most votes shall be used as the basis for the next stage.
If any author fails to get at least one vote, they will drop out and another will be drafted.

Stage 3
Each author shall play the level from the last stage. They shall then make some small alterations to the map - tiles, objects, whatever, as long as it's still more or less the same map.
Each map shall again be judged against the others - and this time, against the original, too.
The most popular will be declared the One Map, and shall be posted and advertised blatantly by me, bringing its contributors worship and praise.

Miscellaneous Stuff (Yes, this is important!)

Since we can't really rank people, there won't be any prizes - other than the huge bragging rights afforded to those who have their maps chosen. Hopefully, the end result will be so spectacularly glorious that merely being associated with it will be enough to attract hordes of screaming fans.

I encourage as many people as possible to participate, whether by voting or signing up as a potential mapmaker. It doesn't require a huge investment of time - just make a map and submit it once a week, or play a bunch of maps and vote for your favourite. Even if you're not in the first nine, you can still get drafted later on, and remember too that if you don't vote for your beloved, they may get kicked out! Also, if this goes well, I might run another one, so if you're interested make sure I know it!

At this point, I intend to give the Nine a week to make a map in each stage. If you don't meet the deadline, you taste the end of my boot and the next person on the list takes your place. I will then give people some time to vote - I'll set the timeframe for this later, depending on how fast votes are coming in on the first round, but it won't be longer than a week. In total, this competition should run no longer than 6 weeks.

#305483 53 2007-03-16T00:01:16Z Atilla
Quote: blue_tetris, 2007-03-15T23:11:07Z
You have to evaluate your definition of "choice", then.  A depressed person chooses suicide in much the same way that I choose to wear jeans in the morning. With a different set of personality traits, I'd have no choice but to choose slacks, instead, right?

I don't think so. I mean, I don't know about you. I usually wear pants, but I could wear shorts instead with a minimum of fuss. I wouldn't need medication and years of counseling to cure me of my pants-addiction. The same isn't true of suicide. You can ask someone not to wear a certain item of clothing and they may well concede, but you can't just ask someone not to be depressed and expect it to happen.

That said, "choice" is always a badly-defined word. There's no one definition which suits all circumstances. I tend to distinguish between things which can be altered without a huge amount of trouble - for example, it's not a huge matter for me wear a red shirt instead of a blue. Likewise, I can "choose" to do study or play games. We also have to consider how circumstances effect these choices - for example, it's a lot harder to study if there's a screaming match going on next door, so people are more willing to sympathise if you choose not to. You shouldn't steal, but if the choice is theft or starvation, people are more understanding - they'll even say you "had no choice".

Now, humans (indeed, all animals) generally have a very strong instinct to preserve themselves and their friends/family/associates. If someone is driven to the point where their desire to live is overridden - particularly when there is no benefit to anyone else - I think it's reasonable to say that their condition and circumstances have lead them to a place where they believe there is no other option, and that we should be cognisant of this and thus allow them some leeway when we consider their actions.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2007-03-15T23:11:07Z
At what point do we allow people to forfeit a degree of liability for the things that they do?  When a doctor labels you with a "disorder", you're a victim.  When society labels you an addict, you're to be worthy of pity, because you're not responsible for your choices.  When you are too oblivious by character to respect someone's race, you're entirely responsible for the words that you've chosen and the rude things you've said.  When you're depressed, you're not liable for the maintenance of your life.

Circumstances must always be considered when judging another's actions. One major cause of social problems is that people neglect to consider them, and instead ascribe things purely to someone's character - for example, the belief that blacks must be stupid and lazy because they tend to be less educated ignores the fact that they are less educated due to the socio-economic disadvantage they were born into as a result of the oppression of their ancestors.

Even things like racism are often the result of ignorance and upbringing, things over which the racist has no control. Yes, racism certainly shouldn't be tolerated, but it's not entirely the fault of the bigot. This is why, in the long term, we need to encourage multiculturalism and education to combat racism. Speaking out against it reduces (or at least suppresses) it to some degree, but ultimately the underlying causes need to be addressed. It's the same in war - always we must seek revenge for the evil atrocities committed against us, by committing the same atrocities against others. We are too stiff-necked to realise that even our enemies are human, too quick to demonise others instead of seeking reconciliation.

Calling those who commit suicide selfish cowards does not help. It does not reduce the rate of suicide. On the contrary, it makes those who are depressed fear to tell anyone because they believe they will be castigated. It reinforces their negative beliefs about themselves. It therefore prevents people seeking proper treatment which may prevent suicide. Is calling someone a coward so important to you that you are willing to risk lives to do so?

Quote: Neil Gaiman in American Gods
There are stories that are true, in which each individual's tale is unique and tragic, and the worst of the tragedy is that we have heard it before, and we cannot allow ourselves to feel it too deeply... if it were to touch us it would cripple us or make saints of us; but, for the most part, it does not touch us. We cannot allow it to.

Tonight, as you eat, reflect if you can: there are children starving in the world, starving in numbers larger than the mind can easily hold, up in the big numbers where an error of a million here, a million there, can be forgiven. It may be uncomfortable for you to reflect upon this or it may not, but still, you will eat.
There are accounts which, if we open our hearts to them will cut us too deeply. Look- here is a good man, good by his own lights and the lights of his friends: he is faithful and true to his wife, he adores and lavishes attention on his little children, he cares about his country, he does his job punctiliously, as best he can. So, efficiently and good- naturedly, he exterminates Jews: he appreciates the music that plays in the background to pacify them: he advises the Jews not to forget their identification numbers as they go into the showers - many people, he tells them, forget their numbers, and they take the wrong clothes, when they come out of the howers. This calms the Jews: there will be life, they assure themselves, after the showers. And they are wrong. Our man supervises the detail taking the bodies to the ovens; and if there is anything he feels bad about, it is that he still allows the gassing of vermin to affect him. Were he a truly good man, he knows, he would feel nothing but joy, as the earth is cleansed of its pests.
Leave him; he cuts too deep. He is too close to us and it hurts.

...We need individual stories. Without individuals we see only numbers: a thousand dead, a hundred thousand dead, 'casuaties may rise to a million'. With individual stories, the statistics become people - but even that is a lie, for the people continue to suffer in numbers that themselves are numbing and meaningless. Look, see the child's swollen, swollen belly, and the flies that crawl at the corners of his eyes, his skeletal limbs: will it make it easier for you to know his name, his age, his dreams, his fears? To see him from the inside? And if it does, are we not doing a disservice to his sister, who lies in the searing dust beside hinm, a distorted, distended caricature of a human child. And there, if we feel for them, are they now more important to us than a thousand other children touched by the same famine, a thousand other young lives who will soon be food for the flies' own myriad squirming children?
We draw our lines around these moments of pain, and... they are covered with a smooth, safe, nacreous layer to let them slip, pearl-like, from our souls without real pain.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2007-03-15T23:11:07Z
Are we wrong to use the word cowardice at all, being that every person is just a just slave to his persona?  At what point am I allowed to make a judgment?  When I can I use the word "coward", or any other subjective definition of someone's will and behavior, Atilla?

I think some distinctions need to be made to define "feeling low" from "being depressed" from "being clinical depressed" from "suicidal behavior".

Suicidal behaviour is attempting to kill yourself or seriously considering deliberately killing yourself.

We could distinguish normal and clinical depression through medical terms (brain activity & chemistry) but that's not terribly practical for the purposes of this discussion, so I'll try and do it a different way. "Feeling low" and the colloquial use of "depression" refer to a temporary bad mood, usually caused by outside circumstances. Once these circumstances alter, the depression should lift. For example, if your grandmother died, yeah, you'd be upset for a while, but eventually you'd move on. Clinical depression, on the other hand, is persistent - even in the absence of negative influences, the sufferer tends to be unhappy (although external circumstances can still help or hinder, of course). Suffering "normal" depression for an extended period of time, or going through a particularly traumatic event (such as sexual assault) can sometimes cause clinical depression.

We may draw several analogies. Say, for example, that each person has a happiness rating between 1 and ten. A "normal" person tends to hover around 5 unless something is making them happy or unhappy. If something horrible happens, them may well plunge to 1, but they should slowly return to 5 as long as nothing else goes wrong. Someone who is clinically depressed might have 3 as their midpoint instead of 5 - they are much more vulnerable to outside events and tend to be less happy in general unless they are well supported. We could also compare depression to a kind of emotional AIDS - without proper treatment, it's difficult for someone who is clinically depressed to maintain their health or recover from injuries which would heal quickly for most people.

A Melbourne supporter (theist) claims that Melbourne is the best team.

#308528 65 2007-03-29T07:34:02Z Atilla
Meaning is not of necessity defined by common usage. For example, "weight" is commonly used to mean "mass". However, this does not mean physicists are incorrect when they define weight and mass as separate concepts. When using these terms in serious discussion, the correct usage is not determined by majority, but rather by the technical meaning which is required in those circumstances. If you say that you've lost 5kg (rather than 49N) since you started going to the gym in casual conversation, that's fine. If, however, you write on your physics exam that something "weighs" 50kg, you will lose marks, because that usage is incorrect for the context regardless of popularity.

By the same token, many people use "atheist" to describe what I would call an "antitheist". Their definition of atheism is used in common speech, but is not suitable for scholarly debate. In a similar fashion, when asked about my religious affiliation I usually say that I am agnostic, rather than that I am an agnostic atheist, because most people would understand what I mean. However, when in-depth discussion arises, we should adhere to the technically correct definitions - that agnosticism is separate from theism and atheism, and that atheism is simply lack of theism.

In upholding the correctness of this definition over macaddict's, we may examine an unfortunate problem with the latter: theistic and atheistic are supposed to be binary descriptors. If you're not one, you're the other. However, under macaddict's terms, there are many positions which are neither. The doctrine which is widely described as "weak atheism", for example, would not be considered a form of atheism. The "common usage" which has been cited for macaddict's definition clashes with other terms when used in philosophical debate.

Then there is simply the fact that there are large numbers of self-described atheists who disagree with that definition. I've known quite a few people who see no difference between "Catholic" ("antitheistic") and "Christian" ("atheistic"), yet it is nevertheless incorrect to describe Protestants ("atheists") as "Catholic" ("antitheistic") or "non-Christian" ("not atheistic"). Attempting to define someone's beliefs in a way they disagree with generally won't get you very far.

You must also consider that "popular usage" depends on circumstance; for example, since I live in a Western country and I am of obviously caucasian appearance, the word "religious" is almost always assumed to be functionally identical to "Christian" when applied to me. However, it would be silly to claim theism means "belief in a Christian God" based on "popular usage".

EDIT: What Kablizzy said, basically.

Firstly, I recommend you skip the level and come back later if it's causing that much grief.

Secondly, your problem is that you are either jumping too early, jumping too late, or you are holding down the jump key instead of just tapping it really quickly. Record a demo in debug mode (Ned) and play it back in frame-by-frame (ie turn off caps lock) to see where you are going wrong.

Unfortunately, the first jump is more unforgiving than normal because the mine blocks some of the space at the end. Even when you get the first jump right, you almost have to get the second frame-perfect. You'll get it eventually if you keep trying (or you could use the enter key to place yourself on the platform and try the second jump, which is a little easier). You might also find practicing the position of the first jump in frame-by-frame helps.

Quote: disconinja, 2007-04-17T22:50:45Z
I support outlawing guns. Hell, why don't we even outlaw murder? I mean, if murder was illegal, surely this guy wouldn't have done it, right?
Murder is outlawed...
He was being facetious. Of course murder is illegal. People do illegal things. Outlawing guns would mean it would be a crime to own a gun. Which means, guns would only be in the hands of people who were going to commit crimes anyway. Do you think outlawing the sale of guns would have made it any more difficult for this person to acquire a gun and shoot up a bunch of his classmates? Perhaps a little. Do you think the extra hurdle of a black market sale would have entirely prevented him from murdering those people, then ending his own life? Probably not.

I disagree. It is of course unreasonable to expect that, say, Mafia hitmen will be affected by a gun ban. However, random lunatics are much less likely to go to the trouble of acquiring a gun via the black market. For example, Australia has tight restrictions on firearm ownership (particularly on automatic weapons, semi-auto weapons with large magazines, and high-powered weapons) and carrying firearms. According to a report from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime in 2000, our non-firearm homicide rate per 100,000 people was about 1.5, and our firearm homicide rate was about 0.3. In the US, the non-firearm homicide rate was 5.5 (less than 4 times Australia's) and the firearm rate was 3.6 (over 10 times as much as Australia's). Why are few homicides committed with guns in Australia? Obviously there are cultural differences, but I would also say that it's simply because most people don't have easy access to firearms, and the weapons which are most readily available tend to be the least dangerous - it's difficult to kill two dozen people with with a low-powered handgun with a 5-round clip.

#314115 53 2007-04-19T00:37:41Z Atilla
Quote: blue_tetris, April 18, 2007 12:10 pm
I think it's, for the most part, cultural. I simply don't think that tightening up gun laws to that extent would be benefitial to the US. I think the US gun culture would resist any progress that could be made in that direction, anyway.

I would agree that there would be strong resistance to tighter restrictions on firearms, and agree that banning guns outright is unnecessary. However, I disagree with the view that preventing the public from carrying guns around at all times will cause a rise in violent crime. Restricting firearms may also change the culture which appears to be partially responsible for violent crime in America.

I think one of the cultural differences you speak of is that, to some degree, there is a perception in America that you can't defend yourself without a lethal firearm*. This is not the case. Aside from the obvious option to just use a blunt object (or, indeed, fight unarmed) there are deterrents such as capsicum spray. I'm sure someone will point out that capsicum spray won't help if someone is already pointing a gun at you - but if you think for a moment, you'll realise that you wouldn't be able to draw your own gun in that situation, either. Another point is that, as I said above, many countries have much tighter restrictions on firearms then America, yet still manage to apprehend gun-wielding criminals fairly quickly. Given the proliferation of mobile phones these days, police are notified of violent crime immediately and turn up promptly, and I'm fairly sure they can usually deal with the situation more effectively than gun-wielding civilians.

Furthermore, lesser restrictions, as opposed to an outright ban on carrying weapons, are a good option (although I realise you were arguing mostly against an outright ban). If you only want a gun to defend yourself, you don't really need an automatic handgun with a large clip - in most cases, you would only need to disable one assailant. Therefore, restrictions on clip size and/or auto and semi-auto weapons could inhibit murderers (killing 30 people is much more difficult if you have to reload after every few shots) while having virtually no impact on the efficiency of legal guns for self-defence. Of course, black market weapons would still be a problem, but at least the nuisance (and, possibly, expense) of obtaining illegal firearms would make the same crime more difficult to commit, and I don't think there's anything wrong with that. There are also reasonable measures which could make black market weapons substantially more difficult to obtain - for example, having more consistent laws instead of the large state-to-state variance which presently exists would prevent powerful weapons being obtained legally in a state with lax gun control, then smuggled into another state.

*This is speculation based on personal experience, so don't get stroppy if you disagree.

Episodic levels play as a coherent unit. They should generally progress in difficulty as they go along, although there are exceptions (for example, putting a short level with lots of gold after a long level is a nice change of pace, and also says "This level is here so you can make up for the time you lost last level, because this is an episode"). They should have enough to gold to be finished as an episode. Each episode should be harder than the last.

Aside from that, there are two ways to make the episodic nature more clear. The first is to group levels with similar gameplay or similar style together (you might have, say, five curvy maps, followed by five mine jumpers). The second, my preferred option, is to put a selection of different level types in each episode, so that it forms a whole which challenges all the player's skills rather than a subset of them.

Making a pack feel "episodic" is as much about organising levels as making them.

I'm no better or worse than most people.


You are hurrying to work, afraid you will be late for the third time this week. Suddenly, a little girl comes up to you distraught that she can't find her puppy. She says, "Please, I need to find my puppy and my mommy will be so upset with me if she finds out I lost it." What will you do?

Tell her I haven't seen a puppy, and that she should really tell her parents before asking randoms to look for it, then hurry off.

You see a man in a bar hitting on a group of women. They complain to the bartender, but he isn't doing anything. The man is a persistent vexation to them, and no one is paying any attention to it except you. The man refuses to leave them alone and the women refuse to leave the bar because of some pig. What will you do?

I would not intervene unless he attempted to assault them. Firstly, I doubt it would help - if the bartender won't do anything and he won't listen to the women, I doubt he'll listen to me either. Secondly, the women should walk out to make a point instead of hanging around giving the recalcitrant barkeep more money. If he lost custom when someone harassed female patrons, he might be more willing to stop it.

You find a wallet laying on the ground. You open it to find some ID, but there is none. Instead, there is only $200. You look around to see if someone is looking for a wallet, but you cannot see anyone searching. What will you do?

I'd take it to the police. Someone might be able to identify the wallet itself, and if they can't, I still get the cash.

You meet this obnoxious person while on a cruise who does nothing but complain and criticize you. When you tried to be nice, he/she only scolded you. When he/she dropped his/her wallet and you tried to give it to him/her, he/she started ranting at you for trying to steal the wallet, and nobody on the boat trusts you. Suddenly, he/she falls overboard, and you are the only person around who can help and who has seen this happen. What will you do?

Of course I'd help. If I was willing to kill someone for being obnoxious, the streets would be piled high with corpses.

A man is walking down the street with his shirt backwards, and everybody is laughing at him. He doesn't realize it, however. How would you respond to this sight?

Given that I live next to a university, I'd probably assume it was supposed to be one of the many bizarre fashion statements perpetrated on campus, and laugh at how silly it looked.

You are placed in a perfect situation to cheat on your boyfriend/girlfriend/spouse. There is no way you will be found out, and the person you have the opportunity to cheat with is particularly attractive. Will you take the opportunity to cheat?

No, unless I was already close to breaking up with my boyfriend/girlfriend/spouse, in which case I would terminate the relationship when I next saw them.

You and another person are competing for a position in a company. You have already seen the test once before and know the correct answers, but the other person has not had the test before. What will you do?

Get the job, I should hope. It's not much different from being experienced with the kind of responses employers like in an interview.

You are picked for a job out of 4 people. You know that you weren't the best for the job and that you were chosen because the boss was racist/sexist. What would you do?

Encourage the person I believe was the best to file a complaint with the Equal Opportunity Commission and testify on their behalf. I would undoubtedly clash with a prejudiced boss sooner or later anyway.

You were supposed to write an essay for your English Professor/Teacher, but you forgot about it completely until the day it is due. You see a well written essay about the very same topic on a table, with no name and is reminiscent of your style of writing. You have 10 minutes to get to class and you need to make a quick decision. Just as well, there is no one around that has claimed it yet or has asked about a misplaced essay. What would you do?

Try to write as much as I can before class. Plead for an extension, and if one is not granted, cop the terrible mark. It's my fault and my responsibility.

You came home early from school one day and caught your father cheating on your mother. You saw him, but he didn't see you. What would you do?

Aside from worrying a lot, I'm not sure. Confront him and urge him to end the affair or end the marriage?

I rarely rate below 2.5, because I don't often play maps which don't seem interesting. After all, when I browse NUMA I'm looking for maps I'll enjoy. I think a lot of people do the same thing, which would explain the above-average average. It's a selection effect - people look for good maps, more good maps are rated than bad ones, and thus the average is higher than you would expect. This can be used to explain the average rating graph:

Atilla's Speculative History of Ratings:

In the beginning, there were few maps, and most of them got rated. This lead to a relatively low average rating. As more maps became available, people stopped voting for maps which were obviously substandard, which caused the average rating to become higher. Unfortunately, because people were now seeing only high ratings, it became perceived that maps must be rated higher and higher, which lead to an overly-lenient period in which the average rating almost reached four. After numerous complaints and the introduction of rating guidelines, the average descended to a more reasonable level.

As for the high number of fives and zeros, I would say the fives are mostly the result of people browsing the top-rated, with a bit of multi-accounting and "mates rates" on the side. The zeros are probably due to the bombardment of offensive or stolen maps with 0s, and sniping. I note that the proportion of 0s and 5s has decreased since the arrival of Maesweep, which I believe is due in part to their efforts to stop abuse, as well as the introduction of the voting guidelines.

#319754 6 2007-05-09T10:49:50Z Atilla
I, of course, am not American, but I'm answering anyway.

1. Do you think citizens should have the rights to criticize elected officials like the president, governor, or city officials?

Yes. The alternative is the path to tyranny.

2. Do you think burning the American flag in anger or protest is an acceptable form of free speech or do you see it as an unacceptable act?

Why not? The country is not so fragile it cannot withstand a bit of fabric being burnt. It's really just a way to make clear your extreme dissatisfaction with the state of the nation. Not terribly tactful, but hardly worthy of banning.

3. Do you think religious beliefs that people hold sacred should be open to comedy, criticism, or insults?

Yes. Religion is a matter of opinion, as are non-religious worldviews, and are therefore subject to criticism. From a practical view, making religion untouchable just doesn't work. For a start, you can just say "I believe God gives me the right to criticise other religions" and no one is allowed to disagree.

4. Do you think books that contain harsh language or controversial subject matter (sexual refrences, fantasy/witch craft, violence, etc...) should be banned from school libraries?

Witchcraft and fantasy, no. For start, that includes things like "The Wizard of Oz" and "Hansel and Gretel". I doubt many people have been turned into blood-drinking, Satan-worshipping murderers because of such stories. Sex, violence, and obscenities should be banned from primary schools, perhaps, but not at secondary school. People need to learn about these things as they mature, and literature can be an important aid to their personal development.

5. Do you think that speakers or groups, whose views may be unpopular or hateful should be allowed to speak their mind?

Unpopular, certainly. Hateful, I'm less happy about, but probably.

6. Would you support limiting the jokes people can tell if it would help to decrease insensitive comments about racism, sexism, and intolerance (No ethnic jokes, blonde jokes, jokes about lifestyles, disabilities, etc...) ?

Yes, though I would prefer to do so simply through social pressure rather than legislation.

7. Do you think that singers/bands should be prevented from writing or performing songs that have profanity or other controversial lyrics in them?

No. Sale of such music might be restricted for minors (as it already is, I believe) but other than that, no.

8. Should the internet be regulated so that dangerous, obscene, hateful, pornographic, etc... websites would not be permitted?

Somewhat. Not block that sort of material outright, but perhaps prevent access by minors. Sites about the construction of bombs and suchlike might be banned, since there's not really a reason for anyone to know that other than behaviour which is likely to harm others.

If it isn't a point mutation, then there's got to be a gene for 'sexual orientation'. That's a gross oversimplification which pays no mind to the realities of genetics. Firstly, these interactions are complex. Genetic code is not a blueprint saying "This leg goes here, and the arms go here, fetish for fuzzy handcuffs goes here..." Nor must sexual orientation necessarily have a huge batch of genetic code simply because it effects behaviour, instincts and emotions; in fact, all three can easily be regulated by controlling the release of a single chemical upon a given stimulus, which would require little code. You may be interested to know that ferns, which do not have the complex mental faculties of humans, have far more genetic code. So do frogs, fungi, insects, algae, and bacteria, among others.

Quote: Shark, 2007-05-10T02:02:31Z
It's actually very relevant. It ties this in with Darwin's theory of evolution. If being gay really wasn't a choice, then it would have genes to code for it. Those organisms that had the gene(s) or genetic structure that made them homosexual would not reproduce, and therefore, the genes for homosexuality would be lost. (eventually, over the course of 100-150 generations.) The organisms best fit to survive their environment survive the rest die off. In this case, the gays lose because they cant reproduce.

Its just like anything else in evolution. Say, for instance, that a bug is born with a mutated gene and it is blue. The blue bug can be spotted more easily by birds and other prey, and is caught and eaten. The green bug that blends in more survives long enough to create the next generation of bugs, and green skin color is passed on. In the next generation of bugs, one certain bug is born with the ability to shift color to imitate its surroundings. It also survives, as there is even less of a chance that prey can see it. It will go on to produce the next generation of bugs that also have color shifting ability.

Homosexuality is a choice. If it wasn't, evolution would kill it. An organism's environment causes the person to be gay.

That's based on the assumption that only people who are explicitly homosexual carry genes which could cause homosexual tendencies, and furthermore that those with homosexual tendencies never breed. Both are incorrect. As was previously stated in this thread, homosexuality is not a binary trait; it's possible for people to have homosexual tendencies, or the potential for such, while remaining heterosexual. Furthermore, all genes are not always expressed. For example, I have green eyes though my parents have blue and brown eyes. In the same manner, a homosexual child may be born from a heterosexual couple. Then, of course, there are bisexuals, and homosexuals who have been forced to dissemble by societal pressures.

There may also be non-genetic factors which nevertheless influence sexuality on a biological level. Some studies show that second-born boys are more likely to be homosexual that the first born, and the third-born more likely than the second, and so on. It is believed this is because the immune reaction of a woman's body to a male embryo becomes stronger with successive pregnancies and that this inhibits masculinisation of the brain to some degree.

Unlike other traits which are detrimental to breeding, homosexuality is not fatal, nor does it inhibit the individual's other faculties. Homosexuals can make as much of a contribution to society as anyone else, and therefore there is less reason to select against homosexuality than against harmful genetic diseases. It may be that behavioural traits linked to homosexuality are in some manner slightly beneficial for society as a whole, in the same way that altruism damages the chances of an individual but still survives because having some altruists around helps the entire group.

The end result of all this is that from a biological standpoint you would expect homosexuality to be rare, but not unknown. Given what we know of the rates of homosexuality, this expectation appears to be upheld.

Quote: Keron Cyst, 2007-05-21T23:37:50Z
I think our definition of "complexity" differs... what do you mean in referring to that? (Not just Atilla... anyone here) Perhaps I was too insisting on merely multiple overlapping melodies. I would at least like however a grabbing one, not one which keeps repeating every four measures.

Very few songs have a melody which repeats every four bars. The melody in a rock song typically consists of the vocals, which usually repeat a verse several times. Most verses are maybe six to twelve lines of vocals, with perhaps two bars per line. Granted, the lines are sometimes repeated (often in twos) but it's still far from every four bars. The chorus and an instrumental section (including the ever-popular guitar solo) are also commonly used to break things up.

Beside which, classical music often has a single motif which is repeated with variations throughout the piece. A degree of repetition is a natural part of music; it is one of the things which makes a piece a coherent whole rather than simply a sequence of notes.

My interpretation of complexity? I naturally tend to lean towards a somewhat mathematical interpretation. It's the relation of elements of music to one other on various levels, particularly pitch and duration. In general, the more information you need to describe something, the more complex it is. For example, a string of 8 C's is very simple, because, well, it can be described as just 8 C's. ACBDEFGA is also very simple - "Start at A and step up a note at a time for 8 notes". GECFDBflat is more complex - "Start at G, step down two notes, step down another two, then start at F and repeat". Having 100 instruments can allow more complexity, but you can also get instructions which are fairly simple, like "10 of the violinists should play C, 10 should play F, and 10 should play A." Having a bunch of instruments is no guarantee of complexity. It also needs to be understood that complexity is not always desirable. Under my complexity scheme, for example, the most complex sound would be a bunch of random notes, which just sounds discordant and horrible.

#329015 28 2007-06-09T03:34:23Z Atilla
So, I was wandering through wikipedia and I found some even more bizarre versions of the Liar paradox.

Quote: Wikipedia
Consider the simplest version of the paradox, the sentence:

    This statement is false. (A)

[explanation of the paradoxical nature of this statement]

However, that the liar sentence can be shown to be true if it is false and false if it is true has led some to conclude that it is neither true nor false. This response to the paradox is, in effect, to reject the common beliefs about truth and falsity: the claim that every statement has to abide by the principle of bivalence, a concept related to the law of the excluded middle.

The proposal that the statement is neither true nor false has given rise to the following, strengthened version of the paradox:

    This statement is not true. (B)

If (B) is neither true nor false, then it must be not true. Since this is what (B) itself states, it means that (B) must be true and so one is led to another paradox.

This result has led some, notably Graham Priest, to posit that the statement follows paraconsistent logic and is both true and false. Nevertheless, even Priest's analysis is susceptible to the following version of the liar:

    This statement is only false. ©

If © is both true and false then it must be true. This means that © is only false, since that's what it says, but then it can't be true, and so one is led to another paradox.

Another interesting variation is:

    The writer of this statement cannot verify it to be true

In this version, the writer of the statement cannot verify it to be true, because in doing so he makes it obviously false, but at the same time cannot verify it to be false, as this would make it obviously true. Anybody else except the writer, however, can easily see and verify the statement's truth

The last one is particularly odd.

I dismiss the second one on account of tiny sample size, poor experimental procedure, and lack of proper, systematic measurements. Furthermore, the condition of plants is hardly a good comparison for effects on humans. Blasting rock at a small plant may damage its stem and leaf structure through vibration, but would not have that effect on a fully-grown oak or the human skeletal structure.

I dismiss the third on the basis that it is a personal account which does not cite sources and, in any event, that an increase in health does not imply enjoyment. Injections may improve your health but this does not mean you enjoy receiving them.

The third also focuses on effects on physiology and temperament rather than enjoyment.

Also, I notice that all these focus on a single piece of classical vs. a single piece of rock or pop (or just classical vs noise or silence). This fails to account for the wide variety inherent in both genres. I'm fairly sure playing Let It Be would have a significantly different effect to, say, Paranoid. In essence, the studies which have been performed were not formulated as a comparison between two genres of music and taking their results as evidence that an entire genre should be condemned would be unwise.

To add to what I said above in a reply to Atilla in general - is there, then, a difference between logic and reason? I agree that many Christians try to rationalise their worldview, as do most people, but I still think it is more accurate to say that God is illogical, but can exist within reason.
If God is truly omnipotent, He could just declare Himself logical and nobody could argue.

Anyway, what you have to remember here is that the issue is not whether or not God is logical, or even whether Christians are logical, but whether Christians are, of necessity, opposed to logic and reason. I am stating that this is not the case.

Belief in an entity which is illogical may not itself be illogical. If something is beneficial to you it is logical to do it, right? What if belief in something illogical is beneficial? Furthermore, being illogical, having a logical blind spot, or applying flawed logic does not necessarily mean opposition to logic and reason. To take the most extreme stance, you believe that you stance is the most logically correct, yes? This means that everyone with a difference stance must be ignoring a logical flaw in their own stance, and is therefore illogical. Thus, everyone who disagrees with you must be opposed to logic itself. I think we can agree that this is a rather silly stance to take. Most people take illogical stances because they do not know better (or they are not convinced that their stance is actually illogical), not because they actually reject logic.

We may also consider that classical logic is not the be-all and end-all. For example, the statement "This statement is not true" cannot be assigned a truth value under classical logic. It could be argued that, in a similar manner, it is unreasonable to attempt to apply classical logic to god because that is a situation where logic cannot apply. This is not opposition to logic, but rather placing a constraint on the bounds of logic; and clearly there must be some restraint, because we can easily come up with paradoxes where classical logic fails. Why "classical"? Because it may be possible to resolve these conflicts using paraconsistent logic (1) (2). I'm not terribly well versed in paraconsistent logic, but it is apparently possible to use it as a logical framework even when there are contradictions under classical logic. This may resolve issues with the omnipotence in a logical manner, thus undermining the proposition that god is illogical.

Is there a difference between logic and reason? Sort of. Reason could perhaps be considered somewhat similar to fuzzy logic, in that there is room for things like "maybe", "somewhat", "both" and "neither" instead of just "true" or "false" (er, obviously I'm comparing with classical logic here). The differences are usually most noticeable in places where logic fails, such as the liar paradox or (as you suggested) the existence of god, where we can point out that something is apparently illogical but nevertheless reasonable. I'd say that the primary difference is that reason doesn't quite have the same rigid, rigorous approach as logic. If we compare to physics, we could say that reason is a macroscopic approach, while logic is a microscopic approach.

You have similar problems even without omnipotence. If someone threatens to kill me unless I give them money, and I refuse, is my subsequent death my choice or theirs? Quote: epigone, 2007-06-24T03:50:35Z
And while the money is initially tax-free, every year you pay income tax (at least you are supposed to, I think we're pretending everything is by the books) and that chips away at your funds. It doesn't "chip away at your funds". It takes a percentage of your interest. So, say you get $70K interest and pay $30K in tax per year. Anyway...

My worldview is closest tp empirical agnostic atheism, also known as "negative agnosticism" and "weak agnosticism". It has not been demonstrated to my satisfaction that gods and suchlike exist or do not exist; therefore, the most rational decision is to withhold judgment. Unlike many people, I have never felt a personal need for religious belief or a connection to any deity, despite years of religious education. Thus, I see no need to believe in or worship a god, and I am therefore an agnostic atheist rather than an agnostic theist. I also have some leanings towards apathetic agnosticism, which is the premise that whether gods exist or not is a largely academic question and not relevant to everyday life. As I said, I have never felt that I have any connection to or that my life is influenced by any gods. Furthermore, I know of no religion whose faithful members all become incredibly lucky or any such. Indeed, atheists tend to have higher levels of education, social status, and wealth than the religious; the gods don't seem to be aiding their followers in any obvious manner.

#344349 7 2007-07-18T03:17:28Z Atilla
Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, July 18, 2007 03:58 am
Many call this an illusion, or a quale. It's not.

Eh? Being a quale does not mean something is an illusion. A quale is the perception of something. If someone else breaks a leg, you know that the leg is broken, and that it would hurt, but you don't experience the feeling of having a broken leg itself. That is, you do not have the quale of having a broken leg. The typical example is the redness of red. We can measure the wavelength and so on and assert that light is indeed red, but this won't let a blind person experience how seeing the colour red feels. A quale is the sensation a thing creates in a given observer, not the thing itself, or a property of the thing. Qualia are by definition subjective.

---

Anyway...

Say you wanted to know what 5*6 was. There are two ways to do this:

1. Go through a mathematical process (eg. 5+5+5+5+5+5).
2. Read the answer from a multiplication chart.

These are clearly quite different ways of looking at it. In the second, we care only that the answer is determined. In the first, we care about the process by which the answer is determined.

This may be compared to compatibilism and incompatibilism, which are two ways of interpreting the same information. Even if the outcome of a choice is deterministic, the process of making that choice still occurs. Compatibilists hold that this process is what is important; it doesn't matter if the outcome is always the same - the choice is still made. Incompatibilism holds instead that the outcome is the most important part; if the answer is the same, it doesn't really matter how you got there - the process may be necessary, but has no true meaning.

Quote: southpaw, 2007-07-19T04:46:51Z
The big bang was the result of all of the universes particles getting squashed into a tiny space and exploding, yet science tells us that the only thing that can be pressurized that much is gas.

Firstly, the big bang is no such thing. It is not a result of anything, so far as we can determine - beyond the big bag the laws of physics as we know them do not apply. Furthermore, the big bang was not an explosion in the traditional sense but rather a rapid expansion of the universe itself.

Secondly, the implication that "the only thing that can be pressurised that much is gas" is not only true but somehow contradicts the big bang is clearly incorrect. For example, black holes contain matter compressed to a point, and it's not accurate to describe a singularity as a gas. There's also the fact that if you apply enough pressure to a gas it turns into a liquid! I think the term you're looking for is "compressed" rather than "pressurised", but again, this is untrue.

I don't think the question is "when life begins" so much as "when personhood begins". As Tsukatu pointed out, bacteria are alive, but I'm perfectly happy killing them by the thousand; and of course sperm and ova are also alive in their way. One of the primary problems with the whole debate about abortion is that people want to draw a clear line between "unperson" and "person", when in reality no such line exists.

In any event, I believe that an embryo is certainly not a person for up to fourteen days after conception, because up until that time it can still split into twins. After that it gradually transitions from "thing" to "person". I believe that abortion of embryos (first 8 weeks of pregnancy for humans) is mostly acceptable, and perhaps up to the end of the first trimester. In general, the earlier done, the better.

I'm theoretically in favour of the death penalty, but the requirements I would place on it would be so strict it would never be used. To quote Gaiman, "I believe in the death penalty provided you can implicitly trust the legal system, and I believe only an idiot would implicitly trust the legal system."

I also think voluntary euthanasia should be legal, but only under extremely stringent requirements to prevent abuse.

#348939 6 2007-07-30T07:15:22Z Atilla
The damage system seems like it would detract from the game. My main concern is that it undermines what has traditionally been the main attraction of NSF - namely, that it encourages flamboyant, risky driving. There are already plenty of racers out there which encourage care, precision and consistency - we don't NSF to join them. As is, it's a nice bridge between the ridiculousness of Burnout - where crashes are so common, they become tedious and uninteresting - and the games which focus on more cautious and realistic driving. I, for one, would like it to remain so.

I've seen persistent damage in other racing games, and it's generally irritating. If people winning by bouncing off all the walls is a problem, then you really need to fix the game engine or track design, not just whack arbitrary penalties onto it. If you look at games with punitive damage, like the F-Zero series, hitting the walls slows you down enough that you would try to avoid it even without a damage system. If you look at games *without* a damage system, this is certainly the case. Furthermore, the shift from street races to proper tracks means you can stick sand patches, hay bales, piles of tyres and other obstacles in front of the wall, thus making scraping along it much slower.

On the shift from street races to track races, I approve with some reservations. On the one hand, it perhaps makes NSF a little more generic, although it must also be considered that many racers have street tracks these days. However, the shift to tracks will allow more emphasis on making tracks which are varied and enjoyable, rather than ones which actually resemble city streets. I actually found many of the specially designed tracks in past games, such as the URL races, Street X and Drifts, to be better than the street tracks. It will also get rid of those mysterious glowing forcefields, which basically turn the streets into a closed circuit anyway. Because of their nicely-curved shape, the forcefields are also particularly prone to being used as a "turning aid".

#349297 6 2007-07-31T07:54:48Z Atilla
Mmm, not a bad suggestion, but there are some major problems.

1. How many options for feedback are too many? If you find a map you really like, you could conceivably have to vote, comment, favourite, bitesize, and float. We're approaching the point where people just can't be bothered doing all that, or where people are so intimidated and confused by all the options that they just don't use them.

2. We already have complaints that people just can't be bothered to rate or even look at maps from relatively unknown authors. It is a concern, then, that this system will merely promote the maps which already receive lots of attention. Particularly with the time restriction, people are more likely to float their favourite author than some unknown.

One alternative is allowing users to search for maps produced after/before date X and sorting in the normal ways, although I'm not sure that this is feasible given the way NUMA stores such data. For example, you might view the most highly-rated maps from the last week. This has problems of its own, of course, but at least it improves the existing system in a manner which is fairly straightfoward, rather than adding more clutter.
#349302 10 2007-07-31T08:23:29Z Atilla
Symmetry does not mean "playing the same map twice", unless the areas are completely isolated. In most cases it means playing in an area which is twice as large. There is also the fact that your direction of approach may necessarily be different for one side of the level. If, for example, you were to traverse the level counter-clockwise, you would approach the left side from the bottom and climb up, whereas you would approach the right side from the top and fall down. This can be a significant difference as far as gameplay is concerned.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, August 11, 2007 11:13 am
Could you give me an example of an illogical truth?
That could be considered a contradiction in terms, given that "truth" is a value defined by logic. I think it would be more accurate to say things which do not have an adequately defined truth value.

There are some things which people accept - and which they must accept to operate - without logical justification.

For example, try to justify the use of logic itself. You can't use logic in doing so, because that would be a circular argument. Circular arguments are not adequate justification under the rules of logic, so you've just invalidated your own argument...

There's also the Problem of Induction.

EDIT:

Quote: mam, 2007-08-11T01:41:33Z
Also, I'm pretty sure predeterminism has been proven. Something to do with quantum physics - a beam of entangled particles is directed towards a separator. The separators were identical, each with two exit points, A1/A2 and B1/B2. It was found that if particle A chose the first route, particle B would choose the first route and if paricle A chose the second route, particle B would choose the second route. As they had no contact after separation, the only plausible explanation is that their paths were predetermined.

No. Entanglement particles will have correlated quantum states - for example, the decay of a pion (spin 0) will produce an electron and positron. By conservation of angular momentum, one must have spin up and the other spin down. As soon as you measure one, you know the spin of the other, regardless of how far away it is. However, this does nothing to prove determinism. Whether you get up or down for a given measurement is a matter of probability. Indeed, this experiment can be used to demonstrate that it is impossible for the state of the particles to be determined by any local "hidden variable".

Quote: Keron Cyst, 2007-08-11T23:30:08Z
Christianity is all about altruism. And what does Evolution regard?: "survival of the fittest," annihilation of the weak? Christ (this is the raw foundation of the religion I'm talking about, yo) willingly sacrificed himself for people who didn't deserve to even talk to or, heck, even see him! How anyone can try to combine that with the idea that all organisms that live now arose out of inorganic materials, on their own, many of which continue to, and all of which began in, destroying everything (or at least not caring about anything other than themselves or immediate family) in their paths that prevented them from developing solely for themselves and offspring of theirs alone just totally beats me. The two cannot possibly click.

Altruism benefits a whole society, and thus increases its odds of survival. This is fully compatible with evolution. Humans are by no means a special case! Wolves form packs, bees form swarms and hives, birds form flocks, cows form herds, fish form schools, lions for prides, and why? Because in many cases, it's easier to survive as part of a group than as an individual. I'd have great trouble fighting a lion alone, but with 20 compatriots I have more chance to survive. Heck, many predators are scared off by sheer numbers, so I might not even need to fight lions. With companion hunters, I can chase prey towards my fellows, increasing the likelihood of both of us getting fed. With fellow builders, I can make a wall to keep the cold out in a matter of days rather than months. As part of a society, I can become a specialist, providing one service of great quality rather then many of poor quality. The advantages of living in a society are huge for many creatures.

Say, for example, that I am a skilled weaver and seamstress, and my neighbour is a highly skilled farmer. If we are in competition and each look after only our own interests, I must farm for six hours a day to produce just enough food to feed myself. I can produce comfortable, strong clothing for myself with just four hours of work per day, being skilled in that art. Meanwhile, my neighbour only takes four hours of work to produce food to feed himself well, but must labour for six hours to produce crude clothing which soon falls apart. Now, in this situation, where both of us only look after our own interests, I work 10 hours a day for good clothing and bad food, and the farmer works 10 hours a day for good food and bad clothing. If I trade my services with the farmer, we can both work 8 hours a day and have good food and good clothing. We have better results for less effort, the advantage of living in a society!

But that is trade, you might say. What of altruism? Well, altruism benefits the group in a manner similar to trade. If I heroically throw myself at a lion to save my tribe's children, for instance, they lose one person instead of many. Yes, I and my altruistic urges are dead. However... compare the situation to a group where the guy looking after the children wasn't quite so heroic. All the tribe's children are eaten by the lion. They can probably have more, but they're badly crippled and their chances for survival and growth are now much lower. Meanwhile, my tribe - which presumably includes my equally altruistic relatives - will continue to flourish. It's a mistake to consider only individuals as part of evolution - societies without altruists will fail, and societies with altruists will flourish. It's true that individuals can gain advantage by being selfish sods - but only if there are altruists around! Otherwise, everyone competes, nothing is produced, and you all lose. This is why humans presently harbour both altruistic and selfish motives - it's a balance created by weighing the advantage of the individual against the advantage of the group.

[/rant]

Anyways, yeah, that's a given (referring to your 1337 synergy examples), but Christianity in particular is so controversial because its doctrine states that you shouldn't retaliate even if an enemy (who makes it clear as an enemy of yours for whatever reason, not an ambiguous neutral person or thing) repeatedly attacks you, on a physical and/or other level, with no justifiable reason whatsoever. So how d'ya tie -those- in?

As I have already demonstrated, a measure of altruism is an aid to survival. So is a measure of forbearance. A number of people have made it clear that they dislike me and will annoy me at every opportunity. However, I have refrained from destroying them utterly. This maintains group cohesion - if people went around retaliating every time someone was annoying them, society would rapidly fall apart. An eye for an eye makes the whole world blind, as the saying runs.

So, having established that a degree of both altruism and tolerance is necessary for a society to operate, we must consider that there is variation in all facets of humanity. There are some who have no empathy for others, who will manipulate without qualm. There are some who have no forbearance, and fly into a rage at the slightest provocation. Neither of these is held to be unnatural or impossible. Why, then, should it be impossible for someone to be abnormally altruistic, when the opposite is generally accepted as entirely plausible? If psychopathy is caused by a natural deficiency, surely abnormal tolerance can be caused by a natural excess?

We may also consider self-control, a trait which allows one to sacrifice a small gain now for a large gain later. If it is believed that God wants X, it might be considered that doing X will eventually benefit you, even if it is not in your immediate interests.

I also question the number of Christians who actually obey that command. I would say very few, which lends weight to the hypothesis that pacifism is the exception rather than the rule.

Besides, if evolution was guided by God - and this thread does regard belief in both evolution and Christianity - surely God could arrange it so that pacifism occurs naturally? He is, after all, omnipotent.

#356252 5 2007-08-17T03:21:27Z Atilla
Time and space are continuous, rather than discreet. However, uncertainty at the quantum level means that objects and events do not exist at an exact point in spacetime.

Also, your discussion of continuous time *is* more or less exactly the same as one of Zeno's paradoxes, and is flawed for the same reason. An infinite number of things can add to a finite sum. Yes, you can divide a second into milliseconds, and microseconds, and nanoseconds, and picoseconds, and so on. However, this doesn't change the fact that it is still a second! The amount of time is not infinite - you're just dividing it into infinitely small pieces.

It's highly linear. Sure, there are some optional quests, but most areas are just a path from A to B, and are arbitrarily unlocked when complete part X of the main quest. Virtually all of them will be visited in the course of the main storyline - from the top of my head, I can only recall one area which wasn't.

The combat is rather shallow and frequently repetitive. You'll run into the same kinds of enemies over and over, and dispatch them in exactly the same way. Furthermore, the magic is highly unbalanced. Slow time is the most powerful spell in the game by far, and will allow you to defeat virtually any foe by mindlessly hacking away. It's particularly foul when used in conjunction with berserk, allowing you to demolish many bosses in a matter of seconds.

The game is also rather short. I completed it in under 20 hours the first time through, and I was hardly in a rush - I collected almost everything and spent quite a while doing silly things like trying to herd a dozen chickens into the local tavern.

On the other hand, the story and dialogue are quite good. Yes, the story is completely cliched, but not through laziness. It's presented in a way which uses the unoriginal plot as a strength, rather than a weakness. The dialogue is often amusing, and the voice acting is good. The graphics are also quite nice, in most places.

As I said in the post that caused this hullabaloo, the difference is that I understand that the scientific method is not "determine a conclusion and then find evidence for it."

Nevertheless, you do not understand the scientific method. Gods are outside the scope of science, and no claim is made as to their existence or non-existence. There are no scientific theories which postulate the existence or non-existence of gods. There are no scientific theories which make any reference to gods. Whether they exist or not, science works the same way.

If gods are not relevant to science, then, what about religion? Yes, it's true that many religions make claims about the physical world, and that these claims may sometimes conflict with scientific theory. However, that doesn't mean science and religion are in opposition! Religious claims do not of necessity conflict with scientific claims. Furthermore, a great part of most religions is concerned with things which lie outside the boundaries of science. Naturally, science cannot make judgments about such things and so there is no conflict in those areas.

Another thing to remember is that in science, if something is done the same way it shouldn't matter who's doing it. No equation demands to be solved by a pure maiden. Similarly, there is no requirement that science be performed by atheists. It doesn't matter how religious a scientist is as long as they adhere to proper scientific practice.

In short, science is not founded on atheism and does not require practitioners to be atheistic. Furthermore, religion does not of necessity make claims which conflict with science. How, then, are they mutually opposed?

I really don't mean to condescend, but there's the right way to interpret statistical data and the wrong way to interpret statistical data.
In this case, we're looking at the difference in proportion of atheist scientists versus religious scientists, so the wrong way to interpret that 15% vs 30% is "most of Australia's scientists are still theists," and the right way to interpret that is "the proportion of scientists who are atheists is fully twice the percentage of atheist population."

Incorrect. The question is not whether atheists are more scientifically inclined; it is whether religion is incompatible with science by definition. Quote: Tsukatu, 2007-08-23T02:26:02Z
Here's another example::
In America (2002), roughly 16% of the population was atheistic, and 0.4% of the American (2002) prison population was atheistic. The wrong interpretation is "atheists are the minority," because that doesn't address the difference in the rate, but only states the amount in one of the relevant places. The correct way to interpret this information is, "the proportion of atheists in prison is one-fortieth the proportion of atheists in the population."
We can therefore conclude that either "atheists are more likely to stay out of prison" or "people are less likely to be atheists in prison."

Which doesn't tell you that religion is incompatible with lawful behaviour. There are plenty of religious people who follow the law, and religions which encourage following the law.

Doesn't the government create a language to cause disinterest in politics because there are no words that directly relate to politics (the language of newspeak)?

Newspeak is a constructed language which was designed to stifle free expression by removing all subtlety and shades of meaning, and replacing them with simplistic binaries. For example, "bad" would be replaced with "ungood", and words like "horrible", "atrocious" or "unethical" might all be described as "doubleplusungood". The plan was to eventually conflate these terms with each other, so that "Big Brother" was synonymous with "good". This was supposed to prevent rebellion because people would only be able to describe dissent in terms which were vague if not completely nonsensical ("Good is ungood"). However, this had not yet occurred in 1984.

Quote: scythe, 2007-09-20T00:24:27Z
Mmm? And if you were drunk too, your lack of inhibition would prevent you from considering that. Why should the judgement be any different for one party than the other? You both got drunk, you both did something irresponsible, so what's the difference?

When one person is sober or near-sober, and the other is inebriated, one person is a position in which they can reasonably foresee that their actions will harm the other, and one is not. Furthermore, the sober person can give consent, and the drunk cannot. Why? Because the sober knows what they're getting into. They probably won't be horrified at what they did when they wake up the next morning. That is, they are unlikely to come to harm from the act. The drunk, on the other hand, might well be horrified. They have a high probably of harm from the act. Because of this imbalance, the sober is responsible for harming the drunk in this case.

By contrast, if you are both drunk, neither of you can think well enough to fully realise the other person will be harmed by your actions. You are both equally at risk of harm. Thus, you are both equally responsible; we cannot single one person out as having acted in a criminal manner as we could in the previous case.

Quote: scythe33, 2007-09-20T00:24:27Z

When a person drink-drives, they are responsible for actions which have a high probability of causing harm to others. When they have drunken sex, they cause harm to themselves. And it takes two to tango - you are taking an action which you know has a reasonable chance of harming someone. You aren't excused simply because the other party was drunk. If a drunk asks you to kill them, and you do it, you're still guilty of murder. You can't just say "Oh, but they gave consent. If they didn't want it to happen they shouldn't have got drunk." Yes, they put themselves in a bad position by getting drunk, but if you hadn't taken advantage of them it wouldn't have happened.

Furthermore, I can make the same sort of argument in the opposite direction, and I doubt you'd agree with the results. Women who get raped are at fault, not rapists, because if the women didn't wear provocative clothing they wouldn't incite lust. People who get mugged are at fault because they choose to go out at night. The real criminals are the victims. It's all their fault for putting themselves in a situation where they can be victims, rather than the fault of others for taking advantage of their poor judgement.

#369284 6 2007-10-03T05:03:07Z Atilla
Light is effected by gravity because gravity distorts space. Light moves in geodesics (the shortest possible paths between two points). In flat space a geodesic is a straight line. However, in curved space (ie. a gravitational field) it is a curve, and thus light curves.

You can think of it this way. On a flat piece of paper, the shortest path between two points is a straight line. On a globe, the shortest path between two points is curved because you have to follow the curve of the surface. For example, when travelling from the north pole to the south pole, the shortest path is a "straight" line south, but this line actually traces out a semi-circle because you follow the curve of the planet. Light works in a similar way, but in four dimensions.

#369950 10 2007-10-06T04:24:01Z Atilla
Quote: smartalco, October 06, 2007 06:59 am
ok, /me is about to correct all your ignorances, even though I do not live on a farm, I know some people who do and my family farms, any questions? direct them at me

Quote: nevermore, 2007-10-05T22:58:04Z
I think I'm the man to ask here. I'm living on a farm for the second half of this year.

If we're all waving our country credentials around, I was raised in a cattle farming district. My parents used to be farmers. My grandparents were farmers. Many of my uncles are also farmers.

Quote: smartalco, 2007-10-05T20:59:20Z
1. farming != sheep, in fact farming is almost entirely referring to the whole plow the field and plant the grain part, not livestock (in other words, they said farmer, not shepherd)

They are referring to a small, more-or-less self-sufficient farm, not the large-scale cash crops which are common today. They would want a mixture of produce, including grain, vegetables, fruit, milk, eggs, and meat. Until tractors became readily available they would also need horses or oxen. Many farms also keep dogs and cats, which also require meat of some description. There's also the fact that without modern fertaliser, fields become depleted unless you allow them to lie fallow and/or rotate your crops. As such, many farmers owned a number of sheep, goats or other grazing animals, as they are useful for fertalising fields which aren't currently producing a crop.

Furthermore, I disagree with the assertion that farming is almost entirely based on crops. Cattle, beef, milk, wool and lambs are among Australia's most valuable agricultural products. Livestock may be less common in the US; I know Australia exports an obscene amount of beef to you.

Quote: smartalco, 2007-10-05T20:59:20Z
2. no one ever said you can't have internet on a farm, it will probably just cost a little to have your provider run a cable out there for you

I live on a residential property in a medium-to-large country town. It would cost several thousand dollars to install cable broadband. It's not going to be cheap on a farm.

Of course, Australia's internet infrastructure sucks badly. It might be cheaper in the US. Or you might be able to get wireless or satellite instead.

Quote: smartalco, 2007-10-05T20:59:20Z
my farm is moderate sized for the area, total, we put maybe an average of like 2 hours a day of work into it (thats average, its more like just an afternoon or 2 during the week, and an 8 hour day on the weekends, plus a full week of 12-14 hour days during harvest and drilling (planting) season

The average farm size for your area must be rather small, or the farm must be heavily populated, then. Or perhaps you only farm low-maintenance crops. All the farms I've been to require more work than that. There's also my next point...

Quote: smartalco, 2007-10-05T20:59:20Z
4. tractors are cool, our tractor could pull 4 of your cars, with the wheels taken off (more friction), through a field without a problem, try that with your car/truck

...which is that we're discussing literature. People were considering farms idyllic long before the invention of modern machinery. Much more manual labour was require in the good old days, and you had to keep horses/oxen/etc., which created a different kind of work. You also had to haul your goods to market if you wanted to sell them, or at least go and barter with your neighbours. These days, people sometimes forget just how long it takes to travel by foot. And, of course, if you wanted heating, or wanted to cook, you needed a fire, which meant cutting firewood...
