Quote: smort, October 24, 2007 11:45 am
My handwriting is very messy, this is true. Does that mean that I'm illiterate, by any definition?

Yes. If your handwriting is so poor other people cannot read it at all, you could be considered illiterate. A large of literacy is your ability to convey meaning through the written word. If the written word is unreadable, no meaning is conveyed.

Quote: smort, 2007-10-24T01:45:50Z
My thoughts are slightly sporadic, and very strange, but highly original. Does this mean I am illiterate?

It does if they are so sporadic you cannot adequately communicate through writing.

Quote: smort, 2007-10-24T01:45:50Z
Yet here I am in academic English, buried so far in deadlines and proper form that I can't write anything half as good as I would be able to otherwise!

The ability to comply with restrictions is an important part of communication. When you submit a job application, for example, you must complete it before the application deadline, and you should adhere to proper form. Your prospective employer does not want a 60-page essay on the role of feminism in postmodernist thought. Nor do they wish you to write your CV in iambic pentameter, or place random comments about how pretty daisies are while listing your qualifications. Even if you're self-employed, you must adhere to the requirements given to you by the client. That's how the world works.

This is not some kind of draconian assault on your intellectual integrity. If you wish to write in a different style, feel free to do so outside class. In class, however, you must demonstrate that you can communicate clearly and concisely about a range of topics. That is what is required to function effectively in the real world. Yes, marking can be bureaucratic and arbitrary, but the mere existence of deadlines and form guides is hardly evidence of this.

#17754 1 2007-11-01T03:48:08Z Atilla
Just thought of this today. It's a blend of those thumbs up/down systems (Is that Dave I hear cheering?) and the favourites system which was tried a while ago. I'm just throwin' it out there to see what people think. I'm not sure whether I'd support it at this stage - I need some more time to think of potential problems - but the concept seems to have some merit.

Rating system:

There would be three ratings, "Good", "Average", and "Poor". Users would also be able to favourite maps just like they can now.

Now, ratings would be calculated as follows:

1. The map must have at least 5 votes.
2. We calculate (Average + Good) - Poor. If this number is less than 0, the map is deemed "Poor".
3. We calculate Good - (Average + Poor). If this number is less than 0, the map is "Average". Otherwise, the map gets a "good" rating.

Obviously, a lot of maps will be "Good" under this system. Will there be a way to sort them? Indeed there shall. We shall use the ratio of favourites to "Good" votes. If lots of people think a map is "Good", but nobody wants to favourite it, then it's a fair bet to say that it's enjoyable but not outstanding. If one or two people particularly like it and decide to favourite it, it probably has a little more merit. If just about everyone who likes it at all favourites, they're calling it "Good" because they all think it's brilliant. We can use a similar system for the remaining levels.

The top-rated would then be sorted as follows:
1. "Good" maps by ratio of favourites to Good votes.
2. "Average" maps by ratio of Good votes to (Average + Poor) votes.
3. "Average" maps which are equal under step 2 sorted by ratio of Average to Poor votes.
4. "Poor" maps by ratio of (Good + Average) votes to Poor votes.

Advantages of this system:
1. Every vote still plays a part.
2. You can't make a map's position swing wildly with a single bad vote. It's only possible to push a map into a lower category if it's already borderline. Furthermore, the lack of extreme voting options makes it more difficult to make ratings change drastically even within a category.
3. There is some mechanism from sorting good maps from great maps.
4. Although the way maps are sorted is a bit complicated, the ratings themselves are pretty intuitive.
5. The limited number of ratings (3 + favourites, rather than 11) would make it easy to just display the actual vote tally, if people wanted to see it.

Example:

Map X has 3G and 2A votes, and has been favourited by one person. This map has a "Good" rating and an F/G ratio of 1/3 (0.333). Map Y, which has been around longer, has 6F, 19G, 10A, and 5P. This map has a "Good" rating and an F/G ratio of 6/19 (0.316). Map X will be higher on the top-rated.

Now, say that someone gives Map X a "Poor" vote. How will this effect things? Not at all. Map X still has the same F/G ratio, and it still qualifies for a "Good" rating, so if that was a sniping attempt it was completely ineffective.

But wait! What if the "Poor" vote is geniune? Shouldn't every vote count? Well, in a way it does. You see, that vote made Map X borderline. The number of Good votes and (Average + Poor) votes is now exactly even. Another Average or Poor vote will tip it into the "Average" class. More good votes will give it a bit of insulation. This prevents a lone idiot messing things up - a map can't pushed into a lower rating unless the majority is on your side. Nor can it be promoted into a higher rating against the majority.

So, Map X now has 1F, 3G, 2A and 1P. Someone thinks it's good but not amazing and gives it a "Good" vote. This causes the F/G ratio to drop to 0.25 and Map Y is now more highly rated. Eh? Giving it a good rating makes it move down? It seems odd at first, but if you think about it it makes sense. What's with the one person who favourited it? Clearly, not many people agree with them - just as not many people agreed with the one person who gave the map a "Poor" rating. Perhaps the mysterious favouriter just likes this kind of map far more than most people, or maybe they're friends with the author, or perhaps they were just in a good mood that day. For whatever reason, if lots of people are giving the map "Good" but not favouriting it, it means they think the map is good but not great. It's rather like giving a map a 4 when it has an average of 4.5 - it's still a good rating, just not as high as it was.

But what if people come along and favourite the map, vindicating the first guy to do so? That works too. Say two people now give the map a "Good" vote and favourite it. This gives us 3F, 5G, 2A, 1P. The map is now up to a .6 F/G ratio. The rating has improved as more people favourite it, just as you would expect.

Potential problems:

1. It's possible to get wacky categorisation in some circumstances. For example, a map with 3 good votes and 3 poor votes would be considered "Good". However, that's not likely to be a huge problem, since that sort of thing is unlikely to occur unless there's a war between snipers and multi-accounters. Not to mention that a single Average vote will fix that problem. I think you'll get anomalies like that in any rating system; the problem with the current one is that they occur in a way which gives the dishonest minority too much influence. At least with this system, they can be eliminated by a couple of normal votes, without that equally-dishonest anti-sniping garbage.

Another anomaly is that favouriting a map without giving it a Good rating can boost its standing more than it should, so long as the map is in the Good category. However, this can only happen a limited number of times before it falls into the Average category. It could also be addressed by only allowing users to favourite a map they have stated is "Good".

2. You can still cause ratings within a category to wobble a bit. Again, I think this is inevitable to some extent, and that it would be less under this system than the current system.

3. This system is a bit more complicated than the current one. Fortunately, the voting portion is pretty straightfoward, so it shouldn't confuse people unless they want to know just how the maps are sorted.





Thoughts? Problems? Issues?

#377407 475 2007-11-07T00:29:43Z Atilla
You should really do more research before you jump in. Or at least take more time to think about what you're saying and look at it from all angles. It's not that hard to work out that there's no reason for evolution to result in a single species.

Firstly, most organisms *have* evolved to more-or-less the same level. Animals are not less evolved than humans simply because they are less intelligent. Try wiping out every cockroach on the planet and see how far you get...

Secondly, not all organisms compete, and most depend on other organisms for survival. For example, if there are too many predators and not enough prey, food becomes scarce and the predator population decreases. The prey then has a chance to breed and repopulate. Both predator and prey will continue to survive. As another example, polar bears and hyenas don't compete because they live in completely different environments, so there's no reason to expect that one would die out. Also, sparrows and humans aren't really in competition, even though we live in the same region, so there's no reason both species can't exist. The fact is that it's not really feasible for a single species to do everything. Thus, organisms inevitably end up specialising to some degree, and you end up with many different creatures inhabiting a single environment.

Even if creatures do compete, you won't necessarily end up with a single species - if the species are more-or-less evenly matched, or if there is plenty of food and suitable habitation, both can survive. Often species compete for the similar resources using different strategies - for example, monkeys eat fruit by climbing trees, while birds just fly instead. Species may also be in limited competition - for example, two types of bird may compete for appropriate nesting sites, but not for food because one eats seeds and the other eats insects. As long as the two types are equally adept at finding nests, and there's enough food for each type, they can co-exist.

We can also look at variation within species as an analogy. Now, it's obvious that there are human traits which are useful in different circumstances. Some people are tall, some are short, some are stocky and strong, others are thin but athletic, some people can stand in the sun for hours without being burned, others have to lurk indoors all summer. I'm going to assume you agree that variations within a species can compete, be passed on through heredity, and thus become more or less common. Now, it's clear that this doesn't result in humans becoming completely uniform, so when similar competition occurs between species, why would you expect only a single species to survive?

#384247 13 2007-11-29T02:00:00Z Atilla
This has been suggested several times before, and it's not going to happen.

Reasons:
- Anything other than MIDI would drastically increase the download size.
- N works fine with a media player in the background.
- Most people would prefer their own music to anything M&R would compose anyway. Especially if it's MIDI.
- The library of music would be very small. Consider the number of hours you've played N. Imagine a two-minute track repeating. Over. And over. And over.
- M&R's time is better spent on other things.

#385185 10 2007-12-02T01:20:48Z Atilla
No, I don't think it's a good idea to completely legalise marijuana. I'm surprised none of you have given much attention to the fact that marijuana use greatly increases the risk of mental illnesses, particularly schizophrenia.

As for addiction, tobacco companies deliberately manufacture cigarettes in a way which makes them much more addictive than necessary because, shockingly, making your product addictive generates more revenue. If marijuana was made commercially available, I wouldn't be surprised if the same sort of thing happened. Indeed, it has already happened to some extent - hemp used to be a mild painkiller, with no real hallucinogenic effects. In modern times, the plants are deliberately bred and grown to maximise the effects of the drug. This also poses a problem with weight limits - potency can be increased to compensate.

I do, however, support the use of marijuana in an appropriate medical context. I would also welcome a greater focus on rehabilitation with regard to drug use; punitive measures do little if anything to reduce the problem.

EDIT: Also, marijuana does have a severe, detrimental effect on driving ability. The number of accidents caused by drugged driving has been rising steadily in my state, which is why all booze buses are now also equipped to test for use of illicit drugs.

uhhh.... no green isn't primary. Where did you learn that?

Green is taught as a primary colour in many science classes. This is because red and green light, when mixed, appear yellow. Also, most humans have three different types of colour receptor in their eye, which are respond most strongly to red, green, and blue light, respectively.

Yellow is taught as primary in art classes because red and green pigment generally don't mix well, whereas red and yellow and yellow and blue do.

#387910 4 2007-12-10T03:40:55Z Atilla
You need to have Caps Lock on to play in debug mode.

To play the level outside debug mode, you copy the level data and paste it into "userlevels.txt" in the format $Level Name#Author#Category#Level Data#. The data must be after the line "&userdata=", and userlevels.txt must be in the same folder as N.

The clipboard is the space where Windows temporarily stores things you've cut or copied, ready for pasting.

That is indeed circular reasoning. Let me demonstrate by replacing some words.

"Atilla's autobiography defines Atilla as all-loving and such. And because consumers believe that Atilla's autobiography was written by Atilla, it's not the consumer who defines Atilla as anything."

On this basis, you say, we should accept that I, Atilla, am all-loving and such. However, the question here is "What reason do you have to believe what Atilla says about himself?"

After all, if I happen to be dishonest, my autobiography may well lie about my nature. By the same token, you can't argue against the assertion that God is not omnibenevolent etc. etc. by referring to divinely-inspired literature; because if God NOT omnibenevolent, He may well be an outrageous liar.

Think about it. If I assert "God is a liar", is it a good idea to respond with "But the Word of God says otherwise!"?

If I assert that Dave is a liar, is it a good idea to respond with "But Dave says he's honest!"?

Quote: Guest, 2007-12-16T04:05:03Z
2.  God above logic does not mean that all of God is above logic.  If it were, then your argument would be acceptable.  However, not all of God is above logic.  We know this because of our experiences of God, and the things that make sense to us.  If God was completely and only above logic, nothing would make sense. Naturally, this isn't true.  Ergo, God isn't completely above logic.  So what does this mean?  It means that certain aspects of God are above human comprehension, but not all of God's aspects.  So now it is possible that God can have logical aspects.  Meaning, God can contradict Himself in some places and make sense, and not contradict Himself and make sense at the same time.

If God was completely above logic, He could make perfect sense. It would be illogical that He do so, of course, but that's not relevant to something which is above logic.

Furthermore, if any part of God is illogical, God Himself is illogical. As in a logical argument, if any part is false or contradictory, the whole fails. Not to mention that the illogical parts of God - being unbound by logical laws - could mess around with the logical parts at any time.

There's also the problem of omnipotence, which causes logical contradictions all over the place. Now, if a part of God which is not above logic is also omnipotent, you have a problem. It follows that only the illogical aspects of God can be omnipotent. But wait! Omnipotence, by definition, cannot be restricted. Thus, declaring that God is omnipotent but partially logical is itself a logical contradiction and can only be accepted if God is completely illogical.

#390110 23 2007-12-17T00:51:17Z Atilla
@Obby:

You don't understand my point. I'm not saying that God or belief in God is bad because He/it is illogical. I'm saying that if God is illogical, nothing meaningful can be said about His nature. For example, "God is X" and "God is not X" can both be true simultaneously, even though this is a logical impossibility. Try substituting "omnibenevolent" for "X" - we can make completely contradictory statements about God and believe them both. If you accept that God is above logic, you must accept that "God is omnibenevolent" and "God is not omnibenevolent" are equally valid, because without logic you have no basis to distinguish between them.

So, no, I'm not saying there's something wrong with God being illogical. I'm saying that this results in certain consequences, namely that anything said about God, by definition, has no logical basis, and therefore arbitrary. If you are not willing to accept these consequences, then you may find the idea of an illogical God to be wrong.

#392498 32 2007-12-23T01:34:16Z Atilla
There are two main problems with Pascal's wager.

The first is that it requires you to believe that you'll be punished/rewarded by some deity if you worship/don't worship them. For reasons already stated, this doesn't work so well with unbelievers.

The second is that it doesn't really rule out any course of behaviour. For example, God's Ineffable Divine Plan may require me to be an atheist to the death to hide my presence from His enemies, who can read minds. It's possible, and indeed fairly easy, to "justify" any possible action using Pascal's wager.

Quote: Catechism of the Catholic Church

#394868 3 2007-12-31T00:23:16Z Atilla
This can be done in one of two ways.

1. Put a locked door on every side of the drone. When they are unlocked, it should remain stationary.

2. Edit the level code manually. The easiest way to do this is to put the drone in, then - without adding any other objects - return to the Ned menu and hit a random letter. This will change the part of the code which describes the drone's path algorithm to "NaN" (Not a Number), which makes it stand still. You can also go through your data and change the last number in the drone's code to "NaN" by hand. There's a basic overview here.

Quote: sweep, January 05, 2008 09:14 am
I think - on the profit/loss side of the argument - what I'm saying is pretty sound. You're right, there are no exact figures to produce but that should not stand in the way of what I am saying any more than it does you.
No, it's not.

Say, for example, that someone has been in an accident and needs CPR. Now, normally you wouldn't go around shoving strangers in the chest, and there's a danger of broken ribs or at least bruising. However, they're more likely to benefit from it than be offended that you've invaded their personal space. We know this. It is well established.

However, if you don't bother checking for a pulse or breathing, and just start performing CPR and mouth-to-mouth on anyone who is lying down, you're going to annoy a lot of people. If the person is already fine, they're going to be pretty irritated when you start whacking them on the chest and breathing down their throat. Yes, it might help them. But you have no assurance that it will, because you haven't got the necessary information to make that judgement.

You're saying that it's okay to infringe someone's rights because it might conceivably, in some circumstances, maybe possibly help them. However, you have no assurance that this is the case. Kablizzy is saying, correctly, that because you lack good reason to believe that what you are doing is beneficial, you should instead respect the rights of others to control the distribution of their works. In the same way, health inspectors don't go around closing random restaurants on the basis that they might be unsafe, and we don't lock up people who might turn out to be criminals; you need to have good reason to believe that what you are doing is beneficial before you start infringing on other's rights. You need to find the rats in the kitchen or the sack of jewelery in the attic, rather than just assuming they're there because it makes things easier for you.

#400329 138 2008-01-13T02:04:58Z Atilla
Quote: Cossack, January 12, 2008 12:43 pm
hardly - if you were to take out the biological advancements
Define "advancement". If, for example, there was a nuclear apocalypse, the environment might select for cockroaches and viruses. Would you consider the annihilation of humanity "advancement"? Because that's what you have to accept if you wish to assert that evolution results in biological advancement.

Evolution results in biological differences which make organisms more or less suited for survival in certain circumstances. This does not necessary constitute advancement. For example, it is believed that pale-skinned humans are an adaptation which allows them to thrive in areas with little sunlight. However, it would be silly to insist that those with pale skin are more advanced than the rest of the species because they have this adaptation. Pale skin has some advantages, but also many disadvantages; its evolution cannot be considered progress or advancement, except in a very narrow sense in a specific environment.

Furthermore, "advancement" is usually taken to mean increasing intelligence and so on. However, this is not a requirement of evolution; there are circumstances where intelligence is not worth the cost - otherwise there wouldn't be any non-sapient life! Thus, the changes wrought by evolution are not necessarily what most people would consider advancement.

Quote: Obby, 2008-01-12T04:35:10Z
That's simply not true. Birds having wings is much more the result of evolution than a mental 'difference' such as homosexuality

Garbage. We're talking about evolution from a non-theistic perspective here. Human psychology is determined in large part by human biology. Furthermore, animals which we would not consider to have a culture have also been observed to display homosexual behaviour, so blaming it on human culture would be dubious.

Furthermore, as has been pointed out, mental differences are important and are selected for in the same way as purely physical traits. A massive homosexuality rate would inhibit the ability of a species to breed; and therefore it is unlikely that a species will have high rates of homosexuality. If you want another example, there are clearly behavioural differences between the males and females of many species. Why do you consider these differences to be magically immune from natural selection?

Besides, the original point I was arguing against was the notion that if homosexuality was right, we would have evolved the necessary equipment to reproduce with the same gender. If homosexuality is to be considered a mental thing to which evolution is not applicable, then - as I said - evolution is irrelevant. Unless you want to declare the rest of human culture and society wrong on the basis that it is not a result of evolution, of course.

Quote: Guest, 2008-01-12T04:35:10Z
After all, reproduction is the reason for any trait animals have.

Riiiiight. There are more right-handed people than left because it's so damn sexy, I expect. And humans come in two flavours and can only have children every nine months because that lets us produce so many more offspring than bacteria. Wait, what? The fact is that there are far more bacteria than mammals. And more insects, too - even if you go by mass. All our intelligence is an evolutionary failure, then. What I'm saying is that it's not as simple as "Oh, this trait doesn't directly lead to breeding, so it's useless." Intelligence and education don't lead to breeding, either - in fact, statistics show that the more educated you are the fewer children you're likely to have. Going by this measure, we should all return to barbarism, marry at the age of ten, and have forty kids each.

Quote: Guest, 2008-01-12T04:35:10Z
Carrying on the species is evolution. Homosexuality is not carrying on the species. It is not the result of evolution.

"Carrying on the species" is not the definition of evolution. Evolution is a biological process where the nature of organisms changes as the result of selection pressure. Humans are the result of this process. That includes the aspect of humans which makes some of them homosexual. This trait can be selected for or against, just like every other; again, it is not somehow magically immune. Therefore, its continued existence is just as much the result of evolution as any other aspect of humanity.

Quote: Guest, 2008-01-12T04:35:10Z
It's also notable that homosexuality isn't heredity. So unless you are saying either that homosexuality is heredity, or nothing is heredity...

Homosexuality is, in fact, hereditary.

I mean, according to one of your own posts:

Quote: Obby, May 10, 2007 10:59 am
No, it's not a choice. It is merely a difference in the genes the affected the way that your brain was wired, hence causing you to be attracted to the same sex.

If genetic differences do not count as hereditary, I'm not sure what does.

Also from a previous thread:

Quote: Atilla, 2007-05-10T13:10:40Z
[The assertion that homosexuality should be wiped out by evolution] is based on the assumption that only people who are explicitly homosexual carry genes which could cause homosexual tendencies, and furthermore that those with homosexual tendencies never breed. Both are incorrect. As was previously stated in this thread, homosexuality is not a binary trait; it's possible for people to have homosexual tendencies, or the potential for such, while remaining heterosexual. Furthermore, all genes are not always expressed. For example, I have green eyes though my parents have blue and brown eyes. In the same manner, a homosexual child may be born from a heterosexual couple. Then, of course, there are bisexuals, and homosexuals who have been forced to dissemble by societal pressures.

There may also be non-genetic factors which nevertheless influence sexuality on a biological level. Some studies show that second-born boys are more likely to be homosexual that the first born, and the third-born more likely than the second, and so on. It is believed this is because the immune reaction of a woman's body to a male embryo becomes stronger with successive pregnancies and that this inhibits masculinisation of the brain to some degree.

Unlike other traits which are detrimental to breeding, homosexuality is not fatal, nor does it inhibit the individual's other faculties. Homosexuals can make as much of a contribution to society as anyone else, and therefore there is less reason to select against homosexuality than against harmful genetic diseases. It may be that behavioural traits linked to homosexuality are in some manner slightly beneficial for society as a whole, in the same way that altruism damages the chances of an individual but still survives because having some altruists around helps the entire group.

The end result of all this is that from a biological standpoint you would expect homosexuality to be rare, but not unknown. Given what we know of the rates of homosexuality, this expectation appears to be upheld.

And also

Quote: Atilla, 2007-05-11T10:21:44Z
Why does altering a gene in fruit flies make them attempt to mate almost exclusively with their own gender? Why are gay men substantially more likely to have gay relatives on their mother's side than their father's? Why are homosexuals less likely to be right-handed than the rest of the population?

I'm not saying environment has no effect, but there are all sorts of odd "coincidences" which don't seem readily explainable by upbringing. I believe there is certainly some biological basis which, at the very least, makes a person more receptive to environmental factors which may produce homosexuality.

Oh, and another thing in regards to evolution, this is interesting. It appears that the mothers of homosexual men are more fertile than those of heterosexual men.

Now, let's examine a couple of things.

The bit about fruit flies is fairly clear, I believe. If fiddling with genes can make an organism homosexual, that seems to be grounds for considering it a genetic trait.

Firstly, it is known that left-handed people tend to produce more left-handed offspring than right-handed people. This would imply that handedness is in some way hereditary. Now, homosexuals have an anomalous rate of left-handedness. We might postulate that this is because they share a heredity, the heredity which lead to their homosexuality. This is far from conclusive, of course, but it's interesting.

At this point we need to address an important assumption which most people make: it is generally assumed that if homosexuality is inherited, it has the same cause in both genders. However, let us instead consider that there is a different cause for homosexuality in each gender.

Now, homosexual men are more likely to have gay relatives though their mother's side of the family. This is precisely what would be expected if homosexuality was an inherited trait whith different causes for each gender. There are few gay relatives on the father's side because gay men do not generally reproduce and therefore there is little chance of the trait being passed on. There are many gay relatives on the mother's side because the trait which causes men to be homosexual can be carried by heterosexual women and can therefore be passed down the matriarchal line from here to eternity.

Furthermore, if you examine the link in my quote, you will note that the mothers of homosexual men tend to be more fertile than those who mother only heterosexual men. If these two thing were caused by the same trait, it would explain everything nicely - homosexuality is hereditary, but the trait persists because increases fertility in one gender and can be passed down through that gender.

So, yes, I'm reasonably sure that homosexuality has a large inherited component, though the environment may have some effect.

#402627 70 2008-01-21T06:14:45Z Atilla
Quote: Arona Daal, January 21, 2008 03:33 pm
...if 8 million people buying a game doesn't prove once and for all it's a great game, I don't know what would.
8 million people buying a game prove that it is popular, not that it is high-quality. After all, millions of people believe newspaper horoscopes are accurate. The reason I mentioned casual games is that unoriginal, poorly-produced connect-3 games sell like hotcakes, even though they're obviously lacking in quality.

Other popular video games which aren't particularly outstanding include Final Fight, which sold well despite being extremely repetitive, involving little to no skill, and primitive graphics, and Uno (yes, the card game) which has sold over a million copies on XBLA - it's certainly nothing special, just an XBox version of a popular card game. If we go by sales, Yoshi's Story, which is widely considered rather poor, is a better game than Pilotwings 64, which received excellent reviews; and they're both better than Paper Mario, which also received a positive reception and has become a successful franchise. Meanwhile, Pilotwings is discontinued, and Nintendo are trying to pretend Yoshi's Story never happened. And, apparently, Wii Play is twice as good as Zelda: Twilight Princess on current sales figures.

EDIT: Beyond Good & Evil is another good example. It received excellent reviews and a good reception from those who actually bought it, but for some reason it didn't sell very well. Psychonauts suffered a similar fate.
#402632 72 2008-01-21T06:47:55Z Atilla
Quote: Arona Daal, 2008-01-21T06:20:40Z
If people enjoyed playing those games more, they would buy them. All the ratings in the world mean nothing if no one buys your game.

You're missing the point. We're talking about quality, not commercial success or popularity. If a bad game sells a billion copies because the Mafia threatens to kill everyone who doesn't buy it, it's still a bad game. If the world is swept by a wave of furrydom and everyone buys Star Fox Adventures so they can ogle Krystal, that won't make the plot any less ludicrous.

Again, I point to Yoshi's Story. It sold reasonably well, not because of the game's merits, but because it followed Yoshi's Island, which was absolutely brilliant. Had Yoshi's Story not been part of the Yoshi franchise, it would have flopped massively. This is a clear case where sales are not an indication of quality.

Meanwhile, Beyond Good & Evil was a stand-alone game released by Ubisoft at the same time as several of Ubi's franchise games which already had a fairly large following (Tom Clancy's, Prince of Persia, XIII). As such, it didn't get anywhere near as much attention as it could have - even Ubi acknowledge that it could have done much, much better if it hadn't been for the release date. It's still a good game, even though it didn't sell well.

Then we have games like Cave Story. It's an obscure freeware game, but that doesn't make it any less brilliant. The same applies to N, the Spirit Engine, Battle for Wesnoth, and pretty much any other indie game you care to name. Most of them wouldn't sell as well as the Finding Nemo ™ Activity Centre, but they're still good games!

From a more direct angle, when you play a game, do you think "I'm really enjoying this game because 8 million people bought it?" I certainly don't. I couldn't care less about how many people bought it; I can't tell you the sales statistics for any game I own without looking them up. My enjoyment of a game, then, and my judgement of its quality are not based on how well it sells, but on factors inherent to the game itself. I think this is true of most people. That is the difference between how well a game sells and how good it is.

Quote: scythe33, January 13, 2008 03:17 pm
By the way, since you argue that the genes for male and female homosexuality are probably different, did the fruit fly gene affect males, females, or both? I'm not attacking you, just curious.

I believe they only fiddled with the genome of the males. Of course, there's also the possibility that things are different for other animals. Also, even it the genome alteration caused an excess of one hormone - so what? Controlling hormones is one of the things genes do, and if a gene causes an excess of a hormone which results in an organism being homosexual, it could be considered a genetic basis for homosexuality.

Quote: scythe33, 2008-01-13T05:17:19Z
Quote: atilla, 2008-01-13T02:04:58Z
Furthermore, if you examine the link in my quote, you will note that the mothers of homosexual men tend to be more fertile than those who mother only heterosexual men. If these two thing were caused by the same trait, it would explain everything nicely - homosexuality is hereditary, but the trait persists because increases fertility in one gender and can be passed down through that gender.
That does suffer the correlation fallacy, especially because the second and third son are more likely to be homosexual-in other words, mothers with more sons ought to be more likely outright to have more homosexual sons.

*shrugs*

That's possible, certainly. I was just putting out a likely hypothesis - I'm not claiming it's conclusive.

However, your explanation wouldn't really explain why gay men only tend to have gay relatives on the maternal side - if it was simply related to the number of kids a woman has, then if the paternal grandparents had twelve kids, there should be plenty of gay relatives on that side of the family.

Besides, even if there isn't a direct genetic link between homosexuality and fertility, there is clearly a link. If the proportion of homosexuals rises with the number of children each woman has, then that creates a difference which can be selected for. A village in which everyone has twelve kids might have considerably more homosexuals than a village where the women only give birth to three. If the rate of homosexuality caused problems, the women would develop in a way which reduced the likelihood of homosexual children - whether through some change which would reduce the effect of multiple children, or through a change which results in fewer children.

Quote: Snooks, 2008-02-15T12:28:08Z
I think that should technology permit it ALL people should be sterilized at puberty.  Couples should apply to have a child.  The fetus should be genetically screened, as the parents were before hand, and aborted should it not meet the standard.  In addition when we can manipulate DNA well enough I fully support manipulation of the fetus's DNA to improve it or change it to suit the parents.  This will lead to a smarter and healthier  human race, as well as allowing for a control over the amount of humans born so that the size of our population never threaten our resources.

The problem with that is that the people who monitor the applications are just as defective as the rest of us, and it gives them far too much power. In an ideal world, yes, having a child would be an intellectual choice made in cold blood. However, unless the entire human reproductive system can be drastically altered, this isn't feasible in the real world.

Furthermore, I'm not sure that aborting every embryo with genetics which don't meet some standard will actually improve the race. Putting aside for the moment that nobody will be able to agree on what standards are appropriate, and that even if they do they'll probably get it wrong, it's not clear that all desired traits can be inferred from genetics. Environment plays a large role, of course, and which genome controls creativity, charisma, determination, compassion? And does having a few "defective" people around really hurt society that much? The primary problem I see in society is not a lack of intelligence, or strength, or speed. It's an unwillingness to accept responsibility, a lack of compassion and consideration for others, and a fear of those who are different. Embracing eugenics would only exacerbate these problems. Humanity already has too much power and not enough wisdom - if technological development slows down, perhaps it will stop us blowing ourselves up before the race develops some collective maturity.

And where do you stop? Say we root out everyone with a major disability. Will the short-sighted be next in line? Those with a history of heart disease? People who are left-handed? Someone has to be on the bottom of the heap. That's the way the world works. 50% of people will always be below the median. At some point you have to accept that. As others have pointed out, somebody has to do the dirty work; society needs considerably more janitors than it does particle physicists. Indeed, if we were all geniuses whose intellect was wasted on manual labour, it might be considered a great and noble thing to become a janitor for the good of others; while everyone can be a molecular biologist, it takes an altruist and a gentleman to clean the halls.

As for your assertion that we'll be overrun by the wretched poor people... I don't believe the poor have substantially lower intelligence than the middle class. They do worse academically, certainly, and they frequently make bad, short-sighted decisions. However, generational poverty is due to culture rather than genetics. The impoverished make poor decisions because they have not been taught to make the right ones. The solution is not eugenics, but education. Many poor people already rise to the middle or even upper classes through hard work, education, and, perhaps, a little luck. If they are as genetically deficient as you claim, this shouldn't be happening.

There's also the traditional argument: Stephen Hawking, world-renowned physicist, is a cripple. Is it more important that we have people like him, or that we don't need to manufacture wheelchairs?

Quote: Snooks, February 16, 2008 12:44 pm
Its hard to wrap you head around but if I was aborted I would not have ever existed. Arguing that my parents would miss me is ridiculous. I never existed to begin with. To say "in your world so and so would never have been born, thats mean" No, the person would never have existed, its different. I can see exactly where this is headed. I don't consider an embryo a person. You can get rid of one, it has no personality. Its pre-person.

That's not the point. The point is that people who are deformed or disabled can and do contribute to society. Many of them display an optimism and an ability to endure hardship which puts the rest of us to shame. Moreover, society is enriched, not lessened, by a diversity of viewpoints. At the very least, those whose daily life is impeded by disability challenge us to reconsider our own lives and values, and that's not a bad thing.

Furthermore, there are some disabilities which are actually helpful in the right circumstances. Sickle-cell anemia, for example, offers considerable protection from malaria, but is considered a disability in areas which are largely free of the disease. Should sickle-cell anemia be eliminated or not? What about savants, who might be extremely skilled at mathematics, but have horrendous social skills? Should this trait also be eliminated?

I don't think humans can make the necessary judgements with any degree of accuracy. This kind of program would require a lot of work and a massive bureaucracy, and I'm just not convinced that it would have any real benefit.

And, for the record, I don't consider an embryo a person either.

Quote: Skyflyer, March 01, 2008 12:23 am
Yes, I am.
Does it matter?

Well, Macs are notorious for having weird problems with saving progress, and the usual solution is different for Windows.

Anyway, the .sol file is created when you run N for the first time. It won't be in the N folder, but rather in some obscure directory where all Flash applications store their info. You need to find this file - it should be called n_v14b_userdata.sol - and back it up. I believe it's in a randomly-named folder in #SharedObjects, on a Mac.

Once you've done that, delete all the random folders from #SharedObjects and empty the trash. Run N to create a fresh .sol file. To get your progress back, close N, find the clean .sol and replace it with the old one.

#413716 38 2008-03-04T04:44:57Z Atilla
There is a difference between "we do not know how to explain this using logic", "this is logically impossible" and "logic does not apply to this". If you do not know how to explain something using logic, there may well be a logical explanation which you are unaware of or lack the background knowledge or mental capacity to grasp. In contrast, if something is logically impossible, you know (or, at least, believe you know) how logic should be applied to the situation, and under the dictates of logic the specified circumstance cannot occur. If logic does not apply to something, on the other hand, then it is exempt from any logical reasoning, including this one, which is why everything gets confusing.

For example, we know of no explanation for the fact that electrons have a mass of 9.11 x 10^-31 kg. However, it's certainly not logically impossible for electrons to have that mass - quite the contrary! Nor do we believe electrons are exempt from logic. In short, "unexplained" is different from "unexplainable", and both differ from "does not need explanation".

Furthermore, there's a difference between something existing and its existence being relevant to us. If God is beyond logic and therefore incomprehensible to humans, then it's not clear that there is any point talking about Him since there is no guarantee that we can gain any understanding of Her, or indeed that It would wish us to understand Them. In such circumstances, ignoring God completely would seem to be as theologically sound as worship...

#413975 43 2008-03-05T00:52:51Z Atilla
Obby: Uh, what? That's not even close to what I was saying. I'll try to explain...

Say, for example, that Priest A and Priest B both believe in an omnipotent god which is exempt from logic in the manner we discussed.

Now, Priest A states that redheads should be removed from society and placed in isolated missions until they die out, because they have no part in God's grand plan for humanity. By making such a statement, Priest A implies that there are two facets of God which are known and comprehensible - that God has a Divine Plan for humanity, and that redheads are not part of it.

Priest B, on the other hand, states that God has a plan for all people, but that this plan is ineffable and beyond the knowledge of mere mortals. This implies that two things about God is known and comprehensible - that He has a Divine Plan for humanity, and that humans are unable to comprehend any part of this plan, save that it is beyond human understanding.

Now, although both priests agree that God is omnipotent and has a Divine Plan, Priest and Priest B disagree about what can be known and what cannot. Priest B claims that God's plan is ineffable; Priest A thinks that it may indeed be effed, though not quite as badly as the poor redheads. Is there any method by which we can determine whether Priest A or Priest B is more likely to be correct, or must we just choose arbitrarily whether we agree with A or B or neither?

If we must choose arbitrarily, then what's the point in even talking about God? In such a situation, there is no objective measure of which beliefs are accurate and which are not. To put it another way, all that matters is that beliefs are internally consistent, rather than externally consistent (ie. matching some objective state of reality). Any reasoning I apply will only serve to reinforce whichever belief system I reason within, regardless of what it is. As such, any evangelism or discussion about the matter is just a way for people to occupy themselves, rather than approach any consensus or truth - they like doing such things and so picked a belief system which allowed them to. In short, everyone just does whatever they are inclined to and makes up a belief system to justify it (or borrows a ready-made one).

I'm not sure how you manage to come up with these interpretations. I don't think I said anything to suggest that I think only one religion is correct, or that we're arguing about the jurisdiction of the Catholic Church.


It's like this.

I said that, if belief is an arbitrary matter - you either believe or you don't and that's that - there is no objective way to determine whether we are actually coming any closer to an understanding of God. This raises questions about the value of theology and religious discussion, since in such circumstances we would not have reason to believe that it actually improves our understanding of God at all.

You responded that prayer and meditation could be used to decide whether one belief gives you a better understanding of God than another. You also stated that, had I been correct in my previous statement, that the Church would be in many factions rather than a united whole.

I responded that prayer and meditation cannot be used to determine that one belief brings you closer to God than another, because many people pray and meditate and come to completely conflicting conclusions - typically reaffirming belief in whatever their current religious stance is. If prayer and meditation resulted in movement towards a true understanding of God, you would expect opinions to converge towards a single belief system. Historically, this has not been observed - as I pointed out, there are many different religions, and many factions within each religion (the many denominations of Christianity, for example). This means that my original question is still an issue - if religious belief is an arbitrary decision, what does this imply about the role and value of theology and religion?

Now, you seem to have got the idea I am somehow saying all religion is bunk solely because people disagree. Nothing could be further from the truth. Rather, that if you believe religious choices are arbitrary - you either believe or you don't - then it would seem that there is little point in theological debate. All religions seem valid to those who believe them, and there is no objective method of distinguishing them, so you might as well just pick one and get on with it. People will believe what they believe and we just have to work around that.

On the other hand, if you reject the notion that we either believe or do not, but instead base our beliefs on some form of reasoning, then there clearly is a need for discussion and debate. When there is reason for belief, we can argue that one reason is better than another, that one belief therefore brings us closer to understanding God, and, therefore, you have a basis for distinguishing beliefs. Just picking a belief is no longer enough - you need to pick the one which you believe is the most convincing and justified, the one which gives you the best understanding of God.

A unified federal approach would aid in their enforcement, however.

#423486 7 2008-03-30T07:24:31Z Atilla
FLail has already been mentioned, but Helix Games also produced Jumper Redux and Jumper 2, which also have editors. Ninjah is another platformer in the vein of N, FLail and Jumper. Pekka Kana 2 is a different style of platformer, somewhat reminiscent of New Zealand Story (aka Kiwi Kraze), which has an editor and level packs available for download.

In other offerings, Zep's Dreamland is a puzzle game which looks like a platformer. Typhoon 2001 is a Tempest 2000 remake (arcade-y shooter) with level editor. Neverball is an action/puzzle game in the vein of Super Monkey Ball. Custom map-packs are available, and ytou can make your own maps if you've experience with GtkRadiant. Battle for Wesnoth is a turn-based tactical game with a map/campaign editor and downloadable content. Battleships Forever is a real-time tactical game with (rather limited) mission editor and ship editor.

#424462 23 2008-04-02T10:58:07Z Atilla
[quote="Grassman7z7" date="April 01, 2008 03:52 pm"]
Quote: Atilla, April 01, 2008 01:38 am
Quote: Grassman7z7, April 01, 2008 11:09 am
The first one is the most magnificent First Person Shooter I have ever played, even if it is largely puzzle based.

Thats because Metroid Prime is a thinking man's FPS. Atilla, do you have any sense of what combat is like? Its not a run-and-gun. It is MUCH more important NOT to get hit than it is to shoot the enemy. In a combat situation, you explore your environment more than you run-and-gun. Just that alone makes it a much more realistic than many FPS's.

Argh. No. You're missing the point. Metroid Prime is not an FPS for much the same reason as Legend of Zelda is not a fencing simulator.

Raven Shield is the kind of FPS you describe. Yes, dodging is an important part of the game, yes, you can't just charge in and blast away. However, the actual shooting still takes skill, and combat is the primary focus of the game.

In contrast, Metroid Prime doesn't even require you to aim. Declaring it an FPS is akin to declaring a roller coaster simulator a racing game. Furthermore, there's a difference between exploration and reconnaissance. In Metroid, you're not trying to flank an enemy, or find the best angle of attack; exploration is an end in itself.

Also, the combat sections of Metroid Prime are very much run-and-gun. Damage is avoided by dashing around like a lunatic. I also find your claim that it is in any way a realistic representation of actual combat quite ludicrous.

Hmm? Studies have shown that playing action games does, in fact, improve your fine motor skills and some aspects of visual perception. Playing games can also help those who have lost movement or coordination as a result of injury to the CNS regain their ability. It's certainly not going to turn you into a professional sportsperson, but there is some effect.

That said, I don't think it's sensible to make a list "justifying" the use of video games. A lot of people who deride games as a waste of time are perfectly happy with TV, Uno, and other pursuits which aren't really the greatest source for essential life skills. The point is that games are enjoyable and, in moderation, they do no harm.

#425863 12 2008-04-07T01:47:42Z Atilla
Quote: Obby, April 07, 2008 06:07 am
Call of Duty 4 teaches me how to shoot Commies and Arabs.

There you have it, folks. Playing video games is the American Way.

@Hendor: Incorrect. I recall a study showing that surgeons who play Halo before an operation actually perform the surgery faster and with greater accuracy. Also, the military is known to use games for training purposes. Even if they don't make you an expert marksman, they can certainly teach you strategy.

I think people who claim that games don't teach you anything aside from pressing buttons have an excessively narrow view. That kind of reasoning ultimately results in the conclusion that reading teaches you nothing, except how to turn pages, and that push-ups don't make you stronger, only better at push-ups. Games stimulate the portion of your brain associated with fine motor skills and visual perception. I don't think it's entirely unreasonable to believe that these functions will improve with use, much like virtually every other brain function.

Really, I think people might be surprised about some of the relations which do exist. For example, despite the drop-out rocker stereotype, musical ability and mathematical ability are correlated. Now, pressing keys or blowing into a tube certainly doesn't teach you how to solve equations. However, harmony, rhythm, even melody all rely on mathematical patterns and relations. Thus, even though there is no direct connection between playing music and adding numbers, there is a correlation because they use some of the same parts of the brain. I think similar relations apply for video games and tasks which rely on similar skills.

#435800 37 2008-05-13T15:19:51Z Atilla
SkyPanda: If God exists outside the universe, He also exists outside the laws of causation as we understand them, because such laws are part of the universe. There is thus no basis to assert that God caused the universe to be created, because the very notion of something being a cause is undefined in those circumstances.

Also, time is internal to the universe. Anything which existed "before" the universe (for want of a better word - without time there is no "before") and which can be said to have "caused" the universe to exist (for want of a better word - without the laws internal to the universe, there does not necessarily have to be causation in the sense that humans understand), you can make exactly the same "unbound-by-your-petty-concepts-of-causality" argument as you can for gods. Think about it for a moment: you're saying that God escapes the infinite recursion problem because He is outside of the universe - but, by definition, isn't anything which exists "before" the universe outside it?

Another problem is defining things like "always existed" without concepts of time and space. How long is "forever"? Because, if you think about it, the universe - by definition - has existed and will exist from alpha to omega, from the beginning to the end of time. To look at it another way, there is no time in which the universe does not exist. That meets at least one definition of "eternal".

Even without these problems, it's quite possible that the universe has "always existed" and has neither beginning nor end. One possibility is that time is finite but cyclical - every event is a cause which ultimately leads to the same chain of events happening again in an endless loop. Another is that the universe has no beginning simply because time extends infinitely back from our current location. We're just a point on the timeline in the same way as (1, 2) is a point on the graph y = 2x.

EDIT: Oh, right. If you're saying the same argument *can* be applied the universe, that's fine, and this post is somewhat redundant.

#439229 9 2008-05-26T02:07:41Z Atilla
NEWMA all the way.

1. The old NUMA captured the simplistic atmosphere of N much better than the new one does in my opinion. I'm not saying that it doesn't look good right now (it looks great), but I prefer the old skin.

The old NUMA looked dull and somewhat amateurish by modern standards (no offence meant to the designers). With web authoring tools becoming more powerful and more widely available, and with presence of a generation that has grown up on the 'net, even small websites have become more stylish and professional in appearance over recent years. NUMA's new look reflects this change. I find it much more attractive and stylish than the old.


2. Point ratings - It is now impossible to rate a map 2.5/5 for average. You can only rate in whole-number intervals now. 2/5 is "below average," and 3/5 is "above average." What happened to "average?" Also, people often dock off 0.5 points for a small flaw on a map that doesn't deserve a 5, but is better than a 4. That is now impossible, and I don't like that. Also, the rating displayed on the maps is only by whole number intervals, too.

Good. Most people only use five rating increments anyway - 0, 3.5, 4, 4.5, and 5. And, really, people aren't perfectly accurate rating machines. It's not worth getting hung up on 0.5 increments for the map average because at that degree of precision differences in the way people rate are just as likely to effect the overall rating as any aspect of the map. Yeah, there are occasionally times when you might want to rate something 4.5 instead of 4, with good reason, but in general I don't think it's a problem. Just recalibrate your ratings to 3, 4, 5 instead of 3.5, 4, 4.5. If you want to be daring, you could even use the whole range of ratings (statistically, the average map gets well over 3.5 4, so perhaps we need to increase our expectations).

3. Featured maps - I'm not particularily bugged about this one, but what was wrong with Bitesizing? "Featured Maps" just doesn't sound as nice as "Bitesized Maps," not to mention that "1 Featured Map a Day" limit.

Eh, I think the reviews and the fact that the featured map pops up on the homepage is nice. If nothing else, it should drastically reduce the number of times people wail "Why was this map bitesized?!" Also, I think decreased volume is a good thing - I've seen people who bitesize every single map their favourite author produces, even though most of them are not exceptionally good for that author or for NUMA as a whole. One per day is perhaps a little stingy, but I understand that this limit is not set in stone (if you look at the home page, it states that featured maps will "initially" be restricted to one a day). Once everyone's settled in and the appropriate privileges set up, I wouldn't be surprised if it increased.


4. No more top-rated page - Sure, there's the "Hot Maps" link, but that doesn't really take the place of it well enough. Classics like "On Route 666" and "Afternoon Dragon 01 Step 04" aren't going to get enough attention now, in my opinion, since now they're almost impossible to find now.

Well, I for one haven't used the top-rated page for quite a while, because I have already seen the overwhelming majority of maps on it. The ones that haven't been there as long and don't have 8000 votes tend to flop all over the place due to sniping, so I'm not sure it was a very good indication of... well, anything, really.

Also, I believe both the maps you mention are immortalised in the Dronies Hall of Fame. There are methods other than the top-rated page for this, is what I'm saying, and I honestly think that a hall of fame works better for this sort of thing.


5. The "Hot Maps" page - I like the idea, but now it's kind of hard to tell what maps really are the newest, and people could snipe other maps to make sure their's is on the top.

Personally, exact chronological order doesn't bother me overly much, as long as one map doesn't stick at the top for ages. I grant you that sniping could be a problem, but it's already somewhat of a problem. So is the large number of poor maps submitted, which few people are interested in playing, and this does something to address that. No net loss, I feel.

6. The disappearance of the top-rated authors page - I liked that page (maybe some of you didn't), because it provided links to the most appreciated authors on NUMA, not to mention that I had hopes of reaching that place some day. Oh well.

I didn't like it in the first place, because I considered it terribly inaccurate as a reflection of map-making ability or how likely I am to enjoy an author's maps. No loss for me, but I can understand that others might feel different.

They're not anti-ratings so much as anti-ratings abuse, or perhaps anti-whinging. It's died down a bit recently, but there was a time when we were getting half a dozen OH NOES I HAVE BEEN SNIPED threads a week. People would spend hours writing huge, hysterical rants asserting that their map having a rating of three was a sign of the impending apocalypse and furthermore NUMA has destroyed their entire life, they cry themselves to sleep every night, and will seriously consider a suicide unless everyone gives their next map fives. Speaking of which, some people started putting complaints about snipers in the description of every map with a rating below 4 purely because this would result in a flood of fives to "counteract the snipe" (I've seen this happen when the only vote on the map was a 3.5 from me). Then, we had the fad of resubmitting every map which didn't get the rating you want and claiming it was sniped, which cluttered up the newest page with maps we've already seen. There was a big multiaccounting scandal a while back, too. And, of course, there have always been the idiots who snipe and multiaccount and otherwise abuse the voting system for petty revenge or to "win" the competition for top-rated maps.

In short, the "ratings don't matter" line gets trotted out so often because in the past, excessive focus on ratings - and particularly on the competitive aspects of ratings - has lead to more complaints and forum drama than anyone would wish to see.

#444126 19 2008-06-13T02:08:40Z Atilla
Whole numbers all the way. People don't rate with enough precision for .5 increments to be very meaningful.
#444166 22 2008-06-13T06:36:45Z Atilla
With the previous system, about the first 500 maps on the top-rated page were all rated 4.5. Changing the increment to .5 isn't going to prevent a lot of maps having the same rating.

More importantly, maps with a 4.5 are in most cases and for most people not noticeably more enjoyable that maps rated a 4, or even a 3.5. .5 variations can easily depend on who rated the map, what mood they were in, who the author is, and perhaps even whether the map has been sniped.

Whether you're looking at maps which are rated 4 or 4.5, you're looking at good maps. You're probably not going to enjoy all of them equally, or in exact proportion to the average rating they have. It's not worth worrying about the .5 because it doesn't mean that much.

There's also the fact that with whole numbers, maps are twice as likely to be rounded up to five (4.5 - 5 instead of 4.75 - 5) which gives a bit more range. Nothing was ever rated five for an extended period under the old system; it's more likely to occur now.

We come to Metanet because we like each other's company, or like to debate, or are bored, or, for some, like to feel powerful in influencing others (or, in a few stupid cases, just want to tick others off). (It's the same problem with the free will issue and Tsukatu's dolls; when the simpler version is eventually, inevitably forced to encompass everything, the analogy doesn't fit.)
No, you're missing the point.

I presently enjoy playing the piano. However, I have been diagnosed with a rare brain disorder which will cause my ability to slowly lose my ability to feel pleasure or pain. In six months, I will be completely incapable of enjoying anything, or even taking pleasure in any of my memories. No matter what I do, it won't possibly affect how happy I am in six months, because I will be incapable of happiness (or unhappiness).

According to you, this should prevent me from doing anything because it'll all be the same in six months. However, I believe most people would take the attitude that it's time to cash in your life savings and enjoy yourself as much as you can, while you can. Simply because you won't enjoy things one day is no reason to refrain from doing so now.

There's also the fact that many people seek immediate pleasures which they know will be harmful in the long run. If it's all about the long-term effect, rather than the immediate, why does this occur? Why do people go out and get drunk rather than studying diligently? Why do people take actions they know they'll regret later?

And, y'know, playing the piano might have a lasting effect. I might give me pleasant memories. But, again, when I remember something, I do so now. I'm not remembering everything I ever did all the time. If I like a memory, I can choose to call it up again - but that's because I want to do so in the present, not because I expect the memory to get better the more I dwell on it.

Also, let us consider animals. Animals, it is said, are without souls. I'm also fairly sure they don't really have a concept of god or religion - I've not caught the local birds holding Sunday mass*. Yet animals grown, learn, play, work, breed, form friendships and animosities, develop social hierarchies, form fears and habits and preferences and do all the things which are part of life. If we assume the world is naturalistic, why should humans be expected to stop living simply because they have neither soul nor faith? Other mammals seem to get on perfectly well without either.



We can also turn the argument around. Why do you, as a Christian, do things you enjoy in this world? After all, you expect to go to either Heaven or Hell, and experience infinite happiness or suffering. Any enjoyment in this world is nothing compared to that. It follows that nothing in this world matters at all, save that it increases your chance of going to Heaven. It doesn't matter how much you suffer in life, because what comes after death will make up for it all. So why don't you give away all your possessions? Why haven't you joined a monastic order? Why are you playing Flash games instead of devoting yourself tirelessly to prayer and the betterment of your immortal soul?


Also, why do you eat? When you die, you won't need to eat. So you should stop doing it now, because you won't be doing it when you die. Right?


*Perhaps because we don't get cardinals.

-----

Omnibenevolence and God's Responsibility for the Evils of the World:

Okay, you don't like Strife's analogy. Here's one which involves humans, which I have borrowed from Good Omens (by Neil Gaiman and Terry Pratchett).


I run a corporate training camp where co-workers who barely know each other run around playing paintball and other "team-building" activities, which are supposed to help them bond.

Now, when my clients arrive, I *tell* them they'll be playing paintball. However, I actually give them real weapons, unbeknownst to them. Stan from sales fires first and accidentally kills Briggs, from marketing. Cooper, who played cards with Briggs every Friday, kills Stan in retaliation. Pretty soon, it's all-out war.

I wash my hands of the matter. Sure, I gave them the guns. I put them in a situation which I knew would result in fatalities. But none of it is my fault, because they chose to shoot each other. Any of them could have refrained from pulling the trigger at any point (well, except for poor Stan, who didn't know any better), but they didn't, and that's no responsibility of mine. My motives were completely pure and benevolent.


By the same token, if I put a hundred people in a cage, starve them for three days, and then toss in a packet of food, it's not my fault if they hurt each other. It was totally predictable, of course, and I deliberately set the situation up when I could have avoided it. But it's not me doing the hurting, oh no, they're doing it to each other. Nothing to do with me. I accept no responsibility.


If I knock the first domino over, I'm not responsible for the next four hundred which fall. Oh, no. It's the dominoes which are knocking things over. Not my fault at all.


In other words, God set up the world in a manner which He knew would result in suffering and pain. He could have designed a world in which no suffering occurred and still achieved whatever his objectives were - after all, He is supposed to be omnipotent. Even if He is not directly causing the suffering, it didn't need to happen and would not have happened had He not created the circumstances which gave rise to suffering. Free will, you say? But God is omnipotent. Surely He could create free will without suffering if He chose? Isn't that what omnipotence means? And can someone who knowingly causes unnecessary suffering be called omnibenevolent?


Also, I note that you agree with Strife's assertion that "God intentionally created a creature to suffer for all eternity". Isn't it a bit cruel to create a creature just so it can suffer unbearable agony for its entire existence? I'm pretty sure people would object if I bred rats and continually shoved hot coals into their face from the moment they were born until the moment they died.


-----

On God's Sovereignty:

What maestro said. Having the right to do something doesn't mean it's kind or good to do so. I have the right to horde all my food while those around me starve - it is my property, after all - but most people would agree that doing so is morally repugnant.

What if you belong to a religion in which there is not an all-encompassing Plan which includes animals? Should people who believe such a religion expect all animals to lie down and die because they don't believe in an afterlife?

Also, let's try some more analogies.

Put your hand on a hotplate. You will automatically withdraw it, even if you *want* to hold your hand there. This is because it is a reflex reaction in which the conscious section of the brain is not even involved - the message to withdraw the hand is sent by the spinal cord before the pain signal even *reaches* the brain, let alone gets processed and waits for your consciousness to catch up. By a similar token, you can't just choose to stop or start liking something. I can't wake up one morning and say ""I'm going to find beans more delicious than chocolate today!" and expect my taste buds to comply.

What I'm saying is that the desire for self-preservation, not to mention a liking or disliking for certain things, are a function of who and what you are rather than what you currently think. People don't lust after one another because they think "Hmm, I must breed to ensure the continuation of my genome. This individual appears to have traits which will give our offspring the greatest chance of survival." Many human behaviours and most human desires arise whether you want them to or not, simply because that's how humans are. Thus, deciding that there is no afterlife doesn't eliminate your desire to enjoy yourself because that's not how people work.

Quote: Atilla, June 25, 2008 09:00 pm
Quote: Ryzor, June 26, 2008 07:57 am
And a fact would be that the sky is blue, or the grass is green...
No, those aren't facts, they're just theories. You may be 99% sure the grass is green, but you can't rule out the possibility that everyone is red-green colourblind and grass is only considered green by convention.
As far as I know, a "fact" in science is a phenomenon that can be verifiable by all competent observers. Because humans are the most competent observers we know of, we consider what we see to be factual, as long as it isn't contradicted by other observations we make.

So, then, if I declare that creationists are incompetent observers (because they don't have sufficient scientific knowledge) can we declare evolution is a fact? This might seem rather underhanded, but remember that to assert that humans are competent observers of which colour grass is, you'll be wanting to exclude people who are red-green colourblind.

My point is that it's rather silly to go around yelling "It's called a theory! Theory isn't 100% proven!" as if it actually means something. Nothing is 100% proven, except perhaps for tautologies and mathematics. Facts can be and regularly are debated. For example, many humans - who are allegedly competent observers - claim to have experienced alien abduction. Now, in most of these cases nobody can prove that they weren't abducted by aliens. However, I certainly don't consider it a fact that these abductions occur regularly. It's also common in court cases, where the two sides will typically claim the facts are different (even though the events which actually occurred were objective and observable).

Quote: smartalco, 2008-07-05T21:09:05Z
@incluye: that is 21% marketshare of the markets Apple targets, basically they have a 21% marketshare in everything but business, if you include business (as I was, because people like Strife get anal if you don't) Apple's marketshare is ~6%

The reason you should include a figure for the wider market is because it's too easy to redefine "the markets we target" to exaggerate your share. For example, if Apple defines their market as "pretentious Arts students who don't know how to use a computer" they probably have a 90% market share.

The other reason is that using your "target market" isn't very useful is that the target market for each company may be different. If you're discussing the use of Macs in C++ programming it might be useful to compare the market share of Microsoft and Apple in that specific market - but, again, this is comparing two companies in the same market. If 68% of graphic designers use a Mac, that might be a good reason for a graphic designer to consider buying one. However, if Apple declares graphic designers to be their targets, financial analysts shouldn't be buying Macs because Apple has a 68% share of their "target market"!

#454537 8 2008-07-23T05:07:19Z Atilla
You don't consider "So-and-so attempts to conquer the world/galaxy/universe" a cliche? It's exactly the same as the fantasy cliche, "So-and-so attempts to conquer the kingdom/world/planes", but with lightsabres instead of magic swords and psionics instead of magi. Indeed, popular sci-fi like Star Wars and other space operas are often the epitome of the "epic war" scenario.

"Machines Go Bad" is also quite the cliche, and sci-fi has the "traipsing though dungeons" thing going too - instead of the Escape from the Demon Lords of Ur, it's Escape from the Crab People of Protolon Five. The fact is that fantasy and sci-fi are quite similar genres and share many of the same tropes, to the extent that it can sometimes be difficult to decide whether a particular work is sci-fi or fantasy (some are termed "science-fantasy" these days). Isobelle Carmody's Obernewtyn series is a good example - I'd call it sci-fi, but to the casual glance it looks like fantasy.

Also, there are plenty of fantasy works which involve neither dungeons or epic wars. Neil Gaiman's Anansi Boys is a good modern example, as are several of Gaiman's other works. Many Pratchett books also avoid standard fantasy plots - Reaper Man and Going Postal are good examples. Also, don't forget that fantasy also includes fairy tales and wacky Japanese stories about a fox and a tanuki placing bets on who is better at shape-shifting.

#455684 577 2008-07-29T02:59:10Z Atilla
Quote: incluye, July 29, 2008 04:58 am
Why doesn't Michael Behe count? What's this supposed refutation to his "irreducible complexity"?

We've been over this before - I believe it starts at about page four of this thread. In short, several things which it has been claimed are "irreducibly complex" have subsequently been shown to have a completely viable path for evolution. Furthermore, humans can produce hardware and software by emulating an evolutionary process - creating some criteria for fitness, creating random designs and testing them against it, then "breeding" or randomly mutating the best performing designs and repeating the process. This can produces results which seem incomprehensible to humans and fit all the requirements for being "irreducibly complex", or even results which look exactly the same as those designed (intelligently, we hope) by human engineers - and yet, we know that they aren't irreducibly complex or human-designed because we know the process by which they were created. In essence, the refutation of the "irreducible complexity" argument is that it has been demonstrated repeatedly that humans cannot reliably determine that something is irreducibly complex, or that it "looks designed", or any other such thing.
