Quote: _makio_, July 29, 2008 01:44 pm
Quote: Qix, 2008-07-28T07:46:20Z
Finally, it addressing your numerous experiences of rapture: you have no proof whatsoever. I could say that I frequently experience connections to the FSM, pink unique, and magical space elves, but no one's converting to these groups. No matter how passionately you describe God speaking to you, how am I supposed to know if it did or didn't. I didn't hear/see/feel anything. Hallucinations don't feel imaginary to those who experience them.
essentially, you're saying that I am lying and I just imagined all of the things that i described vividly. I also imagined talking to my youth pastor afterwards and hearing his account of what I was doing and and seemed to happen to me? If you went to the shops yesterday, but i wasn't there would I just assume, that you didn't see the things you saw, or feel the things you felt? no.
There's a difference between claiming God talks to you and claiming you went to the shop. I can stand outside a shop and confirm that yes, people are walking into it. I can't attach electrodes to your soul and confirm that God is touching it, or anything similar.

As for believing your personal experiences... let's say that person A believes that Christ appeared unto her and told her that there is but one God, the Lord, who created the universe 6000 years ago, and that this God should be served and worshiped. With me so far?

Now, Person B believes that the Buddha Siddhartha Gautama came to him in a dream and told him that attempting to indulge the petty whims of gods will only lead to suffering, and that he should instead focus on the betterment of himself.

Person C believes he was abducted by aliens. They took him aboard a great silver ship, and explained to him that billions of years ago, they had created the planet and seeded it with life as an experiment, to see if sapient life could indeed evolve from microbes if given enough time.

The problem here is that all these people have completely conflicting experiences. A believes the universe is 6000 years old, and C believes it's at least several billion. B doesn't care how old the universe is, but believes serving a god will only cause suffering, while A believes serving her god is virtuous. Unless you want to claim reality is subjective, someone has to be delusional.

There are people who claim to have personally experienced the existence of Christ, the Lord, Yahweh, Allah, Ganesha, Thor, Zeus, and Amaterasu. There are people who claim to be sent from the future, people who honestly believe they remember being a dragon and get depressed because they can't fly anymore, and people who believe they have come from the stars with a mission to save humanity. There are people who believe there is but one god, people who believe there are many gods, and people who believe there are many gods who are ultimately facets of the one. There are people who believe God is the universe and the universe is God.

In short, people claim a lot of things and it's simply not possible for all of them to be right. You claim you've spoken to God? Good for you. However, there are people who claim they have spoken to different gods. There are a lot of former Christians who say they've tried and heard nothing but silence. We can't believe everyone. It's nothing personal, you understand, but we can't all be right, and we don't really have a reason to consider your personal experiences better than anyone else's. That's why such experiences aren't a good argument in favour of your position - a lot of people are wrong and there's no reason for us to believe you aren't one of them.

I think that language can be both subjective and objective, to some degree. What I mean is that most words have a precise, stable definition which is typically found in dictionaries and technical manuals, and a more vague and fluid meaning defined by common usage. #472891 25 2008-09-24T03:14:08Z Atilla
Quote: Calcy, September 16, 2008 04:29 am
I agree with spoon, it never made sense to me to press down to look up and vice versa.

It makes sense if you think of the directions as 'forward' and 'back' instead of 'up' and 'down'. You tilt your head forwards to look down, and backwards to look up. When you use inverted, you tilt the stick forward to look down, and back to look up. Or, to think of it another way, imagine that you strapped a pencil horizontally across the top of your joystick, pointing away from you. When you push the stick forward, the pencil will point downwards, and when you pull it back, upwards. This also explains why people like me use normal with a mouse and inverted with a stick - we feel like we're pointing up or down, rather than tilting forwards or back.

It's also related to the control mechanism in planes, where pulling back on the controls points the nose upwards, and pushing forward points it downwards. Back in the Good Old Days ™ flight simulators tried to emulate the controls of a real plane by using a joystick with inverted controls. As a result, people who were into flight sims before FPSs - or at least FPSs which allow free look - typically use inverted.

This article is kind of interesting, though I'm not sure I agree with the stuff about introversion and extroversion.
